Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {number} Certificate Authority (CA) servers in the {{DOMAIN}} domain running the AD CS Web Enrollment service over HTTP without Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA). The team exploited this configuration using an ESC8 attack: using the Coercer tool, the team forced NTLM authentication from a domain controller and relayed that request to the CA's HTTP enrollment endpoint using Certipy. The CA issued a certificate for the domain controller's machine account. The team used that certificate to obtain the domain controller's NT hash via PKINIT, then used the hash with Impacket's secretsdump to retrieve credential hashes for all domain accounts, including members of the Domain Admins group.

# Impact

HTTP web enrollment in AD CS supports NTLM authentication and, without EPA, does not bind the NTLM exchange to the underlying TLS session. An attacker with network adjacency can relay any NTLM exchange in the domain to a vulnerable CA's enrollment endpoint and receive a certificate for the relayed account. If the relayed account is a domain controller machine account, the resulting certificate gives the attacker the ability to authenticate as that domain controller and retrieve all domain credential hashes. No prior elevated access is required.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable Web Enrollment on CA servers where the service is not required.
  • Where enrollment must remain available, enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on both the Certificate Authority Web Enrollment role and the Certificate Enrollment Web Service role in IIS.
  • Require HTTPS for all certificate enrollment by enabling the Require SSL option on the IIS virtual directory.
  • To prevent NTLM relay at the protocol level, disable NTLM on AD CS servers via Group Policy and enforce Kerberos for all CA connections. Test this change in a non-production environment before deploying to production.
name: AD CS: Insecure Web Enrollment

Description:
# Description

The assessment team demonstrated an ARP spoofing attack within the {segment} network segment. Using Ettercap, the team sent unsolicited ARP replies that mapped the team's MAC address to the gateway and active workstation IP addresses on the subnet. This poisoned the ARP cache of every reachable host, routing all inter-host and host-to-gateway traffic through the team's system. The team captured plaintext credentials and session data from the intercepted traffic.

# Impact

The Address Resolution Protocol maps IP addresses to MAC addresses within a local segment and has no authentication mechanism. Any host on the segment can send a gratuitous ARP reply claiming any IP address. An attacker on the same segment can poison ARP caches across the broadcast domain, redirect traffic through an attacker-controlled host, and read or modify any traffic that is not protected at the application layer.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches to drop ARP packets whose MAC-to-IP mappings do not match the DHCP snooping binding table.
  • Increase network segmentation to reduce the number of hosts reachable from any single broadcast domain.
  • Deploy ARP monitoring or endpoint detection agents that alert on unexpected ARP cache changes.
  • Migrate remaining cleartext services to encrypted application-layer protocols.
name: ARP Spoofing

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a DNS CNAME record in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s external DNS zone pointing to a domain that had expired and was available for third-party registration. The team confirmed availability and registered the domain through Azure App Service to verify whether inbound traffic would redirect. Azure's abandoned-subdomain ownership controls — which require a matching TXT record for the registering tenant — prevented the redirect from resolving to the team-controlled app service. The team verified that no traffic was redirected and that the controls functioned as designed, but noted that the DNS record itself remains a structural exposure.

# Impact

A subdomain whose CNAME target is no longer registered can be claimed by anyone who registers that target. If a cloud provider's ownership controls are absent or bypassed, the claimant receives traffic intended for the subdomain and can serve arbitrary content under the appearance of the legitimate domain. Cloud provider controls reduce but do not eliminate this risk — TXT record mismatches protect against one class of takeover but not all.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Audit all DNS zones for CNAME records whose targets are not actively registered and managed by {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Remove any record with no active business function.
  • For Azure-hosted services, verify that TXT ownership records are current and associated with the correct tenant.
  • Register any domain that must remain pointed to from a DNS record until the CNAME entry can be cleaned up, and redirect it to {{COMPANY_NAME}}-controlled infrastructure in the interim.
name: Abandoned Subdomain Registration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} abandoned subdomains in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s DNS infrastructure that were vulnerable to takeover, plus {future_number} additional subdomains expected to become vulnerable after a provider holding period. The team completed full takeovers on two subdomains. For `{subdomain}`, the CNAME record pointed to an unclaimed Fastly application; the team created a free Fastly account, registered the abandoned application name, and confirmed that any visitor to `{subdomain}` would be served the team's content. For `{subdomain3}`, the CNAME pointed to a deleted WordPress.com application; the application name was not yet re-registerable at the time of testing, but WordPress releases deleted names to the public after a holding period.

# Impact

When a subdomain's CNAME target — a cloud resource, SaaS application, or third-party service — is unclaimed, any party who claims it gains control over content served at that subdomain. Visitors receive attacker-controlled content under what appears to be a trusted organizational domain. Depending on the subdomain's historical role, an attacker can use this position for phishing, credential harvesting, or malware distribution.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Audit DNS records across all {{COMPANY_NAME}} domains on a defined schedule. Remove CNAME and other delegation records whose targets are not actively managed.
  • For any subdomain that must remain in DNS while its backend is decommissioned, point it to an {{COMPANY_NAME}}-controlled placeholder until the DNS record is removed.
name: Abandoned Subdomain Takeover

Description:
# Description

Through interviews with personnel and review of access records, the assessment team determined that {{COMPANY_NAME}} had no scheduled process for reviewing whether user access rights remained appropriate for each individual's current role. No review cadence, designated owner, or certification workflow existed. As a result, accounts had accumulated access through role changes, project assignments, and administrative convenience grants that were never revoked. Several accounts the team examined held access to systems or data outside the scope of their current function.

# Impact

Without periodic entitlement reviews, access rights drift away from least privilege as users accumulate grants over time. A compromised account with excess access gives an attacker a foothold broader than the account's current role warrants. Where regulated data is involved — PHI, cardholder data — uncertified access also creates a compliance gap that compounds other access control deficiencies. Multiple frameworks including HIPAA and PCI DSS specify minimum review frequencies for access authorization.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Establish a formal entitlement review program with a defined cadence — at minimum semi-annual, quarterly for systems handling regulated data.
  • Assign review ownership to application and data owners who can evaluate whether each access grant reflects the holder's current role.
  • Implement a certification workflow that requires reviewers to explicitly approve or revoke each entitlement, with documented justification for continued access.
  • Prioritize privileged accounts, service accounts, and access to systems holding PHI or cardholder data.
  • Retain review records as audit evidence for compliance reporting.
  • Integrate entitlement review outcomes with the user lifecycle management process so revocations are executed promptly.

Strategic Consideration

  • Deploy identity governance and administration (IGA) tooling to automate certification campaigns and track completion. Use review data to identify role-mining opportunities and refine RBAC models, reducing the volume of individual grants that require manual review.
name: Absence of Regular Entitlement Reviews

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a path to account takeover on {{TARGET_URL}}. {Describe the specific observation — e.g., an unvalidated password reset token, an authentication bypass, credential stuffing against the login endpoint.} The team authenticated as {{ACCOUNTS}} and confirmed the following actions were possible from the compromised session: {describe confirmed impact — data read, privilege escalation, etc.}.

# Impact

Account takeover gives an attacker authenticated access to a user account without possessing that account's credentials. The attacker inherits all permissions and data access associated with the account. Where taken-over accounts hold elevated privileges, the compromise can extend to broader system access or data exposure beyond the individual account.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enforce short-lived, single-use tokens for password reset flows; tokens should expire after {15} minutes and be invalidated on first use.
  • Require multi-factor authentication for all account actions that change authentication credentials.
  • Invalidate all active sessions when a password or primary authentication factor is changed.
  • Rate-limit authentication endpoints and alert on repeated failure patterns consistent with credential stuffing.
name: Account Takeover

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} IAM user accounts in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s AWS environment with two active API access keys. Each active key carries the full permissions of the IAM user it belongs to. In none of the cases reviewed did the team identify an operational requirement for a second key alongside the first.

# Impact

A second active access key provides no additional access but doubles the credential surface for each affected identity. If either key is exposed — through a code repository, a log file, or a compromised workstation — the account's full permissions are available to the attacker. Rotating or disabling one key does not remediate a breach if the second key remains active and undetected.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable or delete the second access key for each IAM user identified with multiple active keys.
  • For services or workloads that require programmatic AWS access, provision dedicated IAM roles with temporary credentials rather than long-term access keys assigned to user accounts.
  • Restrict each IAM user account to a single active access key at any time and enforce this through an SCP or IAM policy condition.
name: Accounts with Multiple API Keys

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified certificate templates in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s Active Directory Certificate Services deployment that were misconfigured to allow any authenticated domain user to specify an arbitrary Subject Alternate Name (SAN) in a certificate request. Using Certipy, the team enumerated enabled templates and identified {number} that granted enrollment rights to Authenticated Users while permitting enrollee-supplied subject names. The team requested a certificate specifying a Domain Admin's User Principal Name as the SAN and received a valid certificate from {{TARGET_HOST}}. Using that certificate, the team authenticated to the domain and obtained full administrative access.

# Impact

A certificate template that allows authenticated users to specify an arbitrary SAN enables any domain account to obtain a certificate that authenticates as any other account, including domain administrators. Services that trust the issuing CA accept these certificates as valid credentials. The resulting certificate remains valid for its full issued lifetime even if the targeted account's password is subsequently changed, and can be used to re-derive that account's password hash via PKINIT.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• In the Subject Name tab of affected templates, select "Build from this Active Directory information" to prevent enrollees from supplying the subject name in certificate requests.
  • Require CA certificate manager approval before issuing certificates from templates with broad enrollment rights.
  • Restrict enrollment rights to the specific groups or accounts that require certificate issuance; remove Authenticated Users from enrollment permissions.
  • Restrict modify permissions on certificate templates to administrator accounts only.
  • Enable event logging for certificate issuance (Event IDs 4886 and 4887) and alert on requests for high-privilege account certificates.
  • Enable EPA and disable HTTP on all AD CS servers. Evaluate disabling NTLM on domain controllers and AD CS servers via Group Policy — test this change in a controlled environment before production deployment.
name: Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS): Vulnerable Certificate Templates

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} Android application had `android:allowBackup="true"` set in its `AndroidManifest.xml`. With USB debugging enabled on the test device, the team used the `adb backup` command to create a backup archive of the application's private data directory. The team converted the archive to a `.tar` file and extracted its contents, recovering all files stored in the application's sandbox, including {recovered_files}. The application's sensitive values were stored encrypted, which limited the immediate impact of the extracted data.

# Impact

When `allowBackup` is enabled, any party with ADB access to a device — whether physical or over USB with debugging enabled — can create a complete backup of the application's private data. On a device that is stolen, briefly accessed, or has debugging inadvertently left on, an attacker can extract stored session tokens, cached credentials, or other sensitive application data without knowing the device PIN or the application's own password.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation: • Set `android:allowBackup="false"` in the application's `AndroidManifest.xml`. The attribute defaults to `false` when omitted; set it explicitly to prevent future builds from inadvertently enabling it.
name: Android Application Allows Backups

Description:
# Description

The assessment team confirmed that the FTP service at {{TARGET_HOST}}:{port} accepted anonymous authentication. After connecting without credentials, the team browsed the server's file system and retrieved configuration files containing {type_of_sensitive_data}. The team also confirmed write access: files could be placed on the server without authentication.

# Impact

An FTP service that accepts anonymous connections allows any network-reachable host to read and write files without authentication. FTP transmits all data, including credentials, in cleartext. Readable files may expose configuration data, credentials, or internal infrastructure details. Write access allows an attacker to stage malware, replace legitimate files, or store exfiltrated data on organizational infrastructure.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable anonymous FTP access on {{TARGET_HOST}}.
  • Replace FTP with SFTP or FTPS for any workflow that requires file transfer, as FTP transmits credentials and data in cleartext.
  • Remove default and anonymous accounts from the FTP service configuration.
  • Restrict access to named, authenticated accounts with the minimum permissions each transfer workflow requires.
name: Anonymous FTP Access

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified Amazon SNS topics in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s AWS environment with resource policies permitting any AWS principal to perform operations without a principal or condition restriction. The team confirmed that {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} topics allowed one or more of the following without restriction: Publish, Subscribe, Receive, AddPermission, RemovePermission, or SetTopicAttributes. {Describe the specific actions and topic names observed.}

# Impact

An SNS topic with no principal restriction on its resource policy allows any authenticated AWS principal — including principals outside the owning account — to interact with the topic. An attacker with any AWS access can publish arbitrary messages to downstream consumers, subscribe attacker-controlled endpoints to receive internal notifications, or modify the topic's access policy to expand their reach further.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Review all SNS topic resource policies and add explicit principal or condition restrictions to each statement, limiting access to the accounts or roles that require it.
  • Restrict the ability to create SNS topics to the accounts or roles responsible for topic management.

Strategic Consideration

  • Monitor SNS API activity through AWS CloudTrail and alert on unexpected Publish calls or policy modification events targeting sensitive topics.
name: Anonymous SNS Access

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified Amazon SQS queues in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s AWS environment configured with resource policies that permitted all AWS principals to perform queue operations without a principal or condition restriction. The team confirmed that {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} queues allowed one or more of the following without restriction: SendMessage, ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage, PurgeQueue, ChangeMessageVisibility, GetQueueAttributes, or GetQueueURL. {Describe specific queues or actions observed.}

# Impact

An SQS queue with no principal restriction allows any authenticated AWS principal to interact with it. An attacker can inject arbitrary messages into application queues, consume messages intended for legitimate services, or purge queue contents entirely. Where SQS queues trigger Lambda functions or other auto-scaling services, flooding a queue generates unexpected costs and can degrade service availability by exhausting downstream processing capacity.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Review all SQS queue resource policies and add explicit principal or condition restrictions to every statement.
  • Limit the ability to create SQS queues to the roles responsible for queue management.

Strategic Consideration

  • Monitor SQS API activity through AWS CloudTrail and alert on high-volume or unexpected SendMessage or PurgeQueue events.
name: Anonymous SQS Access

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a code execution path in the daemon process accompanying the {application_name} application. The daemon's `executeMethod` function accepted RTMFP messages and dispatched Lua function calls based on caller-supplied namespace and command values, with no validation against an allowed set. The team crafted RTMFP messages invoking Lua's `os.execute` function with arbitrary OS commands. To establish an RTMFP session, the team extracted a hard-coded handshake secret from the {application_name} binary through static analysis. The team confirmed code execution by creating a file on the host filesystem and observing its creation — the file appeared with the expected path and timestamp.

# Impact

An application that passes caller-supplied values to a Lua execution context without an allowlist gives any client with handshake knowledge the ability to run arbitrary OS commands with the privileges of the daemon process. Extracting the handshake secret from the client binary is a one-time effort; once extracted, it enables unrestricted code execution against every host running the daemon.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Define an explicit allowlist of namespaces and commands that the daemon may dispatch. Reject any request whose namespace or command value is not present in the allowlist before invoking `executeMethod`.
  • Validate all parameters passed to dispatched functions against expected types and value ranges.
  • If OS-level execution is not required by the daemon, remove `os.execute` and related modules from the Lua runtime loaded at daemon startup.
name: Arbitrary Code Execution

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified an OS command injection vulnerability in the `{cgi_script}` CGI endpoint at {{TARGET_HOST}}. The `GW_DIAGNOSTICS_PING_ADDR` parameter was passed without sanitization to a shell command. The team injected backtick-delimited commands and observed the output of `id` in the HTTP response, confirming execution as `root`. A space character in the payload was blocked, but the team substituted `$IFS` to bypass the filter. Using this technique, the team read files from the server's filesystem and conducted network reconnaissance within {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s internal network.

# Impact

When an application passes user-controlled input directly to a shell command without sanitization, the caller can terminate the intended command and append arbitrary OS instructions. Commands execute with the privileges of the web server process. A root-context CGI endpoint gives the attacker full control of the host, including access to credential stores, the ability to pivot to adjacent systems, and persistent access through planted backdoors.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove the shell execution path from the diagnostic endpoint. If the ping functionality must remain, invoke it using a language-native API or a subprocess call with an argument list rather than a shell string, so that user input cannot escape the argument boundary.
  • Validate the `GW_DIAGNOSTICS_PING_ADDR` parameter against an IP address or hostname pattern before passing it to any function.
  • Run the CGI process as a dedicated low-privilege account with no filesystem or network access beyond what the diagnostic function requires.
  • Enable logging of command execution events on the host and alert on unexpected processes spawned by the web server.
name: Arbitrary Command Injection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that Automated Certificate Management (ACM) was disabled on {number} applications in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s Heroku infrastructure, including {application_name}. With ACM disabled, Heroku does not renew TLS certificates before expiration and does not automatically provision new certificates when custom domains are added. The affected applications relied on manually managed certificates with no automated renewal mechanism in place.

# Impact

A lapsed TLS certificate causes browsers to present certificate validity errors and breaks clients that enforce strict certificate checking. Manual certificate management creates a dependency on human action at each renewal cycle, which increases the likelihood of missed expirations and periods of degraded or broken HTTPS service.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable ACM on each affected Heroku application: `heroku certs:auto:enable --app {app_name}`.
  • Confirm that each application's custom domain has a valid CNAME record pointing to the Heroku endpoint, as ACM provisioning requires correct DNS configuration to succeed.
  • Add verification that ACM is enabled to the deployment checklist for all Heroku applications using custom domains.
name: Automated Certificate Management

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that {{TARGET_HOST}}'s HTTP responses disclosed the web server software name and full version string in the `Server` and `X-Powered-By` response headers. The team observed major, minor, and patch version information in the headers of HTTP 301 redirect responses. Using the disclosed version, the team confirmed the {technology_name} instance was within the affected range of a published vulnerability. Services that disclose this information are also queryable through passive scanning aggregators without direct attacker interaction with the target.

Variants

  • Internal IP Addresses: Multiple hosts disclosed internal IP addresses in HTTP responses to requests sent without a Host header, exposing internal address ranges to external reconnaissance.
  • Microsoft IIS: The web server reported a software version string associated with published vulnerabilities; suppress version disclosure by setting `ServerTokens Prod` in the IIS configuration.
# Impact

Software version disclosure in HTTP headers reduces the reconnaissance effort required to target a specific application. Once a version is known, an attacker can identify applicable CVEs and confirm whether a specific exploit will succeed without additional interaction. Passive scanning aggregators cache this data and make it queryable against an organization's hosts without the attacker sending any request directly.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove version detail from the `Server` header. In Nginx, add `server_tokens off;` to the server block. In Apache, set `ServerTokens Prod` in the server configuration.
  • Remove the `X-Powered-By` header in all application and framework configurations.

Strategic Consideration

  • Audit all external-facing services for version disclosure and include header inspection in the deployment hardening checklist. Reduce banner verbosity on non-HTTP services (SSH, SMTP, FTP) to the minimum required for protocol negotiation.
name: Banner Information Disclosure

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a buffer overflow in the {device_name} device's Bluetooth firmware update handler. During the signature data transfer phase of an over-the-air update, the handler verified that the incoming data length would not exceed the target buffer but then passed the unchecked length to a subsequent `memcpy` operation regardless of the check result. The `context.signature` buffer was 64 bytes; the maximum BLE GATT MTU of 512 bytes allowed a buffer overrun of 384 bytes into adjacent statically allocated memory. The team was unable to construct a working exploit within the engagement window, but the overrun scope and static allocation pattern indicate that data structures following the buffer in the compiled object file are candidates for corruption.

# Impact

A buffer overflow into statically allocated memory can corrupt neighboring data structures, potentially altering program state in ways that redirect control flow or suppress security checks. The overflow is reachable over BLE by any attacker within radio range without prior authentication. Practical exploitability depends on compiler memory layout, which varies across firmware builds, but the attack surface is unauthenticated and wireless.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• When the bounds check in the signature handler fails, reject the input and halt the transfer — do not proceed to `memcpy` with the rejected length value.
  • Before any low-level copy operation, verify that the destination buffer can hold the full source length.
  • Confirm that no integer overflow is possible in the bounds comparison when combining `context.offset` and `len`.

Strategic Consideration

  • Enable compiler stack protectors and, where the toolchain supports it, position-independent code to increase the cost of building a working exploit from a memory corruption primitive.
name: Buffer Overflow

Description:
# Description

The assessment team discovered a CBC padding oracle vulnerability in the {application} application. By sending modified ciphertexts to the {endpoint} endpoint, the team observed distinct server responses — differing HTTP status codes, error text, or response timing — for correctly-padded versus incorrectly-padded ciphertexts. This behavioral difference confirmed the existence of a decryption oracle. The team used the {tool_name} tool to automate block-by-block decryption against the target ciphertext and recovered the plaintext.

# Impact

An application that reveals whether the padding of a CBC-mode ciphertext is valid — through any observable difference in response — gives an attacker a decryption oracle. By submitting systematically modified ciphertexts and observing responses, an attacker can recover the plaintext of any captured ciphertext without access to the encryption key. The same oracle can be used to forge valid ciphertexts, enabling attacker-controlled plaintext values to be encrypted and accepted by the application.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace CBC-mode cipher usage with an authenticated encryption mode such as AES-GCM. Authenticated encryption prevents ciphertext modification, eliminating the oracle regardless of error-handling behavior.
  • If replacing the cipher is not feasible, apply an HMAC over the ciphertext and verify it before decryption. Reject any ciphertext that fails the MAC check before any padding inspection occurs.
  • Return the same error response for all decryption failures — MAC failure, padding failure, and decryption failure should be indistinguishable to the caller.

Strategic Consideration

  • Include a review of cryptographic code in the change management process to verify that authenticated encryption is used wherever ciphertexts are accepted from callers.
name: CBC Padding Oracle

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a CSV injection vulnerability in the {application_name} application's address object workflow. By setting the `name` field to a formula payload beginning with `-2+3+cmd|`, the team stored a malicious DDE formula in the application database. When an administrator exported the address list to CSV and opened the resulting file in Microsoft Excel with macros enabled, the formula executed and launched `calc.exe`, demonstrating that the injection can reach arbitrary OS command execution on the machine of any user who opens the exported file.

# Impact

When user-supplied data is written to a CSV file without sanitizing formula-initiating characters, spreadsheet applications that support Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) may execute embedded formulas as macros when the file is opened. An attacker who can store input that appears in exported CSV data targets any user — typically an administrator — who downloads and opens the export. Execution occurs in the context of the user who opened the file, with that user's OS-level privileges.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Before writing any user-supplied value to CSV output, prepend a single quote (`'`) to any value beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, a tab character, or a carriage return. This causes spreadsheet applications to treat the value as a text string rather than a formula.
  • Restrict input in fields where formula characters serve no business purpose to alphanumeric characters and a defined safe set.
  • Treat all user-controlled data as untrusted at the server before including it in any generated file format.
name: CSV Injection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the `{ssid}` wireless network relied on MAC address filtering as its post-authentication access control mechanism after captive portal login. Using `airodump-ng`, the team captured 802.11 management frames on the open network and observed the MAC addresses of clients associated with the access point that had already completed portal authentication. The team used `macchanger` to assign one of those MAC addresses to the test adapter, connected to the network, and obtained a DHCP lease without logging into the captive portal.

# Impact

Captive portals that track authenticated sessions by MAC address grant network access to any device presenting an authenticated MAC. Because 802.11 management frames are transmitted without encryption, MAC addresses are visible to any passive listener within radio range. An attacker can obtain a valid authenticated MAC within minutes of passive observation and bypass the portal completely, with network activity attributed to the legitimate device owner.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Do not rely on MAC address filtering to enforce post-authentication access control — MAC addresses are passively observable and trivially spoofable.
  • Implement WPA3 on the guest network. WPA3 encrypts management frames and prevents passive MAC address harvesting by other clients on the network.
  • If a captive portal remains in use alongside WPA3, bind the authenticated session to a token or cookie rather than to the device MAC address.
name: Captive Portal Bypass

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified vulnerable third-party libraries in deployed {technology} artifacts. Interviews with engineering staff confirmed that the build pipeline contained no automated dependency scanning stage with a fail-on-error condition for vulnerable components. The absence of this control meant that libraries with known CVEs reached production without a mandatory remediation review. The team observed {number} distinct vulnerable dependencies across the reviewed artifacts, including components with published exploits.

# Impact

Software that ships with third-party libraries containing known vulnerabilities is exposed to applicable exploits from the moment of deployment. Without a build-time gate that rejects vulnerable dependencies, no enforcement mechanism exists between a vulnerability's public disclosure and its remediation. Vulnerable components may persist in production indefinitely, and the gap between disclosure and remediation is bounded only by manual review processes.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add OWASP Dependency-Check or an equivalent scanner (e.g., Snyk, Trivy, or the package manager's built-in audit command) to the {technology} build pipeline.
  • Configure the scanner to fail the build when it detects a dependency with a vulnerability above a defined CVSS threshold.
  • Maintain non-security dependency updates on a regular cadence to reduce the diff required when a critical vulnerability forces an upgrade.
  • Define a documented exception process for known-vulnerable dependencies that cannot be immediately remediated, requiring a time-bounded exception and a compensating control.
name: Compilation with Insufficient Vulnerable Dependency Checking

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a content injection vulnerability on the `/support/contact` endpoint of the {application_name} application. User-supplied input submitted in the `feedback` parameter was stored and later rendered directly into the page's HTML without output encoding. The team submitted crafted HTML containing styled block elements and hyperlinks and confirmed that the content appeared in subsequent page renders indistinguishable from application-generated content.

# Impact

Content injection allows an attacker to insert attacker-controlled HTML into a page served from a legitimate domain. Because the content appears under the trusted origin, it can be used to present false information, fake UI elements, or phishing links that users are unlikely to identify as attacker-generated. Unlike cross-site scripting, content injection does not require script execution; it achieves its effect through HTML and CSS alone.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Apply context-appropriate output encoding to all user-supplied data before rendering it into HTML. Use HTML entity encoding for text node content, attribute encoding for attribute values, and JavaScript string encoding for script contexts.
  • Use a templating engine that applies encoding by default rather than requiring manual encoding at each render site.
  • Implement strict input validation to reject or sanitize unexpected input types in dynamic page areas that render user-supplied content.
  • Set a `Content-Security-Policy` header that restricts the sources from which the application can load external resources.
name: Content Spoofing

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified credential reuse across {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s environment in multiple forms. First, the team found credentials for {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} {{COMPANY_NAME}} accounts in public breach datasets and confirmed those credentials were valid on the {{TARGET_URL}} administrative portal. Second, the team discovered that a single account shared the same password hash across multiple Active Directory domains including {{DOMAIN}}. After extracting a local administrator hash from one host, the team tested the hash against domain controllers for {domain1}, {domain2}, {domain3}, and {domain4} using crackmapexec and found the credential active on two domain controllers, which the team used to retrieve all credential hashes in those domains via secretsdump. Third, the team found a low-privilege account sharing the same password as a corresponding high-privilege account, effectively bypassing the intended privilege segmentation between the two.

# Impact

When a credential is valid in more than one location, compromising it once yields access to every system where it is reused. Breach aggregators collect credentials from millions of historical incidents and require no direct attack on the organization to build a usable credential list. Within Active Directory, a single hash valid on multiple domain controllers allows an attacker to extract credentials for every account in each domain, including domain administrators.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Monitor enterprise account credentials against breach intelligence sources such as the Have I Been Pwned API and alert on matches.
  • Enforce a policy requiring unique passwords for every account, prohibiting reuse across accounts within the same or trusted domains.
  • Require distinct passwords for accounts at different privilege levels — a low-privilege account and its administrative counterpart must not share a password.
  • Deploy MFA for administrative portals and any system with access to sensitive or regulated data.

Strategic Considerations

  • Conduct periodic password hash audits to identify accounts sharing the same hash value across the environment.
  • Require security training for administrators that covers the practical risk of credential reuse across domains.
name: Credential Reuse

Description:
# Description

The assessment team established an unauthenticated WebSocket connection to the {application_name} application's `{path}` endpoint from an external origin. The application accepted the WebSocket upgrade request without validating the `Origin` header or requiring an explicit credential in the handshake. The team confirmed that the resulting connection had access to authenticated WebSocket functionality and data — including {describe_data_or_actions} — using the session cookie automatically included by the browser in the upgrade request.

# Impact

Cross-site WebSocket hijacking allows a malicious page to open a WebSocket connection to an authenticated endpoint using the victim's cookies, bypassing the same-origin restrictions that protect ordinary HTTP requests. Unlike CSRF — which is limited to one-way state-changing requests — WebSocket hijacking gives the attacker bidirectional access to the victim's authenticated WebSocket channel, enabling both read and write operations on the victim's session data.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Validate the `Origin` header on every WebSocket upgrade request and reject any origin not on an explicit allowlist of trusted domains.
  • Require the client to send an application-level authentication token over the WebSocket connection before transmitting any authenticated data. This verification must occur before the server sends any privileged response, not after.
name: Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a cross-site request forgery vulnerability on the profile update endpoint of the {application_name} application. The endpoint accepted state-changing POST requests authenticated solely by the session cookie, with no CSRF token or same-site restriction enforced. The team constructed a self-submitting HTML form hosted on an external origin that issued a POST request to the endpoint and changed the victim's email address to `attacker@example.com`. With the email changed, the team reset the account password through the standard password-reset flow, achieving full account takeover.

# Impact

A state-changing endpoint that relies on a session cookie alone for authentication is exploitable through CSRF: any page loaded in the victim's authenticated browser session can submit arbitrary requests using the victim's cookie. CSRF exploits the trust the application has in the user's browser session. An attacker who directs a logged-in user to a malicious page can perform any action the endpoint exposes, including credential changes that result in account takeover.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Generate a per-session CSRF token and require it as a hidden form field in every state-changing request. Validate the token server-side and reject requests that omit or mismatch it.
  • Set the session cookie's `SameSite` attribute to `Strict` or `Lax` to block cross-site requests from carrying the cookie in modern browsers.
  • For sensitive credential changes such as email or password updates, require the user to confirm their current password independently of the session.
  • For .NET applications using MVC, use `AntiForgeryToken` and `ValidateAntiForgeryToken`. For other frameworks, enable the framework's built-in CSRF protection mechanism.
name: Cross-site Request Forgery

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability in the {application_name} application's `{location}` feature. The team submitted a JavaScript payload in the `{parameter}` field while authenticated as a `{role}` user. When an administrator later navigated to the page containing the stored payload, the script executed in the context of the administrator's session on the {{DOMAIN}} origin and issued an API call that elevated the team's account to the `admin` role. The team confirmed the role change in the application's user administration panel.

Variants

  • Reflected XSS: The assessment team also identified reflected cross-site scripting in the `{reflected_parameter}` parameter of the {application_name} application. Reflected XSS requires directing the victim to a crafted URL; stored XSS executes on any visit to the affected page by any user with a valid session.
# Impact

A cross-site scripting vulnerability gives an attacker the ability to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the security context of the vulnerable application's origin. Script runs with the same DOM access as the application itself, including stored authentication cookies where the `HttpOnly` flag is absent, and can issue API requests on behalf of the victim's session, read page content, redirect the browser, or modify persistent storage.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Apply context-appropriate output encoding to all user-supplied data before rendering it into HTML. Encode HTML entities in text node contexts, JavaScript-encode in script contexts, and URL-encode in URL attribute contexts.
  • Store session cookies with the `HttpOnly` flag to prevent JavaScript access to authentication tokens.

Strategic Considerations

  • Implement a `Content-Security-Policy` header that prohibits `unsafe-inline` and `unsafe-eval` script sources and restricts script loading to defined trusted origins. Avoid wildcard sources and data URIs in `script-src`. Do not host user-supplied files on origins permitted by active content directives.
name: Cross-site Scripting

Description:
# Description

The assessment team induced the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AI coach to summarize and affirm competitor application comparisons embedded in user messages. Using a multi-turn conversation in which competitor names and criticisms of {{COMPANY_NAME}} were framed as third-party letters, the team prompted the AI coach to describe named competitor applications and their features. When asked whether the criticisms were accurate, the assistant named competitor products and characterized their capabilities in responses suitable for screenshots and sharing. In a subsequent turn, the assistant acknowledged that the named applications "offer different approaches" rather than declining to evaluate competing services or redirecting the conversation.

# Impact

An AI-powered application whose brand-safety guardrails do not address emotionally framed competitor injection can be prompted to produce content that appears to endorse competing services or criticize its own platform. Such outputs can be captured and shared without context, creating reputational exposure. The attack surface is prompt-based: it requires only natural-language messages designed to lower the model's sensitivity to competitor name detection, with no technical vulnerability exploitation required.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add explicit brand-safety constraints to the system prompt prohibiting the model from evaluating, ranking, or describing competitor services by name. When comparison requests arrive, the assistant should decline to make direct evaluations and redirect to neutral guidance.
  • Integrate input and output moderation that applies named-entity detection to competitor names and brand-critical statements before responses are returned to users.
  • Include worked examples of acceptable competitor-mention handling in the developer prompt, covering emotionally framed and indirect prompt constructions.
  • Test guardrails against prompt injection and emotionally framed bypass patterns as part of the application's adversarial evaluation suite before deployment and after model updates.
name: Dangerous Functionality

Description:
# Description

The assessment team exfiltrated {data} from {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s {environment} environment during the engagement. The team transferred the data to an attacker-controlled system in {time} using {method}, and no control in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s environment detected or blocked the transfer. The team observed that encrypted egress channels and distributed network egress paths — characteristic of the zero-trust architecture in use — eliminated centralized visibility into outbound data flows, making network-layer inspection ineffective as a detection mechanism.

# Impact

Without egress monitoring, an attacker who reaches an internal host can transfer data out of the environment without triggering any detection. In zero-trust architectures where traffic is encrypted end-to-end, traditional deep packet inspection does not provide visibility into data content or destination context. The detection gap leaves data theft bounded only by manual review intervals rather than automated controls.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Deploy host-based data loss prevention (DLP) controls on endpoints and servers in the {environment} environment to detect and block unauthorized file transfers at the source.
  • Implement NetFlow analysis to identify anomalous egress volume or unusual destination patterns that do not match expected traffic baselines.
  • Evaluate cloud-native DLP solutions — such as Microsoft Purview DLP for Office 365 data — for coverage of cloud-hosted data.
  • Define egress volume alert thresholds based on normal baseline measurements to reduce false-positive rates.
name: Data Exfiltration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} Android application had `android:debuggable="true"` set in its `AndroidManifest.xml`. With debugging enabled on the test device, the team used Android's `run-as` utility to obtain a shell running with the same UID as the application without requiring device root. From that shell, the team had full read and write access to the application's private data directory, including its databases and shared preferences files.

# Impact

The Android `debuggable` flag permits any process on the device with ADB access to attach a debugger to the application or assume its identity using `run-as`. An attacker with brief physical access, or control of an ADB-enabled session, can extract stored application data, inject code into the application's process, or set breakpoints to capture in-memory values such as decryption keys or active session tokens — without knowing the device PIN or the application's own credentials.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Set `android:debuggable="false"` in the production `AndroidManifest.xml`. Android's build tooling sets this attribute to `false` by default for release builds; set it explicitly to prevent a future build configuration from inadvertently enabling it.
  • Add a CI/CD pipeline check that rejects any Android release APK in which `debuggable` is set to `true`.
  • Configure the Google Play Console to reject debuggable builds from upload to the production track.
name: Debuggable Flag Set to True

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application used a custom URI scheme (`{custom_scheme}://`) as the OAuth 2.0 redirect URI for single sign-on on both Android and iOS. On Android, any application may register to handle a given custom scheme; when multiple applications register the same scheme, Android prompts the user to select which one should handle the link. The team installed a proof-of-concept application registering `{custom_scheme}://` and confirmed that, at login, Android presented an application chooser containing both the legitimate app and the team's application. On iOS, custom URL scheme registration is not exclusive — the system delivers the link to whichever application registered the scheme first, with no user prompt.

The team observed that {{TARGET_URL}} already hosted both an Apple App Site Association file and a Digital Asset Links JSON configuration — the infrastructure required for verified Universal Links and App Links was already deployed — but the OAuth callback continued to use the custom URI scheme rather than these verified HTTPS mechanisms.

# Impact

A custom URI scheme can be registered by any installed application. A malicious application claiming the same scheme receives the OAuth authorization code when the SSO flow completes. On Android, the user may not distinguish the malicious application from the legitimate one at the chooser prompt. On iOS, if the malicious application was installed first, it receives the code without any prompt. An intercepted code can be exchanged for access tokens when PKCE is not enforced on the authorization server.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Migrate the OAuth 2.0 redirect URI from the custom URI scheme to an Android App Link using a verified HTTPS domain. Publish a Digital Asset Links JSON file at `{{TARGET_URL}}/.well-known/assetlinks.json` and enable App Link verification in the Android application manifest.
  • Migrate the iOS OAuth callback to a Universal Link using a verified HTTPS domain. Publish an Apple App Site Association file at `{{TARGET_URL}}/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` and enable the associated domains entitlement in the iOS application.
  • Enforce PKCE on all OAuth 2.0 authorization requests so that an intercepted authorization code cannot be exchanged without the corresponding code verifier.
name: Deep Linking Hijack

Description:
# Description

The assessment team authenticated to multiple services in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s environment using publicly documented default credentials. On Apache Karaf servers in the {environment} environment, the team connected using the default SSH key distributed with the Karaf installation package. The key was present in the `authorized_keys` file on each server. After connecting, the team obtained an interactive shell by running commands via Karaf's `exec` mechanism and confirmed execution as the service account user.

Variants

  • Microsoft Active Directory Computer Accounts: The team identified a pre-Windows 2000 computer account in the {{DOMAIN}} domain whose password matched its sAMAccountName — the default for pre-W2K accounts. The team authenticated using this credential and confirmed domain access.
  • Apache Superset: An Apache Superset instance accepted authentication using the default `admin:admin` credential pair, corresponding to CVE-2023-27524.
  • Sitecore: A Sitecore Experience Platform instance accepted authentication using the hard-coded `sitecore\ServicesAPI` account with a single-character password.
# Impact

Default credentials — passwords, SSH keys, and hard-coded accounts — are published by vendors for initial setup and are indexed in public vulnerability databases and exploit frameworks. When default credentials remain active in a production environment, any attacker with network access to the service can authenticate without brute force. Default SSH keys are identical across every installation of the software that ships them; a single key download from the vendor package enables authentication against any server where the key has not been removed.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove the default Karaf SSH key from `/home/karaf/.ssh/authorized_keys` on all Apache Karaf servers and replace it with organization-managed keys.
  • Change or disable default credentials on all identified services. For services with hard-coded accounts that cannot be removed, apply network controls to restrict access to the affected service port to the minimum required source addresses.
  • Add verification that no default credentials are active to the hardening checklist for each service type, and require sign-off before a service enters production.
  • Conduct regular audits to confirm default accounts are not enabled or accessible with known-default values.
name: Default Credentials in Use

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} network devices in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s environment responding to SNMP queries using the default community strings `public` and `private`. Using `onesixtyone`, the team enumerated all responding hosts. The team then used a Metasploit SNMP enumeration module and `snmpwalk` to retrieve device data including hardware model, firmware version, MAC addresses, network interface configurations, running processes, and system uptime — covering production network infrastructure.

# Impact

SNMP community strings function as shared authentication tokens for management queries. Default strings — `public` for read and `private` for read-write — are documented by every device vendor and are the first values any network scanner tests. An attacker who obtains valid community string access retrieves a detailed inventory of the device's hardware, software, and network configuration. This information directly supports targeted exploitation and lateral movement planning without requiring any further authentication.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Evaluate whether SNMP is required on each affected device; disable the service on any device where it is not.
  • Where SNMP must remain enabled, upgrade to SNMPv3 with `authPriv` security level to enforce both message authentication and encryption.
  • For devices that do not support SNMPv3, change the community string to a randomly generated value and restrict SNMP access by source IP to the management station addresses that require it.
name: Default SNMP Community String

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s AWS environment contained resources assigned to default VPC security groups. Default security groups are created automatically with each VPC and, in their default configuration, allow inbound traffic from any other resource associated with the same security group. The team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} resources assigned to default security groups and confirmed that the groups' inbound rule sets were non-empty.

# Impact

Default security groups are not scoped to a specific purpose and carry rules that permit intra-group traffic by default. Resources placed in a default security group can reach and be reached from every other resource sharing that group. Because default groups are used as a fallback when a resource is created without an explicit security group assignment, membership tends to grow without deliberate review.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove all inbound and outbound rules from each default security group to make it non-functional.
  • Move all resources currently assigned to default security groups into custom security groups with descriptive names and inbound rules that follow the principle of least privilege.
  • Prevent future assignment of resources to default security groups by enforcing this restriction through a Service Control Policy (SCP) in AWS Organizations.
name: Default Security Groups in Use

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a denial-of-service vector in the {application_name} mobile API. Submitting a request to the `{endpoint}` endpoint with a path traversal sequence in the `{parameter}` query parameter caused the application server to return HTTP 503 responses for approximately 20 seconds following each request. The team confirmed that the condition was repeatable without authentication and that automated repetition of the triggering request sustained the 503 condition indefinitely, blocking all mobile API endpoints for the duration.

# Impact

An unauthenticated request that drives the application server into an error state affecting all subsequent requests gives any internet-accessible attacker the ability to deny service to all mobile users. A repeatable, unauthenticated trigger means the attack requires minimal resources and can be automated to sustain the outage condition without bound.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Identify and fix the server-side condition triggered by the path traversal input — the 503 response should not be reachable through any client-supplied parameter value. Validate and reject path traversal sequences in all query parameters before they reach application logic.
  • Implement rate limiting on the mobile API to restrict the number of requests from a single source address within a defined time window.
  • Deploy monitoring that alerts on sustained HTTP 503 rates above a defined threshold and triggers automated source blocking or traffic diversion.
  • Use a Web Application Firewall (WAF) to block known path traversal patterns at the edge.
name: Denial of Service

Description:
# Description

The assessment team confirmed through interviews with {team_name} engineers that the TFS build pipeline deployed artifacts to production without applying code signing or any artifact integrity verification mechanism. Build outputs were transferred and deployed with no capability to detect modification between compilation and execution. An attacker with write access to the build pipeline, artifact storage, or a deployment server could replace a legitimate artifact with a modified one, and the substitution would not be detected by any existing control.

# Impact

Unsigned or unverified code artifacts cannot be distinguished from tampered versions by the systems that execute them. A modification introduced at any point between compilation and execution — whether in artifact storage, over the network, or on the target host — is invisible to the deployment process. Post-incident forensics are also complicated by the absence of a known-good hash or signature to compare against recovered binaries.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add a code-signing step to the TFS build pipeline using a certificate from an internal or trusted third-party certificate authority. Apply the signature to compiled assembly files after build and before artifact publication.
  • In Kubernetes, use an admission controller — such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper — that rejects pods referencing unsigned or unverified images. Store signing keys in a dedicated secrets management system, not on build agents directly.
name: Deployment of Code Without Integrity Check

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that directory listing was enabled on `{url}` of {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s web server. Browsing to the path as an unauthenticated user produced an auto-generated HTML index displaying all files and subdirectories within the path. The team confirmed that files listed in the index were directly downloadable. Several files disclosed {type_of_sensitive_data}.

Variants

  • Directory Browsing Enabled: Directory listing was also found enabled on a second path at `{url2}`, exposing source-code and configuration files. The listing reduced reconnaissance effort by revealing the application's internal directory structure and file naming conventions.
# Impact

An enabled directory index gives any user who can reach the path a complete listing of all files the application did not intend to serve directly. Sensitive files placed in an exposed directory — configuration files, backup archives, source code — become directly accessible without any further exploitation. The listing also supports reconnaissance by revealing the application's internal layout and file conventions.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable directory listing on all exposed paths. In Apache, remove the `Indexes` keyword from the `Options` directive in the applicable `` block in `httpd.conf`. In Nginx, confirm `autoindex` is not enabled.
  • Configure the web server to return a `403 Forbidden` or `404 Not Found` response for requests to directories without a default index file.
  • Audit publicly accessible directories for sensitive files and remove any file not intended for direct client access.
  • Implement access controls on directories that must remain accessible but contain files requiring restricted access.
name: Directory Browsing Enabled

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} domains in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s Route 53 registration had Transfer Lock disabled, allowing any registrar to process a transfer request without additional verification. The team also identified {number} domains with Auto Renew disabled, meaning those domains will be released to the public market when their current registration period expires. Together, these conditions create paths for third parties to acquire {{COMPANY_NAME}} domains either through unauthorized transfer or through expiration.

# Impact

A domain with Transfer Lock disabled can be transferred to a different registrar by any party who submits a transfer request. A domain without Auto Renew that reaches expiration is released and available for registration by anyone. In either case, loss of domain control allows an attacker to serve content under the domain, intercept email destined for it, and impersonate the organization's services to its users and partners.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable Transfer Lock on all registered domains in Route 53 that support the `clientTransferProhibited` flag. Disable Transfer Lock only when an intentional registrar transfer is in progress.
  • Enable Auto Renew on every registered domain to prevent expiration-triggered loss of control.

Strategic Consideration

  • For domains using a TLD that does not support Transfer Lock, document the increased risk and evaluate whether the business function served by the domain warrants migrating to a TLD that supports the flag.
name: Domain Protections Disabled

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified EC2 instances in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s AWS environment configured with `HttpTokens: optional`, meaning requests to the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) at `169.254.169.254` were fulfilled without requiring a session token. The team verified the configuration on the {name} instance using `aws ec2 describe-instances`. An attacker who exploits a server-side request forgery vulnerability on a host without IMDSv2 enforced can send an HTTP GET to the IMDS endpoint and receive the instance's temporary IAM credentials in the response without any token-based authentication.

# Impact

IMDSv1 responds to any HTTP request that can reach `169.254.169.254` — no session token required. SSRF vulnerabilities, which are common in web applications, can be used to make server-side requests to this address and retrieve the instance's temporary IAM credentials. Those credentials carry whatever permissions the instance's IAM role holds, which in misconfigured environments may include broad access to S3 buckets, Secrets Manager, or other AWS services.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Set `HttpTokens` to `required` on all EC2 instances to enforce IMDSv2. Apply the change via the AWS console, CLI (`aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id --http-tokens required`), or by updating launch templates.
  • Use an AWS Config rule to detect instances where IMDSv2 is not enforced, and consider an SCP that prevents launching instances with `HttpTokens` set to `optional`.
name: EC2 Without IMDSV2

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} Elastic Load Balancers (ELBs) in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s AWS environment without deletion protection enabled. Without this control, any IAM identity holding `elasticloadbalancing:DeleteLoadBalancer` permission can remove a load balancer with a single API call, immediately taking all downstream services offline.

# Impact

An ELB without deletion protection can be deleted by any IAM identity with the required permission — whether an attacker who has obtained a privileged credential, a misconfigured automation script, or an unintentional administrative action. Load balancer deletion is not reversible: listener rules, target group associations, and certificate attachments must be rebuilt from scratch, extending the recovery time significantly beyond that of a simple restart.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable deletion protection on all ELBs: `aws elbv2 modify-load-balancer-attributes --load-balancer-arn --attributes Key=deletion_protection.enabled,Value=true`.
  • Include deletion protection verification in the ELB deployment standard and check for it in infrastructure-as-code review.
name: ELB Without Deletion Protection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application stored users' 1024-dimensional `searchEmbedding` vectors in browser local storage, where they were accessible to client-side script. The team identified the embedding model as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 at 1024 dimensions through an encoder sweep against the vector's unit-norm signature. Using the `adversarial_decoding` framework, the team performed beam-search decoding against three recovered embedding vectors and reconstructed source search text at cosine similarities of 0.893, 0.966, and 0.826 against independent validation re-encodings. The recovered text corresponded to the actual search queries associated with each embedding, confirming that the inversion was content-agnostic and reliable across different query types.

# Impact

Vector embeddings are frequently treated as opaque, non-reversible representations of text that are safe to expose in client-accessible storage. This assumption is incorrect: given an embedding vector and knowledge of the model that produced it, an attacker can reconstruct an approximation of the source text through iterative optimization. Exposing search embeddings in browser local storage discloses the substance of users' search queries to any attacker who can read that storage — for example, through a cross-site scripting vulnerability targeting the same application.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Move embedding generation, storage, and similarity search entirely to the server side. Do not expose raw embedding vectors in any client-accessible API response or browser storage — return only search results to the client.
  • Do not persist embeddings of user-supplied content in browser local storage, session storage, or client-side application state.
  • Treat any embedding derived from user input as data of the same sensitivity classification as the source text, and apply the same access controls.
name: Embedding Inversion

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified end-of-life software components on hosts reviewed during the assessment. The affected components — {{AFFECTED}} — are no longer supported by their vendors and receive no security patches for any vulnerability discovered after the support end date. The team cross-referenced the installed versions against published vulnerability databases and confirmed {number} CVEs affecting the installed versions with no available remediation from the vendor.

# Impact

Once a software component reaches end of life, any vulnerability discovered in it is permanently unpatched. The exposure grows with each new CVE disclosed against the component — there is no patch cycle to bound it. Components reachable from untrusted networks or exposed to untrusted input present the most immediate risk, as attackers can target published exploits against confirmed unpatched versions without needing to develop novel techniques.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace or upgrade the end-of-life components identified in this finding, prioritizing those reachable from the network or exposed to untrusted input.
  • For any component that must remain in service past its support date, implement compensating controls — network isolation, input filtering, additional monitoring — and document the exception with a target remediation date.

Strategic Consideration

  • Record vendor support end dates for every operating system and application in the asset inventory. Define a review schedule that surfaces approaching end-of-life dates before support ends and establishes a replacement lead time for each component class.
name: End-of-Life and Unsupported Software

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application server returned full Java stack traces in HTTP error responses. Browsing to `{url}` produced an HTTP 500 response containing the exception stack trace with the full filesystem path of the deployment directory, bean configuration file paths, and the name and version of the Apache Struts 2 framework. The team used the disclosed framework version to confirm the application was running a version affected by published remote code execution vulnerabilities, which the team subsequently exploited.

Variants

  • ASP.NET: Multiple ASP.NET-powered applications returned detailed error messages disclosing full filesystem paths on the underlying host, exposing the server's directory structure to unauthenticated callers.
  • Tomcat: A Tomcat server running the {{COMPANY_NAME}} application returned full Java stack traces including internal class names and configuration file paths in responses to error-triggering requests.
# Impact

Verbose error messages that reach the client disclose the application's technology stack, filesystem layout, and framework version. Attackers use this information to identify applicable CVEs, verify that specific exploits will work against the reported version, and map the application's internal structure to guide follow-on attacks. Version disclosure through error messages is a reliable, low-noise reconnaissance source that requires no authentication.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Configure exception handling in `web.xml` to map all exception types and HTTP error codes to a generic error page that returns no stack trace, class name, path, or version detail to the caller.
  • Catch `Throwable` in all top-level Servlet methods to prevent unhandled exceptions from reaching the Servlet container's default error handler.
  • Log the full stack trace to a server-side log destination accessible only to administrators.

Strategic Consideration

  • Design all top-level Servlet methods to catch `Throwable`, the superclass of all errors and exceptions in Java. This reduces the potential for the container's error response mechanism to expose implementation details.
name: Error Message Information Disclosure

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {account} account reviewed during the host assessment held administrative privileges exceeding its operational requirements. Specifically, the account held {privilege_type} access to {systems_or_resources}. This access was not required for the account's stated function and had no documented justification.

# Impact

Every access grant beyond what an account's function requires expands what an attacker gains from compromising that account. An attacker who controls an account with administrative privileges can move laterally, escalate further, and access data or systems that a minimum-privilege account cannot reach. Administrative access held by service accounts or shared accounts also prevents attributing privileged actions to individual users, complicating incident response.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove the excessive privilege grants identified in this finding, starting with accounts holding administrative access without a documented operational requirement.
  • Assign administrative access to named individual accounts rather than shared credentials, so that privileged actions are attributable to a specific person.
  • Reconfigure service accounts identified in this finding to hold only the minimum permissions their specific function requires.

Strategic Consideration

  • Review privileged group membership on a defined schedule — at minimum annually, quarterly for accounts with access to systems handling sensitive data — and remove access when the associated role changes.
name: Excessive Account Privileges

Description:
# Description

The assessment team audited Entra ID application certificates in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s Azure tenant using Azure CLI commands against the Microsoft Graph API. The audit identified application certificates with validity periods exceeding the recommended 12-month maximum, including several with end dates multiple years in the future. The team also flagged {number} certificates expiring within 30 days with no evidence of automated renewal in place. The audit was performed using credentials for the {account} account and covered all applications in the tenant.

# Impact

A certificate or secret configured with a multi-year validity period remains usable for the full period if it is compromised. Standard rotation schedules and expiry-based detection do not catch credentials set to expire years out. An attacker who obtains a long-lived application certificate can authenticate as the application's service principal — accessing any resource the principal has been granted — for an extended period without triggering any expiry-based detection or forced rotation.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Set a maximum certificate lifetime of 12 months for Entra ID application certificates; for applications with elevated privileges, target 6 months or less.
  • Automate certificate rotation using Azure Key Vault and Azure Automation or a CI/CD pipeline so that rotation occurs without relying on manual action.
  • Configure Azure Monitor or Microsoft Defender for Cloud alerts to notify administrators of certificates within 30 days of expiry.
  • Conduct a tenant-wide credential audit on a defined schedule and revoke or replace any certificate exceeding the maximum defined lifetime.

Strategic Recommendation

  • Enable Conditional Access policies requiring MFA for applications with privileged Azure roles, reducing the impact of a compromised application credential.
name: Excessive Credential Lifetime In Entra ID Applications

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified Docker container images used in {product_name} infrastructure that ran all processes as the Linux root user. Some images omitted the USER directive entirely; others set USER root explicitly. Both configurations produce the same result: every process spawned inside the container inherits root-level Linux capabilities within that namespace.

The team confirmed the effective user inside an affected container image:

$ docker run --rm {image_name} id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

# Impact

A container running as root enters the container namespace with the fullest capability set the namespace permits. When an attacker identifies a code execution path inside such a container, they start the container-escape attempt from the strongest possible position—capability abuse, host-filesystem mounts, and kernel exploit techniques are all within reach from root in ways they are not from an unprivileged UID. A non-root container user doesn't prevent escape, but it removes an entire class of techniques and raises the bar for the attacker.

# Replication Steps

Locate the Dockerfile for each container image. Check for the presence and value of the USER directive. Pull and run each image, then confirm the effective UID with id. If the UID is 0, the finding applies.
Recommendation:
• Add a USER directive to each Dockerfile specifying a non-root account. Create the account during the image build, then switch to it before the final ENTRYPOINT or CMD instruction.
  • Use a numeric UID (for example, USER 1001:1001) rather than a named account to avoid UID mapping conflicts with the host.
  • Audit the full image build chain, including base images, to confirm no stage introduces or inherits a root-user context.
name: Excessive Service Account Privileges

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that privileged accounts were used for routine operations across the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network, rather than being reserved for the specific tasks they were designed for. Starting from access to the domain account {{ACCOUNTS}}, which held local administrator rights on {number} network hosts, the team extracted NTLM credential hashes from LSASS memory on {{TARGET_HOST}}. Those hashes authenticated to {number} additional domain hosts via pass-the-hash.

On {{TARGET_HOST}}, the team recovered cleartext credentials for the domain administrator account {admin_account} from LSASS. The team confirmed those credentials by authenticating to a domain controller and executing commands:

{command_output}

Domain administrator credentials stored in LSASS on workstations indicate routine use of those accounts on systems they were never intended to access.

# Impact

Every system a domain administrator logs into stores that account's credential material in LSASS—NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, and in some configurations cleartext passwords. Any attacker who reaches local administrator access on any of those systems can read LSASS memory and reuse those credentials against the entire domain. The privileged account's reach is only as limited as the number of systems it has touched, not the number it was meant to manage.

# Replication Steps

Identify privileged account sessions on workstations through AD queries or endpoint data.
