On a system where a privileged account has an active or cached session, dump LSASS memory with an appropriate tool and inspect the output for credential material. Attempt authentication to a domain controller with the recovered credentials.
Recommendation:
• Establish a written policy prohibiting domain administrator accounts from authenticating to systems other than domain controllers. For day-to-day administration of workstations and member servers, provision separate administrative accounts without domain controller access.
  • Monitor domain administrator account activity for authentication events on non-domain-controller hosts. Treat such events as incidents requiring investigation.
  • For Unix environments: prohibit direct root login except from the physical console. Require privilege escalation through sudo with logging, and review sudo logs regularly.
name: Excessive Use of Privileged Credentials

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} hosts on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network exposing the Intelligent Platform Management Interface (IPMI) service on UDP port 623. Using Metasploit's ipmi_dumphashes module, the team retrieved HMAC-SHA1 password hashes for administrative accounts—including root and Administrator—from multiple hosts without authenticating first. The team subjected those hashes to offline recovery, obtained the plaintext passwords, and authenticated to the management interface using ipmitool, confirming the ability to power cycle hosts, establish out-of-band network routes, and modify firmware configurations.

{ipmi_dumphashes_output}

Variants / affected technologies
  • SFTP: The assessment team identified a publicly exposed SFTP service on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network with password authentication enabled. Any network-reachable host could attempt credential guessing against the service. A successful authentication would give an attacker access to whatever files the account was permitted to read or write.
  • WordPress: The assessment team identified a publicly exposed WordPress administration interface on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network. An unauthorized party with valid credentials—whether obtained through guessing, phishing, or credential reuse—could access the administration panel and modify site content, install plugins, or execute server-side code.
# Impact

IPMI v2.0 contains a protocol-level flaw in its cipher negotiation: any host with network access to the IPMI port can request password hash material for configured accounts without presenting any credential (CVE-2013-4786). The recovered hashes are suitable for offline password recovery. A successful recovery gives the attacker hardware-level control over the system—power state, serial console access, firmware modification—independent of the host operating system and its security controls.

# Replication Steps

Scan the target network range for hosts listening on UDP 623. Run ipmi_dumphashes against identified hosts and collect returned hash values. Submit hashes to an offline recovery tool. Authenticate to the IPMI web interface or via ipmitool with the recovered credentials and confirm the available management actions.
Recommendation:
• Disable the IPMI service on any host where out-of-band management is not required. There is no patch for the IPMI v2.0 hash disclosure flaw; network isolation is the only complete mitigation.
  • Move IPMI, BMC, iLO, DRAC, and equivalent out-of-band management interfaces to a dedicated, isolated management network not reachable from the production environment or the internet.
  • Configure unique, randomly generated passwords for each device's IPMI interface. Do not reuse passwords across devices or with any other service account.
  • Disable IPMI cipher suite 0 on all affected devices. Cipher 0 allows an attacker to authenticate without presenting a valid credential by bypassing the authentication step entirely.
name: Exposed Administration Interface

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a {name} administration interface reachable from the {network_name} network at {{TARGET_URL}}. The team navigated to the login page without authentication and confirmed the interface was accessible to any host that could reach it. The team did not obtain working credentials during the assessment.

{screenshot}

Variants / affected technologies
  • Adobe Experience Manager: The assessment team identified Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) interfaces on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network that disclosed version and configuration information without authentication. The team used this information to identify the specific AEM version in use and assess applicable known vulnerabilities.
  • Apache Airflow: The assessment team identified a publicly exposed Apache Airflow administration interface on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network. The team did not obtain valid credentials; however, the interface disclosed DAG names and scheduling information before authentication.
  • Jaspersoft: The assessment team identified a publicly exposed Jaspersoft administration interface on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network. An authenticated user could access business intelligence reports and data exports.
  • Lantronix: The assessment team identified a Lantronix device management interface on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network. Lantronix devices use well-known default credentials that the team recommends testing.
  • Redis: The assessment team identified Redis services exposed to the internet on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network. All instances enforced authentication; the team notes that unauthenticated Redis exposure is a critical severity finding in other contexts.
  • SAP: The assessment team identified SAP administrative interfaces on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network through domain and TLS certificate enumeration. The interfaces were reachable from the internet and presented login forms.
  • SSH: The assessment team identified SSH services with password authentication enabled on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network. Password-authenticated SSH accepts credential guessing attempts from any source.
  • Siemens Teamcenter: The assessment team identified a Siemens Teamcenter product lifecycle management system at {hostname} exposed to the public internet. The PLM platform was reachable without network restrictions.
  • cPanel and Fortinet: The assessment team identified cPanel and Fortinet administration interfaces on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network. Neither required network-level access controls to reach the login page.
  • phpMyAdmin: The assessment team identified phpMyAdmin interfaces on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network. phpMyAdmin provides direct database access to any authenticated user.
# Impact

Administration interfaces reachable from untrusted networks become authentication targets for any internet-connected attacker. Credential guessing attacks, exploitation of known vulnerabilities in the management software, and information disclosure from pre-authentication responses are all possible without network proximity. The larger the number of hosts that can reach the interface, the larger the pool of potential attackers.

# Replication Steps

Navigate to {{TARGET_URL}} from an external or internal host, as appropriate to the network exposure. Confirm the administration interface loads without requiring a network-layer access control. Document the interface version and any pre-authentication information disclosed.
Recommendation:
• Disable the {name} administration interface on any host where it serves no current business purpose.
  • Restrict access to the administration interface to a defined set of source IP addresses—the management workstations or bastion hosts that legitimately need it. Deny all other sources at the firewall or host-based packet filter.
  • Conduct a periodic audit of {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s public IP space to identify and inventory all externally reachable services. Remove or restrict any service that does not require internet exposure.
  • Establish a change management gate requiring security review before any new service is exposed to an external network.
name: Exposed Administration Interfaces

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified an exposed Java Debug Wire Protocol (JDWP) port on the application server {{TARGET_HOST}}. JDWP requires no authentication. The team attached to the debug service using jdb, set a breakpoint in java.lang.Thread.sleep, and injected an arbitrary expression into the JVM when the breakpoint hit:

eval java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec("cmd.exe /c ping {kali_ip}")

The team's listener received ICMP traffic originating from {{TARGET_HOST}}, confirming that the JVM executed the injected command.

The team also attempted to deliver a reverse shell payload via an MSBuild configuration file retrieved from a team-controlled SMB share. The target retrieved the file, but full payload execution was not achieved within the assessment window.

# Impact

JDWP gives a connected client unrestricted control over the target JVM: arbitrary method invocation, class redefinition at runtime, thread suspension, and direct memory inspection. An attacker with network access to the debug port executes code as the OS user running the JVM—no credentials, no exploit development, no vulnerability research required. The Java debug protocol was designed for development environments and has no authentication mechanism in its specification.

# Replication Steps

Scan {{TARGET_HOST}} for open TCP ports. Confirm a JDWP banner on the target port. Attach using jdb -attach {{TARGET_HOST}}:{port}. Set a breakpoint in a method the application calls frequently (such as java.lang.Thread.sleep). When the breakpoint hits, use the eval command to invoke java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec() with a command that produces a verifiable out-of-band signal (ICMP, DNS, or HTTP to a team-controlled listener).
Recommendation:
• Disable JDWP on all non-development systems. Debug ports should never be reachable in staging or production environments.
  • Restrict access to JDWP ports using firewall rules, cloud security groups, or host-based packet filters so that only the specific host running the debugger can connect. 0.0.0.0 binding is not acceptable for a debug port.
  • Audit JVM startup arguments across the environment for -agentlib:jdwp or -Xrunjdwp flags that may have been added during troubleshooting and never removed.
name: Exposed Java Debug Port

Description:
# Description

The assessment team confirmed that the Kubernetes API server for the {{COMPANY_NAME}} cluster was reachable from the internet. The team made an unauthenticated request to the /version endpoint and received a full version response including the Kubernetes release, git commit, and build platform. Using a service account token for the clusterrole-aggregation-controller account, the team queried the API from an internet-connected host and confirmed the account had permission to create pods:

kubectl --token [REDACTED] auth can-i create pods
yes

The team did not attempt to create pods or modify cluster resources beyond confirming the authorization check.

# Impact

A Kubernetes API server reachable from the internet extends the cluster's authentication boundary to every internet-connected host. Any valid credential—a service account token stored in a CI/CD secret, a kubeconfig file committed to version control, a token recovered from a compromised node—can be used against the cluster without network proximity. New vulnerabilities in the Kubernetes API server are exploitable by any attacker globally, not only those with internal network access.

# Replication Steps

Confirm the API server IP and port are reachable from an external host. Send an unauthenticated request to /version or /openapi/v3 and confirm a response. If a service account token is available, use it to run kubectl auth can-i --list and document what actions the account can perform.
Recommendation:
• AKS: Update the API server authorized IP ranges: az aks update --api-server-authorized-ip-ranges {cidr_list}. Restrict to a set of trusted CIDR ranges that excludes 0.0.0.0/0. For new clusters, use --enable-private-cluster to remove public API server access entirely.
  • EKS: Update publicAccessCidrs via aws eks update-cluster-config --resources-vpc-config publicAccessCidrs={cidr_list}. For new clusters, set endpointPrivateAccess=true and restrict publicAccessCidrs.
  • GKE: Enable Master authorized networks in the cluster settings and add only the CIDR ranges that require API access. For new clusters, configure Private Endpoint Enabled, Public Access Disabled, and Private Nodes Enabled at creation time.
  • Bare-metal / generic: Apply CIDR-based allowlists at the load balancer or firewall in front of the API server. Require VPN or bastion host access for all Kubernetes administration.
name: Exposed Kubernetes Administration Interface

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {service} running on {ip}:{port} and reachable from the internet. A network scan confirmed external connectivity to the service:

{nmap_output}

The service required credentials. The team confirmed that authentication was enforced but did not attempt to guess or brute-force credentials. Any internet-reachable service that accepts incoming connections exposes its authentication interface to the global adversarial community.

Variants / affected technologies
  • Amazon Connect: The assessment team identified a web application exposing an Amazon Connect dashboard on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network, displaying real-time status and resource information about the {{COMPANY_NAME}} contact center infrastructure without requiring additional authentication beyond the web application session.
  • Dagster: The assessment team identified a Dagster orchestration instance on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network with no authentication, allowing any visitor to view pipeline definitions, trigger runs, and inspect run history.
  • Jenkins: The assessment team identified a Jenkins build server reachable from the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network. The Jenkins login page was accessible from any source address, exposing the build credential store and pipeline configurations to credential guessing attacks.
  • MailDev: The assessment team identified unauthenticated email inboxes on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network actively receiving email including password reset messages. Any visitor could read those messages and use the reset links.
  • MySQL: The assessment team identified MySQL database services accessible from the internet on TCP port 3306. The services accepted connections from any source address, placing the database authentication interface within reach of any internet host.
  • Prometheus: The assessment team identified a Prometheus monitoring interface on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network without authentication, disclosing infrastructure metadata, metric labels, and internal hostnames to any visitor.
  • RDP: The assessment team identified {number} servers on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network with Remote Desktop Protocol exposed. Any internet host could initiate RDP authentication attempts.
  • Telnet: The assessment team identified a Telnet service at {ip_address} reachable from the internet, transmitting credentials and session data in cleartext.
# Impact

A service reachable from the internet can be targeted by any attacker globally. Credential guessing, zero-day exploitation, and authentication bypass vulnerabilities require only network connectivity. Version information disclosed by service banners informs attackers about applicable vulnerabilities. Each exposed service is a persistent attack surface that exists as long as the service runs.

# Replication Steps

Scan the target IP range from an external host. Confirm that {service} on {ip}:{port} accepts inbound connections. Attempt to negotiate a session without valid credentials to confirm the service is accessible without a prior network-layer restriction.
Recommendation:
• Restrict each service to accept connections only from the hosts and networks that have a legitimate need to reach it. For most internal services, this means removing internet exposure entirely.
  • Place public-facing servers in a network segment isolated from internal systems. Services that must be reachable from the internet should not have direct layer-3 access to sensitive internal resources.
  • For services running in AWS: review all security group rules for any rule with a source of 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 on service ports. Replace broad source rules with the specific CIDR ranges that require access.
name: Exposed Services

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application passed the value of the cmd HTTP parameter directly to a PHP function call without validating that the value named an authorized function. Supplying phpinfo as the parameter value caused the application to execute PHP's built-in phpinfo() function and return its output in the HTTP response. The output included environment variables containing database credentials:

{request_response_evidence}

The team retrieved the database username, password, and host from the phpinfo() output. The database was not directly reachable from the team's network position, and the team could not supply function arguments, which limited further exploitation.

# Impact

When a PHP application uses user-supplied input to select which function to call, an attacker can invoke any function the PHP runtime can resolve. The scope of exploitation depends on the PHP configuration. Functions such as phpinfo() disclose environment variables and configuration details. Functions such as system(), exec(), and passthru() execute operating system commands as the web server user. The disable_functions directive limits this list, but does not eliminate the class of risk as long as input reaches a function call without validation.

# Replication Steps

Identify the cmd parameter in the POST /configuration/ request. Submit the value phpinfo. Confirm that the response body contains the phpinfo() output. Attempt additional function names (system, passthru) to determine the scope of callable functions.
Recommendation:
• Replace the dynamic function call pattern with an explicit allowlist. Define a map of permitted operation names to their corresponding functions, and reject any input that does not appear in the map.
  • Apply input validation at the parameter level: if cmd must accept values, enumerate the complete set of valid values and reject all others before the value reaches any function call.
name: Function Injection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} iOS application wrote {information} to the system-wide general UIPasteboard without configuring an expiration date or restricting the data to the local device. The team built a pasteboard monitor application and confirmed that it could read the {application_name}'s pasted data while running in the foreground.

{tool_output}

# Impact

iOS's general pasteboard (UIPasteboard.general) is accessible to every application that reaches the foreground after data is written. Without an expiration date, data persists in the pasteboard until the device restarts or the entry is overwritten. A malicious application that reaches the foreground—whether by the user switching to it or through a notification—can silently read the pasteboard contents. iOS 10 introduced the expirationDate option specifically to limit this exposure window; without it, sensitive data has an indefinite lifetime on the clipboard.

# Replication Steps

Build a companion application that monitors the general pasteboard. Trigger the {application_name} operation that writes {information} to the pasteboard. Switch to the monitor application and confirm the data is readable.
Recommendation:
• Set an expiration date on pasteboard items by calling setItems(_:options:) with the UIPasteboard.OptionsKey.expirationDate key. Set the expiration to the shortest interval that does not break user workflows—typically a few seconds after the write.
  • Where data should not follow the user across their other Apple devices via Handoff or Universal Clipboard, also pass the UIPasteboard.OptionsKey.localOnly option in the same call.
name: General Pasteboard Without Timeout

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {graphql_endpoint} GraphQL endpoint accepted unauthenticated introspection queries. The team sent a full introspection query and received a complete schema response listing every type, query, mutation, subscription, field name, and argument in the API. The response revealed API operations not surfaced in the application's user interface and field names that indicated sensitive data handled by the API.

{introspection_response_excerpt}

# Impact

A GraphQL introspection response is a complete, machine-readable map of the API surface. An attacker uses it to identify high-value operations—administrative mutations, queries that accept object IDs without authorization checks, operations that return sensitive fields—that would otherwise require guessing or extensive trial-and-error. Introspection itself does not grant access to data, but it converts a black-box API into a documented one, substantially reducing the work required to find exploitable operations.

# Replication Steps

Send a GraphQL introspection query to {graphql_endpoint} without an authentication header. Confirm the response contains type definitions. Review the returned schema for sensitive query and mutation names that are not documented or exposed in the application UI.
Recommendation:
• Determine whether public introspection access serves a documented business need. For internal or authenticated APIs, it typically does not.
  • If introspection is not needed by anonymous users, disable it at the GraphQL server configuration level or require a valid session token before the server processes introspection queries.
name: GraphQL Schema Information Disclosure

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified active guest user accounts in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Azure Entra ID tenant. Guest accounts are provisioned outside the standard employee lifecycle process and are not subject to the same periodic review and deprovisioning controls. Several of the accounts the team examined had not recorded recent authentication activity.

# Impact

Azure guest accounts remain active in a tenant until someone explicitly revokes them. Because they are created through a different path than employee accounts, they are more likely to be missed during access reviews. An attacker who compromises a guest account credential can authenticate to any resource the account has been granted access to, for as long as the account remains active.

# Replication Steps

Query the Azure Entra ID tenant for accounts with a userType of Guest. For each guest account, note the last sign-in date and the resource permissions assigned. Identify accounts with no recent activity or no current business justification.
Recommendation:
• Remove all guest user accounts that do not have an active, documented business purpose. For accounts that do serve a current purpose, record that purpose and assign an expiration date or review date.
  • Establish a recurring access review process for guest accounts, separate from the employee access review cycle, on a schedule appropriate to the sensitivity of the resources guests can reach.
name: Guest User Accounts in Use

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that an Nginx redirect rule at {{TARGET_HOST}} inserted an unsanitized URL path segment directly into the HTTP Location response header. The segment was captured by a regular expression that accepted any character except the forward slash, then substituted into the redirect URL at the $1 placeholder. Injecting CRLF sequences (%0d%0a) into that position split the Location header and appended an arbitrary header to the response.

The team submitted a request with CRLF sequences in the captured path segment and received a response containing an injected Set-Cookie header:

{request_response_evidence}

The injected cookie appeared in Firefox. Chrome did not process headers following the Location redirect header. The team confirmed that HTML and JavaScript could be injected into the response body but was unable to achieve XSS in this configuration because browsers do not render content in HTTP 3xx redirect bodies.

# Impact

HTTP response splitting allows an attacker to write arbitrary headers into a server response. An injected Set-Cookie header can fix a session identifier, enabling session fixation attacks. If the modified response passes through a caching proxy, the injected content can be stored and served to subsequent users who did not interact with the malicious link. The severity depends on the response path—a cached response from a CDN multiplies the audience for the injection.

# Replication Steps

Identify redirect rules that include user-supplied path components in the Location header. Inject CRLF sequences (%0d%0a URL-encoded) into the captured group and observe the response headers. Confirm the injected header appears in the response.
Recommendation:
• Sanitize all user-supplied input included in HTTP response headers before insertion. Reject or strip any input containing CR (\r) or LF (\n) characters.
  • Apply strict allowlist validation to path components used in redirects: permit only the characters the application actually expects (alphanumeric, hyphen, underscore), and reject anything outside that set.
  • For Nginx configurations specifically, run gixy against all server configuration files to identify redirect rules vulnerable to header injection and other common Nginx misconfigurations.
name: HTTP Response Splitting

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined that the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment did not require multi-factor authentication (MFA) when principals assumed IAM roles. The AssumeRole trust policies for {number} roles lacked a condition requiring aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent to be true. A principal whose static credentials were compromised could assume any of those roles using only the key ID and secret, without needing physical access to an MFA device.

# Impact

MFA in an AssumeRole trust policy gates privilege elevation on physical device possession in addition to credential knowledge. Without it, a compromised IAM access key or session token is sufficient to assume elevated roles. The attacker does not need to steal a device or intercept a one-time code—the static credential alone crosses the authorization boundary.

# Replication Steps

Retrieve the trust policy for each IAM role using aws iam get-role --role-name {role_name}. Inspect the Condition element of each Allow statement in the trust policy. Confirm whether aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is present and set to true. Attempt to assume a role without MFA from a test principal to confirm the behavior.
Recommendation: • Add an MFA condition to the AssumeRole trust policy for any role whose permissions warrant additional authentication assurance: {"StringEquals": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}}. Apply this condition to all roles that grant access to sensitive resources or administrative actions.
name: IAM AssumeRole Policy Without MFA

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified IAM policies in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment that used Allow statements with the NotAction element. The {policy_name} policy, for example, excluded only iam:* from its permissions while granting unrestricted access to all other AWS actions across all resources. This means the policy permits every AWS action that is not an IAM action, including actions in Lambda, Glue, and other services that can be used to escalate privileges without any IAM permission.

{aws_iam_get_policy_version_output}

AWS services beyond IAM can create or invoke execution environments that run with other principals' permissions. A principal that cannot call IAM APIs directly may still be able to escalate by creating a Lambda function with an over-privileged execution role, or by modifying a Glue job that runs under a sensitive role.

# Impact

An Allow statement with NotAction grants every AWS action introduced now and in the future, minus the listed exclusions. This is structurally unauditable: the set of permitted actions is open-ended and grows automatically as AWS adds new services. It also makes privilege escalation paths harder to enumerate, because the policy's effective permissions cannot be determined by reading it—only by enumerating all AWS actions and subtracting the exclusion list.

# Replication Steps

Enumerate IAM policies using aws iam list-policies and retrieve each policy's default version with aws iam get-policy-version. Inspect each policy document for Allow statements that contain a NotAction key. For each match, identify the principal types the policy is attached to and assess the escalation paths available through the permitted actions.
Recommendation:
• Replace all NotAction constructs in Allow statements with explicit Action lists. Enumerate the complete set of AWS actions each principal requires and list only those.
  • For AWS-managed policies that use NotAction, create custom replacement policies with explicit Action lists, detach the AWS-managed policy, and attach the custom policy in its place.
name: IAM Policy Allows NotAction

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that IAM roles in the {company_name} GCP environment were assigned directly to individual user and service accounts. Permissions granted per-account must be updated manually on each account whenever a privilege change is required. During the assessment, the team identified user accounts that had accumulated permissions from previous roles that were never revoked when those roles changed.

# Impact

Per-account IAM role assignments make privilege auditing labor-intensive and error-prone. When a user changes teams or a service account's purpose changes, the relevant assignments must be found and updated individually. Group-based assignment means that changing a group's policy updates every member simultaneously, and auditing a user's effective permissions requires only reading their group memberships. Per-account assignment has neither property.

# Replication Steps

Enumerate IAM bindings in the GCP project using gcloud projects get-iam-policy {project_id}. Identify any binding where the member is a user: or serviceAccount: principal rather than a group:. For those accounts, review whether the assigned role is current and appropriate.
Recommendation:
• Assign IAM roles to groups rather than individual users or service accounts. Provision users and service accounts into appropriate groups, and manage permissions through group policy changes.
  • Document a formal IAM change process that requires group assignment for all new permission grants. Record each permission change, the business justification, and the approving authority.
name: IAM Role Assigned to Accounts

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{COMPANY_NAME}} IIS servers vulnerable to short-name enumeration. Using iis_shortname_scanner.jar to identify vulnerable hosts and the sns tool to enumerate content, the team recovered 8.3-format file and directory names from server file systems without reading the files themselves. Enumerated entries included a directory named backup~1 and a file named web.config—content that was not listed in any publicly accessible directory listing.

{sns_output}

The team was unable to read the contents of the enumerated files during the assessment, but their existence was confirmed and their names disclosed.

# Impact

Microsoft IIS generates 8.3 short-name aliases for files and directories and returns distinct HTTP response codes to certain request patterns that probe for these names. An unauthenticated attacker can observe these response differences to enumerate file and directory names without authentication and without triggering a directory listing. The disclosed names reveal backup directories, configuration files, and staging paths that can be targeted in follow-on attacks such as direct file retrieval, local file inclusion, or brute-force enumeration of known-sensitive paths.

# Replication Steps

Run iis_shortname_scanner.jar against the target URL. For hosts reported as vulnerable, use sns to enumerate short names. Review the enumerated names for indicators of sensitive content (backup directories, configuration files, deployment artifacts).
Recommendation:
• Install Microsoft UrlScan and add the tilde character (~) to the DenyUrlSequences section. This blocks the request pattern that exposes short-name responses without affecting normal browsing.
  • Remove all files and directories from the IIS web root that are not required for the application to function. Backup files and deployment artifacts should not reside in the web root.
  • Apply a web application firewall rule to reject requests containing the tilde character in the path, if a WAF is in use and the tilde is not required by any in-scope application.
name: IIS Short-name Information Disclosure

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified two access control gaps in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} sandboxed container environment. The first was read access to /proc/{pid}/mem, which the team exploited to dump memory from the co-resident process_api process. The memory dump contained EdDSA and RS256 JWT credential material. The RS256 token was a Google service account JWT with three bytes of signature missing due to dump imperfections; the team brute-forced the missing bytes against Google's public JWKS endpoint and reconstructed a valid token, which Google's /tokeninfo API confirmed as authentic.

The second gap was the presence of CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_NET_RAW in the container. The process_api binary used --block-local-connections to reject connections from loopback addresses. The team created a virtual network interface using the available network capabilities and bound a connection from a non-loopback address on that interface, bypassing the restriction. The team established a WebSocket connection to the /mount_root endpoint (101 Switching Protocols confirmed) but could not exploit the endpoint further within the assessment window.

Variants / affected technologies
  • Improper Access Controls (deprecated): This template has been superseded. Use Insufficient Authorization Controls for future findings of this class.
# Impact

Improper access controls allow an attacker to read memory belonging to co-resident processes and recover credential material those processes hold. Internal service JWTs recovered this way can authenticate to whatever services they were issued for. The presence of network capabilities beyond what the container's security model requires enables attackers to bypass IP-address-based restrictions by spoofing traffic—a restriction based on source address is not a cryptographic control and fails when the attacker controls the network interface.

# Replication Steps

From within the sandbox, confirm read access to /proc/1/mem. Dump the memory of the target process. Parse JWT fragments from the dump and brute-force any missing signature bytes against the issuer's public key material. Validate the recovered token against the issuer's token info endpoint. To test the network restriction bypass, confirm CAP_NET_ADMIN with capsh --print, create a virtual interface, and attempt a connection from a non-loopback address to the restricted service.
Recommendation:
• Remove read permissions on /proc/*/mem for unprivileged users within sandboxed containers. The process memory of container infrastructure services should not be readable by the container's user.
  • Clear sensitive credential material from process_api memory before the container user's first interaction. Credentials used during container initialization should not persist in heap memory once initialization is complete.
  • Remove CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_NET_RAW from the container capability set unless a specific, documented workload requirement justifies each capability. Drop all capabilities not required.
  • Add prompt-level detection for requests that attempt to read process memory, manipulate network interfaces, or interact with infrastructure services, and decline to assist with those requests.
name: Improper Access Controls

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the claude_code workflow node's allowedNetworkDomains egress allowlist was not enforced at the network layer. The team authenticated as a standard user, submitted a workflow execution with allowedNetworkDomains set to [""] and permissionMode set to bypassPermissions, and instructed the agent to make an outbound HTTP GET request to a team-controlled listener. The agent's first two attempts failed because curl and wget were absent from the sandbox. The agent then used Python's urllib module to open the connection. The team-controlled server returned a unique token, which appeared in the workflow's output stream:

python3 -c "import urllib.request; print(urllib.request.urlopen('https://{listener_url}').read().decode())"

Response: <html><body>{unique_token}</body></html>

The presence of the unique token in the agent's output confirmed that the request left the sandbox and reached the team's external host, despite the allowlist permitting no domains.

Variants / affected technologies
  • Improper Egress Filtering (application server): The assessment team found that the {application_name} application server did not enforce outbound connection restrictions. The team configured an external listener and confirmed the server could open connections to arbitrary internet hosts from the application runtime.
# Impact

An egress allowlist enforced only in application logic, not at the network layer, is bypassed by any interpreter with socket access. Any data available within the workflow workspace—uploaded files, environment variables, API responses, secrets injected into the execution environment—can be exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server. The allowlist value in the request has no effect when the network path to external hosts remains open.

# Replication Steps

Submit a workflow execution with an effectively empty allowedNetworkDomains value. Provide a task that instructs the agent to connect to an out-of-band listener using any available interpreter (python3, node, ruby, or similar). Confirm the listener receives the connection and returns a unique token that appears in the agent's output.
Recommendation:
• Enforce the allowedNetworkDomains allowlist at the network layer—firewall rules or a network proxy that drops outbound connections to non-allowlisted destinations—rather than relying on application-layer enforcement alone. Application-layer controls can be bypassed by any interpreter or library with socket access.
  • Monitor outbound network connections from workflow execution environments for traffic to unexpected destinations and alert on connections to hosts outside the expected allowlist.
name: Improper Egress Filtering

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined through interviews with {organization} developers that the sandbox environment shared user and network namespaces with the host but isolated PID, mount, and UTS namespaces. Outbound network access was restricted using a denylist that blocked connections to known-sensitive internal destinations, including the GCP metadata endpoint. The team confirmed that connections to external hosts not on the denylist—including arbitrary internet hosts—were possible from within the sandbox.

Variants / affected technologies
  • Improper Network Segmentation (protected network): The assessment team identified insufficient network segmentation between the {network1} protected network and the {network2} less-trusted network. Traffic was permitted between the two segments that should have been blocked by a trust boundary.
  • Wireless guest network: The assessment team found that the {ssid} guest wireless network did not enforce segmentation from the {company_name} corporate network. Devices on the guest network could reach internal corporate resources.
# Impact

A denylist-based network control blocks access to destinations that are known to be sensitive. It does not prevent data from leaving the environment to destinations that are not yet known, are not yet documented, or are registered after the denylist is written. An attacker performing reconnaissance inside the sandbox can exfiltrate findings incrementally to an external listener that appears on no internal denylist. An allowlist—permitting only the specific external resources the workload actually requires—is the only model that contains this risk.

# Replication Steps

From within the sandbox, attempt an outbound connection to an external host that is not on the denylist. Confirm the connection succeeds. Attempt the connection to a known-blocked destination and confirm it fails. This demonstrates that the control is a denylist, not an allowlist.
Recommendation: • Replace the denylist-based outbound network control in the sandbox with an allowlist that permits connections only to the specific external resources the sandbox's legitimate workloads require. Deny all other outbound traffic by default.
name: Improper Network Segmentation

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified two flaws in the {application_name} application's session management logic. In both cases, the application issued a valid API session token before the authentication flow was complete. The team reproduced each issue by sending requests that triggered token issuance without presenting valid credentials, then used the resulting tokens to access authenticated API endpoints and confirm user-level access.

# Impact

A session token issued before authentication completes is a credential the application hands out without verifying identity. An attacker who triggers either condition obtains access to whatever API surface the token unlocks, at whatever privilege level the application assigns, without knowing a valid password. Authentication controls applied after token issuance are bypassed because the attacker already holds a valid token.

# Replication Steps

Intercept the authentication flow using an HTTP proxy. Identify the request that triggers session token issuance. Manipulate the authentication flow to bypass or skip credential verification steps while still receiving the token. Use the issued token to make authenticated API requests and confirm access.
Recommendation:
• Enforce that session tokens are issued only after all authentication steps complete successfully—credential verification, MFA confirmation if required, and any step-up checks for the account type. A partially completed authentication flow should not produce a usable token.
  • Terminate sessions explicitly on logout, password changes, and after defined periods of inactivity and absolute session lifetime. Sessions should not outlive the authentication event that created them.
  • Bind session tokens to client attributes (IP address, user agent, or device identifier) so that a token stolen from one context cannot be replayed from another.
name: Improper Session Management

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified CloudWatch alarms in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS account that had no actions configured. When the alarm state transitioned to ALARM, no notification was sent, no auto-scaling action was triggered, and no Systems Manager automation was invoked. The alarms existed in the console but produced no operational response.

# Impact

A CloudWatch alarm without an action is a threshold monitor that records when conditions are met but does not tell anyone. Security-relevant conditions—unusually high API call rates, root account usage, unauthorized configuration changes—can trigger an alarm state that resolves without investigation because no one receives a notification. The alarm log is not checked proactively in most environments; only actions make the alarm operationally useful.

# Replication Steps

Enumerate CloudWatch alarms using aws cloudwatch describe-alarms. For each alarm, inspect the AlarmActions, OKActions, and InsufficientDataActions arrays. Alarms with empty arrays for all three fields have no configured actions.
Recommendation:
• Delete CloudWatch alarms that monitor conditions no one is acting on. An unused alarm creates false confidence and adds noise to alarm inventories.
  • For alarms that should exist, configure at least one action—an SNS topic that notifies the responsible team—so that state transitions produce a response.
name: Improperly Configured CloudWatch Alarms

Description:
# Description

Through interviews with {organization} personnel and review of documentation provided by {{COMPANY_NAME}}, the assessment team determined that the organization did not maintain a current, comprehensive inventory of systems, applications, data stores, and network assets in its environment. During the assessment, the team identified systems and services that were not present in the documentation provided at engagement kickoff.

# Impact

Security controls can only be applied to assets that are known. Without a complete inventory, vulnerability scanning cannot guarantee coverage, patch management processes cannot confirm all affected systems received an update, and incident response teams have no baseline against which to identify unexpected systems. Assets not present in the inventory are the most likely to carry unpatched vulnerabilities—no process tracks or remediates them.

# Replication Steps

Compare the asset documentation provided by {{COMPANY_NAME}} against the systems and services identified during active reconnaissance. Note discrepancies—hosts that appear in scanning but not in the inventory, or vice versa.
Recommendation:
• Develop and maintain a comprehensive asset inventory covering all hardware, software, cloud resources, data stores, and network components. Include owner, classification, data sensitivity, and regulatory scope for each asset.
  • Deploy automated asset discovery tools that continuously scan the network and update the inventory when new assets appear. Manual inventories become stale; automated ones do not.
  • Assign each asset an owner responsible for its security and maintenance. Assets without owners are not managed.
  • Integrate the asset inventory with vulnerability management and incident response processes so that any asset can be located, assessed, and remediated from a single source of record.

Strategic Considerations

  • Conduct periodic reconciliation between the asset inventory and network discovery scan results to identify rogue or unmanaged assets before an attacker does.
  • Use the inventory as the scoping document for security assessments and compliance audits to ensure coverage is complete.
name: Incomplete Asset Inventory

Description:
# Description

Through interviews with {organization} leadership, the assessment team learned that {{COMPANY_NAME}} did not conduct penetration testing on a defined schedule. Testing had occurred in response to specific compliance requirements or individual incidents rather than as part of a recurring program. The organization could not produce documentation of testing performed within the past {months} months covering the in-scope environments.

# Impact

Penetration testing produces findings that automated scanning cannot: exploitation chains, business logic flaws, and attack paths that span multiple systems. A scanner identifies known vulnerabilities in isolation; a penetration tester chains them together and demonstrates realistic impact. Security controls that have degraded or failed without triggering automated detection go undetected until a test or a breach surfaces them. The longer the gap between tests, the larger the window in which a viable attack path exists undetected.

# Replication Steps

Request documentation of penetration testing performed within the past 12 months for the in-scope environments. Note the date, scope, and performing organization for each test. Identify environments with no recent test coverage.
Recommendation:
• Establish an annual penetration testing program covering at minimum external network, internal network, and web application scope. Scope should expand to include cloud configurations and any other environments that handle sensitive data.
  • Engage qualified penetration testing providers that follow recognized methodologies (OWASP Testing Guide, PTES, OSSTMM, or equivalent). Verify that the provider's methodology covers the environments in scope.
  • Conduct additional testing after significant changes to infrastructure, application architecture, or network topology. A security control validated before a major change may not apply to the post-change environment.
  • Track remediation of penetration testing findings with defined timelines by severity, and verify fixes through retest before closing findings.

Strategic Considerations

  • Consider a continuous penetration testing or red team program to supplement annual assessments and provide ongoing adversarial perspective.
  • Use penetration testing findings to drive security awareness training content and inform defensive detection engineering.
name: Inconsistent Penetration Testing

Description:
# Description

Through interviews and documentation review, the assessment team determined that {{COMPANY_NAME}} did not run vulnerability scans on a defined schedule. Scanning was conducted on an ad hoc basis, and coverage did not extend uniformly across all production and non-production environments. The team identified hosts in scope that had not been scanned within the past {months} months.

# Impact

A vulnerability scanner identifies known weaknesses against a current CVE database. A scan run at deployment captures the state at that moment; vulnerabilities disclosed afterward are unknown to the organization until the next scan runs. Without defined frequency and coverage requirements, entire asset classes can go unassessed for extended periods. Attackers exploit newly disclosed vulnerabilities within days of public disclosure; an organization without regular scanning has no mechanism to detect that window.

# Replication Steps

Request documentation of vulnerability scans performed within the past 90 days. Note the scan dates, tools used, and hosts covered. Identify asset classes or network segments with no recent scan coverage.
Recommendation:
• Establish a formalized vulnerability scanning program with defined frequencies: at minimum quarterly for all systems, more frequently for internet-facing and high-criticality assets.
  • Ensure scanning coverage extends to all environments—production, staging, development, and test—and to all asset types: operating systems, applications, databases, network devices, and cloud infrastructure.
  • Define remediation timelines by severity (for example, critical within 15 days, high within 30 days) and track compliance against those timelines.
  • Generate and distribute scan reports to asset owners on a regular cadence. Track remediation progress and vulnerability trend data over time.

Strategic Considerations

  • Integrate vulnerability scanning into CI/CD pipelines to detect vulnerabilities before deployment, not after.
  • Establish an exception management process for vulnerabilities that cannot be immediately remediated. Document the risk acceptance decision, compensating controls, and review date for each exception.
name: Inconsistent Vulnerability Scanning

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that a removable panel on the exterior face of the {device_name} exposed a test harness interface on the device's SoC. The panel was accessible without tools from outside the secured area the lock was intended to protect. Documentation for the SoC indicated that connecting pins 3 and 7 on the test interface triggered a factory reset. The team connected those pins, confirmed the reset completed, and entered the default numeric code 12345 to open the lock.

{photo}

# Impact

An attacker who can reach the exterior face of the lock can trigger a factory reset without knowing any configured credential. After the reset, the device accepts its default code, giving the attacker full access to whatever the lock protects. The attack requires no specialized knowledge of the target installation—only knowledge of the SoC datasheet, which is publicly available.

# Replication Steps

Access the removable panel on the exterior face of the {device_name}. Locate the test harness pins using the SoC datasheet. Briefly connect pins 3 and 7. Confirm the device resets by entering the default code 12345.
Recommendation: • {context-specific remediation required}: Recommendations depend on the specific attack surface and production deployment context. At minimum, consider whether the test harness interface can be physically removed, potted, or relocated to the interior face of the device in a production hardware revision. Evaluate whether the factory reset function should require a distinct hardware action not performable from the exterior of the device.
name: Ineffective Physical Access Controls

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified AWS resources in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment with missing baseline hardening configurations. The following resources were improperly configured:

  • {number} RDS instances without automated backups enabled
  • {number} RDS instances with a snapshot retention period shorter than {days} days
  • {number} RDS instances without automatic minor version updates enabled
  • {number} Redshift clusters accessible from the internet

Production databases without backups cannot be restored after accidental or malicious data modification. Redshift clusters reachable from the internet place the database authentication interface within reach of any internet-connected attacker.

# Impact

Missing backups mean data destruction—whether accidental or intentional—is permanent. A short retention period narrows the window in which a compromise can be detected and a clean state restored. Deferred minor version updates allow known vulnerabilities to persist in production. Internet-accessible Redshift clusters extend the attack surface for credential guessing and direct exploitation to any internet host.

# Replication Steps

Enumerate RDS instances and Redshift clusters using aws rds describe-db-instances and aws redshift describe-clusters. For each instance, check BackupRetentionPeriod, AutoMinorVersionUpgrade, and whether the cluster is publicly accessible. Note any Redshift cluster with a publicly routable endpoint.
Recommendation:
• Enable automated backups for all production RDS instances and set the retention period to at least 30 days.
  • Enable automatic minor version updates for all RDS instances and Redshift clusters in production environments. Minor version updates include security patches.
  • Remove internet exposure from Redshift clusters. If a cluster's business purpose does not require public reachability, remove its public endpoint and restrict access to VPC-internal sources only.
name: Insecure AWS Resource Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified Amazon S3 credentials stored in plaintext in the {repository} source code repository. The file {path} contained an AWS access_key_id and secret_access_key. The team loaded those credentials into environment variables and used the AWS CLI to list and download objects from the affected S3 bucket, confirming full read access to {{OBJECTS}}.

{aws_cli_evidence}

# Impact

Credentials in source code are available to every person who has read access to the repository—current and former developers, CI/CD systems, and anyone who finds the repository if it is ever exposed. Unlike a rotated production secret, a key committed to git persists in the repository's history after the file is edited. Anyone who can clone or access the history retrieves the original credential. The credential's effective lifetime is not bounded by the rotation date of the current secret but by whether the old commit has ever been purged from the repository.

# Replication Steps

Clone the repository or access it through the source control interface. Search for AWS key patterns (AKIA prefix for access key IDs) across current files and git history. Extract the key and secret. Use aws sts get-caller-identity to confirm the credential is valid, then enumerate accessible S3 buckets and objects.
Recommendation:
• Treat the exposed credentials as compromised. Deactivate and delete the IAM access key immediately. Create replacement credentials for the environments that need them, using a secrets management solution rather than plaintext files.
  • Audit the S3 bucket's access logs for the period the credentials were exposed. Determine whether any unauthorized access occurred.
  • Remove the credentials from all repository files and purge them from git history using git filter-repo or an equivalent tool. Notify all repository collaborators that a rebase or fresh clone is required.
  • Migrate credential injection to environment variables provided by the deployment platform (EC2 instance profiles, ECS task roles, GitHub Actions secrets) rather than files committed to version control.

Strategic Considerations

  • If the workload runs on EC2, assign the instance an IAM role with S3 access permissions rather than using static access keys.
  • Consider AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault for managing credentials that cannot be provided through instance profiles.
name: Insecure Application Credential Storage

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} Android application wrote sensitive data to the Android system log, including session identifiers and {financial_information}. The team retrieved this data using standard Android debugging tools. The log entries persisted until the log buffer wrapped or the device was rebooted.

{log_output_evidence}

# Impact

The Android log buffer is accessible to any process holding the READ_LOGS permission. On Android versions prior to 4.1, this permission was available to any application. On more recent versions, access requires a privileged application or device root. An application that writes sensitive data to the log exposes it to any privileged observer while the entry remains in the buffer—which is an indeterminate period, depending on log volume and buffer size.

# Replication Steps

Install the {application_name} application on an Android device or emulator. Perform an action that produces sensitive output (login, payment, account retrieval). Run adb logcat and search for session identifiers, account numbers, or other sensitive strings in the output.
Recommendation:
• Delete all previously generated log files that contain sensitive user data from production devices and application backends.
  • Remove all Log.d, Log.i, Log.v, and Log.e calls that write sensitive data in production builds. Use ProGuard or DexGuard with a rule that strips android.util.Log method calls in release builds to prevent debug logging from reaching production.
name: Insecure Application Logging

Description:
# Description

The assessment team reviewed the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Azure Entra ID tenant authorization policies and identified multiple settings that exceeded secure defaults. These configurations allowed any tenant user to invite external guests, consent to unverified OAuth applications, create new tenants and subscriptions, and register applications requesting elevated permissions—all without administrator approval. The full set of insecure configurations is listed below:

{configuration_table}

# Impact

Overly permissive tenant authorization policies expand what an attacker can accomplish with any compromised account. A guest invitation policy open to all users allows an attacker to introduce accounts they control into the tenant. Application consent settings without admin approval allow a malicious OAuth application to request data access permissions and harvest tokens from users who click through the consent screen. Tenant and subscription creation without governance approval means an attacker can spin up shadow resources outside the organization's visibility.

# Replication Steps

Use the Microsoft Graph API or the Entra ID portal to retrieve authorization policy settings. Compare each setting against the recommended values. For settings that allow all users to perform privileged actions, confirm by attempting those actions as a standard test user account.
Recommendation:
• allowEmailVerifiedUsersToJoinOrganization: Set to Disabled. Require administrator approval for any external user requesting tenant access.
  • allowInvitesFrom: Set to AdminsOnly. Users should not be able to introduce external accounts into the tenant without approval.
  • allowUserConsentForRiskyApps: Disable for general users. Require administrator consent for any application requesting access to organizational data.
  • allowedToSignUpEmailBasedSubscriptions: Disable. Subscription creation should require governance approval.
  • allowedToUseSSPR: Require MFA or a strong verification method before allowing self-service password reset. Unverified SSPR enables account takeover through social engineering.
  • blockMsolPowerShell: Enable. Legacy MSOL PowerShell modules bypass modern conditional access controls.
  • allowedToCreateApps: Disable for general users. Restrict application registration to administrators and designated personnel.
  • allowedToCreateSecurityGroups: Restrict to administrators or a designated set of users. Unrestricted group creation leads to permission sprawl.
  • allowedToCreateTenants: Disable for regular users.
  • allowedToReadBitlockerKeysForOwnedDevice: Restrict to enrolled devices only. Audit access logs for anomalous key retrieval activity.
  • allowedToReadOtherUsers: Restrict to the minimum attributes required. Exposing full directory profiles to all users discloses PII unnecessarily.
name: Insecure Azure Authorization Policies

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} iOS application protected its UI with biometric authentication using a LAContext local authenticator, rather than securing the Keychain item itself with the userPresence access control flag. The Keychain item holding the session token was created without user-presence protection. As a result, the session token was retrievable directly from the Keychain without triggering the biometric prompt.

{code_or_decompilation_evidence}

# Impact

Biometric authentication in a mobile application protects stored credentials only when the OS credential store—iOS Keychain or Android Keystore—enforces the biometric requirement at the item level. A local authenticator (LAContext) that gates the application UI is a UI-layer control: it prevents the application from proceeding, but does not prevent another process or tool from reading Keychain items stored without the userPresence flag. An attacker who extracts the Keychain—whether through a jailbroken device, a backup, or physical access—can read the session token without interacting with the application UI at all.

# Replication Steps

Enable biometric authentication in the {application_name} application. Using a jailbroken device or a Keychain dumping tool, extract the session token from the Keychain without invoking the biometric prompt. Confirm the token is valid by using it to make an authenticated API request.
Recommendation:
• For iOS: create Keychain items with a SecAccessControl attribute that includes the .userPresence flag. Use kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly as the accessibility level. This causes the OS to enforce biometric or passcode authentication at the Keychain level, not the UI level.
  • For Android: generate the secret key with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) in the KeyGenParameterSpec. Set setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) so that enrolling a new biometric credential invalidates existing keys.
name: Insecure Biometric Authentication

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {device_name} used the U-Boot bootloader with the bootdelay variable set to three seconds, allowing the boot sequence to be interrupted from a serial console. The team connected to a serial header on the device's CPU board, interrupted the boot, and modified the flash_self environment variable to add single to the kernel boot arguments. The device booted into single-user mode as root. The team then added a no-password root account to /etc/passwd and rebooted normally:

echo example:x:0:0:root:/:/bin/ash >> /etc/passwd
echo example::10957:0:99999:7::: >> /etc/shadow

# Impact

An attacker who can interrupt the boot sequence and modify kernel boot arguments gains root on the device without knowing any configured credential. From root, firmware images can be read, modified, or replaced; stored credentials and configuration data can be extracted; and any OS-level protection applied after normal boot is irrelevant. The attack requires only physical access to the serial header and knowledge of the SoC datasheet, both of which are achievable for a motivated attacker with access to the device.

# Replication Steps

Connect a serial adapter to the CPU board header. Power the device and interrupt the U-Boot countdown. At the U-Boot prompt, use setenv to modify kernel boot arguments to include single. Issue boot and confirm the device drops to a root shell. Add a test account and reboot normally to confirm persistence.
Recommendation:
• Set the U-Boot bootdelay environment variable to -2. A value of -2 prevents the bootloader from accepting any console input during the boot sequence, making interactive U-Boot access unavailable through normal means.
  • Review the U-Boot configuration for options that disable the console entirely, such as CONFIG_DISABLE_CONSOLE. Evaluate whether the console can be removed from the production build without affecting the manufacturing test process.
name: Insecure Bootloader Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified GCP Cloud Storage bucket configurations in the {company_name} environment that granted access to allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers. Additionally, {number} buckets containing sensitive data did not have versioning enabled. The overly permissive buckets allowed the team to list bucket contents and retrieve objects without authenticating with any {company_name} credential.

# Impact

A bucket granting access to allUsers is fully public—any internet user without a Google account can list and read its contents. A bucket granting access to allAuthenticatedUsers is accessible to anyone with any Google account. Both configurations violate the principle of least privilege at a basic level and are commonly exploited through automated scanning tools that probe GCP buckets for public access. Without versioning, object deletions and overwrites are permanent: there is no recovery path if data is removed, whether accidentally or as part of a destructive attack.

# Replication Steps

Use gsutil ls gs://{bucket_name} without authentication or with a generic Google account. Confirm whether objects can be listed and retrieved. Check versioning status with gsutil versioning get gs://{bucket_name}.
Recommendation:
• Remove allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers from all bucket IAM policies. Grant access only to the specific service accounts and user accounts that require it.
  • Apply the principle of least privilege when writing bucket policies: grant read, write, or admin permissions only to the principals that need them, and scope permissions to the minimum set of operations required.
  • Enable versioning on all Cloud Storage buckets that contain sensitive or operationally critical data.
  • Remove any bucket that no longer serves an active business purpose.
name: Insecure Bucket Configurations

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} iOS and Android applications did not clear the visible UI or replace it with a neutral image before entering the background state. When the user pressed the Home button or switched to another application, the iOS task switcher and Android recent-apps view captured and stored a screenshot of whatever was visible on screen, including {leaked_info}.

{screenshot_evidence}

# Impact

Both iOS and Android capture a screenshot of the application UI at the moment the application enters the background. The screenshot is stored on the device filesystem and displayed in the app switcher. A malicious application with screen-capture access on a rooted device can read those cached screenshots from persistent storage. An attacker with physical access to an unlocked device can view them by opening the task switcher. The exposure exists regardless of whether the user takes an explicit screenshot—it is an automatic OS behavior triggered by backgrounding the application.

# Replication Steps

Navigate to a screen in the {application_name} application that displays {leaked_info}. Press the Home button to background the application. Open the iOS app switcher or Android recent-apps view. Confirm that the sensitive data is visible in the cached preview image.
Recommendation:
• For Android: set FLAG_SECURE on sensitive activities before calling setContentView. This prevents the system from capturing the window content in screenshots and the recents thumbnail.
  • For iOS: override applicationDidEnterBackground in the app delegate. Before the method returns, replace the key window's content with a blank view or the application logo. Restore the real content in applicationWillEnterForeground.
name: Insecure Caching of Application Snapshots

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {device_name} validated TLS connections to the cloud API at {host} by checking hostname matching and whether the issuing CA's common name contained the string {customer}. No cryptographic signature chain validation was performed for either the leaf certificate or the CA. The team generated a self-signed CA whose common name contained {customer}, issued a leaf certificate for {host}, and configured a local DNS server to redirect the target hostname to a team-controlled nginx instance. The {device_name} connected and transmitted user credentials to the team's server.

{credential_capture_evidence}

# Impact

TLS certificate validation exists to bind a server's public key to its identity through a chain of trust rooted in a trusted CA. An implementation that checks only hostname and a string pattern in the issuer CN—without verifying the cryptographic signature at each step in the chain—accepts any certificate that passes the text check, regardless of who issued it. An attacker on the same network, or in a position to influence DNS resolution, presents a self-signed certificate that passes the string check and decrypts or modifies all traffic between the device and the real cloud service.

# Replication Steps

Generate a self-signed CA with {customer} in the common name. Issue a leaf certificate for {host} signed by that CA. Configure a local server to serve HTTPS using the forged certificate. Redirect the target hostname to the local server via DNS. Connect a {device_name} and confirm that it completes the TLS handshake and transmits session data.
Recommendation:
• Use a well-vetted TLS library (OpenSSL, mbedTLS, or the platform's native TLS stack) and perform full cryptographic certificate chain validation. This means verifying each certificate's signature against the issuing CA's public key, checking the CA's signature against a trusted root store, confirming validity periods, and checking revocation status.
  • Do not implement custom certificate validation logic based on string matching or partial attribute checks. Custom validation is difficult to get right and consistently produces bypasses.
name: Insecure Certificate Validation

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified Cloud SQL instances in the {company_name} GCP environment that lacked baseline hardening. The team found instances without automated backups configured, instances without binary logging enabled for point-in-time recovery, MySQL instances where the root account was permitted to connect from any source host, and instances with public IP addresses.

# Impact

Cloud SQL instances without automated backups have no recovery path after data is accidentally or maliciously deleted or modified. Without binary logging, point-in-time recovery is unavailable—the organization cannot restore the database to a specific moment before a harmful query ran. A root account that accepts connections from any host broadens the authentication attack surface to any IP with network access to the instance. A public IP address extends that surface to any internet host.

# Replication Steps

Enumerate Cloud SQL instances with gcloud sql instances list. For each instance, retrieve the configuration with gcloud sql instances describe {instance_name}. Check settings.backupConfiguration.enabled, settings.backupConfiguration.binaryLogEnabled, and whether a public IP address is configured. Query the MySQL user table to confirm the root account's host column value.
Recommendation:
• Enable automatic backups on all production Cloud SQL instances: gcloud sql instances patch {instance_name} --backup-start-time {HH:MM}.
  • Enable binary logging on MySQL instances to allow point-in-time recovery.
  • Restrict the MySQL root account to connect only from localhost or a defined set of administrative IP addresses.
  • Remove the public IP address from Cloud SQL instances that do not require external connectivity. Use Private IP and Cloud SQL Auth Proxy for application connections.
name: Insecure Cloud SQL Configurations

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified Compute Engine instances in the {company_name} GCP environment with the deletionProtection flag disabled and no disk snapshot policy configured. Production instances storing application data could be deleted by any principal holding the compute.instances.delete permission, and no disk snapshot existed to restore data after a deletion.

# Impact

Without deletion protection, a single IAM permission grants the ability to permanently destroy a production instance. Without periodic snapshots, that deletion is unrecoverable—there is no prior state to restore. Both gaps compound each other: an attacker who compromises an account with deletion permission and finds no snapshots eliminates the data permanently. The same applies to accidental deletion by an operator.

# Replication Steps

Enumerate Compute Engine instances with gcloud compute instances list. For each instance, check the deletionProtection field in gcloud compute instances describe {instance_name}. Check whether a snapshot schedule policy is attached to the instance's disks using gcloud compute disks describe {disk_name}.
Recommendation:
• Enable deletion protection on critical production instances: gcloud compute instances update {instance_name} --deletion-protection. Apply this to any instance whose loss would cause a service outage or data loss.
  • Configure periodic disk snapshot schedules for production instances: gcloud compute disks snapshot {disk_name} --storage-location {region}. Automate this through snapshot policies rather than manual runs.
name: Insecure Compute Engine Configurations

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified session cookies issued by the {application_name} application without the Secure flag. A browser receiving a Secure-less cookie will include it in HTTP requests to any URL within the cookie's domain and path scope. If the user navigates to any HTTP URL—whether by direct request, a redirect, or a sub-resource load—the session cookie is transmitted in plaintext.

{cookie_evidence}

# Impact

The Secure flag is the only mechanism that prevents a browser from transmitting a cookie over unencrypted HTTP. Without it, session credentials travel in cleartext whenever any HTTP request falls within the cookie's scope. An attacker positioned on the same network—on public Wi-Fi, at a network appliance in the path, or at any unencrypted hop—can read the session identifier and replay it against the application to take over the session without knowing the user's password.

# Replication Steps

Authenticate to the {application_name} application and capture the Set-Cookie header in the response. Confirm the Secure flag is absent. Make an HTTP (non-HTTPS) request to a URL within the cookie's scope and confirm the cookie is transmitted in the clear request.
Recommendation:
• Set the Secure flag on all session and authentication cookies. In framework terms: configure the session cookie options to include secure=true before any response that sets a session cookie is sent to the client.
  • For Java Servlet applications, set secure=true in the cookie configuration or via response.setHeader("Set-Cookie", "JSESSIONID=" + sessionId + "; Secure").
  • For Tomcat-based applications, set secure="true" in the Context element of context.xml, or configure the cookie-config element in web.xml with <secure>true</secure>.
name: Insecure Cookie Transmission

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified session cookies issued by the {application_name} application without the HttpOnly flag. A cookie without this flag is readable by any JavaScript executing in the same origin. The team used an existing XSS vulnerability to run document.cookie in the page context and confirmed the session cookie value was accessible to the script.

{xss_poc_evidence}

# Impact

The HttpOnly flag instructs the browser not to expose a cookie through the document.cookie API. Without it, any JavaScript running in the same origin can read and transmit the session cookie to an attacker-controlled server. Every XSS vulnerability in the application—whether a stored payload, a reflected parameter, or an injected frame—becomes a session hijacking vector. The attacker receives the session identifier and can authenticate as the target user for as long as the session is valid.

# Replication Steps

Authenticate to the {application_name} application and inspect the session cookie in the browser's developer tools. Confirm the HttpOnly attribute is absent. Inject a JavaScript payload that calls document.cookie and exfiltrates the value to a team-controlled listener. Confirm the session cookie appears in the exfiltrated data.
Recommendation:
• Set the HttpOnly flag on all session and authentication cookies. Apply this at the framework level so it is enforced consistently across all responses.
  • For Java applications, set HttpOnly in the cookie configuration or via response.setHeader("Set-Cookie", "JSESSIONID=" + sessionId + "; HttpOnly").
  • For Tomcat, set useHttpOnly="true" in context.xml or configure the cookie-config element in web.xml with <http-only>true</http-only>.
name: Insecure Cookie Transmission: Lack of HttpOnly Flag

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified cleartext credentials in locations accessible to domain-authenticated users in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment.
