Group Policy Preference (GPP) XML files on the {{DOMAIN}} domain controller contained AES-256-CBC encrypted passwords. Microsoft published the decryption key in 2012; the team decrypted the values and confirmed that credentials for {{ACCOUNTS}} were valid against the domain controller. The team also found unattend.xml sysprep answer files on an accessible file share containing Base64-encoded and cleartext passwords. The account {domain}-sysprep was still active and the recovered password authenticated successfully.

{gpp_output}

{crackmapexec_output}

Variants / affected technologies
  • Cloud developer credential exposure: The assessment team identified multiple types of insecure credential storage in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} cloud environment, including credentials embedded in infrastructure-as-code templates, environment variable files, and CI/CD configuration with access equivalent to that of a {{COMPANY_NAME}} developer.
# Impact

GPP passwords use a fixed AES key that Microsoft published in MSDN documentation in 2012. Every domain-authenticated user can read SYSVOL, where GPP files live. A GPP file that hasn't been deleted is a live credential if the account is still active. Sysprep answer files store administrator and local account credentials for domain-join operations; files left on accessible shares after deployment are accessible to any user who can browse the share. Both classes of stored credential are a single PowerShell command away from any domain user.

# Replication Steps

From a domain-joined system, run Get-GPPPassword (PowerSploit) against the domain controller's SYSVOL share. For each returned credential, test validity with CrackMapExec. Search public and internal file shares for unattend.xml files and extract the Password elements.
Recommendation:
• Remove all GPP XML files from SYSVOL on all domain controllers. Do not use Group Policy Preferences to distribute or manage passwords.
  • Search all accessible file shares for unattend.xml and sysprep answer files. Remove any found and treat the credentials they contain as compromised.
  • Expire and reset all accounts whose credentials were found in GPP files or unattend files, regardless of whether the existing passwords still work.
name: Insecure Credential Storage

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} API at {hostname} reflected the value of the request Origin header directly into the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header without any allowlist check. The API also returned Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true by default. Together, these two headers instructed the browser to send the user's credentials with cross-origin requests from any origin, and to expose the response to the requesting script.

The team hosted a proof-of-concept page on a separate origin that made a credentialed XMLHttpRequest to the API's profile endpoint. When a logged-in user visited the page, the script read the API response and recovered personally identifiable information from the user's profile.

{cors_poc_evidence}

# Impact

CORS with a reflected origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true tells the browser to treat every origin as trusted. The same-origin policy exists to prevent one website from reading another's authenticated responses; this configuration explicitly disables that protection. Any malicious page a logged-in user visits can make API requests with the user's credentials and read the results. The attacker receives whatever the authenticated user has access to—profile data, financial data, account settings—without the user's knowledge.

# Replication Steps

Send an authenticated request to the {application_name} API with an arbitrary Origin header (for example, Origin: https://attacker.example). Confirm the response includes Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Host a page on that origin that makes a credentialed cross-origin request and reads the response.
Recommendation:
• Maintain an explicit allowlist of trusted origins. Validate the Origin request header against the allowlist, and set Access-Control-Allow-Origin only if the origin matches. Never reflect the Origin value without validation.
  • Avoid setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true unless a specific, documented cross-origin workflow requires it. If it is required, the origin allowlist must be strict—the combination of reflected origin and credentials-allowed is the highest-risk CORS configuration.
name: Insecure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} Android application stored sensitive user data in plaintext XML files in the application's shared preferences directory. The team inspected the userdata.xml file at /data/data/com.{package}.android/shared_prefs/ and found cleartext values including email address and social security number.

{xml_file_contents}

On modern Android versions, reading another application's shared preferences requires root access to the device. However, an attacker who roots the device, takes a physical backup, or exploits a local privilege escalation vulnerability can read these files.

# Impact

Shared preferences XML files are stored on the device filesystem without encryption. On a rooted device, any application with filesystem read access can read another application's shared preferences. Physical access to the device is also sufficient: an attacker who boots into a custom recovery environment can read the filesystem directly. Sensitive data stored without encryption is available to any process or person who can reach the file.

# Replication Steps

Root an Android test device or emulator. Install and authenticate to the {application_name} application. Use adb shell or a file manager to read /data/data/com.{package}.android/shared_prefs/userdata.xml. Confirm that sensitive fields are stored without encryption.
Recommendation:
• Determine whether each piece of sensitive data must be stored on the device at all. If it can be fetched from the server on demand, do not persist it locally.
  • For data that must be stored locally, encrypt it using the Android Keystore before writing it to shared preferences or any other persistent storage. Decrypt it in memory only when needed, and clear the plaintext value immediately after use.
  • Store encryption keys in the Android Keystore, not in shared preferences or application code. The Keystore is the only mechanism that prevents key extraction on a rooted device.
name: Insecure Data Storage

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that {{COMPANY_NAME}} iOS and Android mobile applications retained sensitive data in process memory after the user logged out. Using memory inspection tools on a test device, the team located {sensitive_data_type} in the application's heap memory that persisted after session termination.

{memory_dump_evidence}

# Impact

Mobile platforms use garbage-collected runtimes that do not guarantee memory zeroing when an object is released. Data in NSString (iOS) or java.lang.String (Android) objects remains in RAM until the garbage collector reclaims that region—a timing the application cannot control. An attacker with a debugger, a kernel module, or a co-resident process with memory-read access can recover data the application considers cleared. Physical access to the device is also sufficient on some configurations: memory can be extracted by forcing a crashdump or by using low-level forensic tools.

# Replication Steps

Authenticate to the {application_name} application on a test device. Log out. Use a memory inspection tool (strings, objection memory dump, or equivalent) to scan the process heap. Confirm that access tokens or other sensitive values are still present in memory after the logout operation completed.
Recommendation:
• For sensitive values that cannot be avoided in memory, prefer mutable types that can be overwritten: character arrays rather than NSString in iOS, char[] rather than java.lang.String in Android. Overwrite the array with zeroes after use.
  • Trigger explicit memory clearing for sensitive objects on logout and session timeout. For objects that use immutable types, remove all references and encourage garbage collection, though note that garbage collection timing cannot be guaranteed by the application.
name: Insecure Data Storage In Memory

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the database connection accounts used by the application on {server1} and {server2} held the sysadmin role on the MS-SQL instances. The team enabled the xp_cmdshell stored procedure using the database connection and executed operating system commands through it, confirming code execution as the {service_account} domain user running the SQL Server service.

{xp_cmdshell_evidence}

# Impact

A database connection with sysadmin privileges can reconfigure the database engine itself. xp_cmdshell, disabled by default but re-enableable by any sysadmin, executes OS commands as the service account running SQL Server. When that service account holds domain privileges—common in Windows environments—a SQL injection vulnerability in the application becomes a path to domain credential access. The gap between a database connection and a domain account is one stored procedure away.

# Replication Steps

Connect to the MS-SQL instance using the application's database credentials. Run SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin') and confirm the return value is 1. Enable xp_cmdshell with sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1; RECONFIGURE. Execute EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami' and confirm the output shows the service account identity.
Recommendation:
• Create a dedicated database account with only the permissions the application requires: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE on the specific tables the application uses. Remove all other permissions, including server-level roles.
  • Update the application's database connection string to use the least-privilege account.
  • Review the database account's permissions periodically and confirm they remain at the minimum required level as the application evolves.
name: Insecure Database User Privileges

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {device_name} did not remove customer data when a customer removed the device from their account. After completing the account removal process, the team confirmed the device reconnected to the previously associated Wi-Fi network on the next boot, demonstrating that Wi-Fi credentials persisted through decommissioning. The team attempted to extract flash chip contents directly; partial data was recovered, but complete extraction would require more specialized equipment than was available during the assessment.

{wifi_ap_log}

# Impact

A device that retains customer data after account removal carries that data into whatever context it enters next: the next owner, transit, secondary market resale, or a physical attacker who obtains a used device. Wi-Fi credentials allow the device to reconnect to the prior customer's network without authorization. Other retained data—account tokens, network configuration, user preferences—remains accessible on the hardware until it is overwritten or the chip is physically destroyed.

# Replication Steps

Pair the {device_name} with a test account. Unpair the device through the account management interface and confirm the removal was acknowledged. Power the device off and on. Confirm it reconnects to the Wi-Fi network associated with the removed account.
Recommendation:
• When a customer removes a device from their account, immediately send a command to the device instructing it to delete all customer data and await positive confirmation of completion before marking the decommissioning as successful. If the device is offline at the time of removal, queue the deletion command and confirm execution before the account-to-device association is dissolved.
  • If the device cannot confirm deletion within a defined timeout, inform the customer that decommissioning is pending, not complete, and that the device should not be physically transferred until confirmation is received.
name: Insecure Decommissioning Process

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a dynamic group in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Entra ID tenant whose membership rule evaluated properties that authenticated users could modify. The team met the conditions for the {group} group by updating a controlled attribute on a test identity, which triggered automatic enrollment into the group without any administrative action.

The group's dynamic membership rule was defined as:

```bash {insecure_rule} ```

FIGURE TEXT — Dynamic rules for ``{group}``

Entra ID evaluated the rule on the next synchronization cycle and added the team's identity. The group held access to {group_resources}, which the team confirmed after automatic enrollment completed.

# Impact

Dynamic groups in Entra ID add or remove identities automatically based on attribute rules. When a rule depends on properties that an attacker can write to their own account — such as department, job title, or extension attributes — any tenant user can manufacture group membership. Depending on what the group is authorized to reach, this provides lateral movement to other resources or privilege escalation within the tenant without any administrative interaction.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Audit all dynamic group membership rules. Confirm that each evaluated attribute is directory-owned and not writable by the identity being evaluated. Properties such as department, jobTitle, and custom extension attributes can often be modified by the user or through self-service flows and should not gate access to groups with elevated permissions.
  • For groups that grant access to sensitive resources, replace dynamic membership with static assignment or an approval-gated workflow.
  • Exclude guest identities from dynamic rules intended for employee accounts unless guest access to the group-controlled resources is explicitly required and reviewed.
name: Insecure Dynamic Group Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} Elastic Load Balancers in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment with security options disabled. The affected ELBs included instances missing deletion protection and instances with the Drop invalid header fields option disabled on ELBv2 configurations.

Deletion protection requires an additional confirmation step before an ELB can be removed from the console. Without it, the resource can be destroyed in a single operation — by accident or as part of a destructive attack following unauthorized AWS account access.

The Drop invalid header fields option instructs ELBv2 to reject HTTP requests carrying header names that contain characters outside letters, numbers, and hyphens. This filtering reduces exposure to request-smuggling attacks that rely on nonstandard header characters — newlines and spaces — to split a request across different parsing stages in the application stack. Applications that depend on underscore-containing header names must be evaluated before this option is enabled, as it can break those applications.

# Impact

An ELB without deletion protection can be removed in a single operation, intentionally or otherwise, taking dependent services offline with no automatic recovery. An ELBv2 with header dropping disabled gives back-end servers less protection against HTTP request smuggling, a class of attack that abuses parsing differences between the load balancer and the application tier to bypass controls, poison caches, or hijack user sessions.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable deletion protection on all ELBs in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment.
  • Enable Drop invalid header fields on all ELBv2 configurations. Before enabling, confirm that no application behind the load balancer depends on HTTP header names containing underscores or other non-alphanumeric characters.
name: Insecure ELB Configurations

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified an unrestricted file upload endpoint in the {application_name} application that accepted files without validating type, extension, or content. The team uploaded a server-side script to the application and retrieved it over HTTP, confirming that the server executed its contents.

To demonstrate the issue, the team registered a test account, navigated to the document upload function, and submitted a file with a server-side scripting extension. The application stored the file inside the web root and returned a URL at which the file was directly accessible. The team requested that URL and confirmed code execution on the server under the application's process identity.

The {user} account running the application process was a domain administrator for the {domain} domain. The team used that position to pivot to additional systems and ultimately to complete compromise of the Active Directory environment.

# Impact

An unrestricted file upload allows an attacker who can reach the endpoint to place executable content on the server. Once the uploaded file is accessible over HTTP and the server is configured to execute scripts in that directory, the attacker has remote code execution under the application's process identity — with no vulnerability beyond the upload itself required. From that position, an attacker can read credentials, access connected systems, and establish persistent access.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove file upload functionality that has no confirmed business purpose.
  • Require authentication and authorization before the upload endpoint accepts a request. Confirm the authenticated identity is permitted to upload files before processing the submission.
  • Store uploaded files outside the web root so they cannot be requested over HTTP directly.
  • Disable script execution in every directory that stores user-uploaded content. On IIS, set the execute permission to None; on Apache and Nginx, remove CGI handlers and deny access to executable extensions.
  • Generate a random, server-assigned filename for each upload. Do not use any portion of the client-supplied filename or path.

Strategic Considerations

  • Store uploads in object storage (such as S3 or Azure Blob) rather than on the application server's filesystem.
  • Validate file type by inspecting file content — magic bytes — not by trusting the extension or the Content-Type header. Reject files that do not match the expected format for the upload context.
  • Do not serve uploaded files to other users directly. If sharing is required, proxy the content through a controlled endpoint that streams it rather than executing it.
name: Insecure File Upload

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found files and directories on {{COMPANY_NAME}} systems set to world-readable permissions, including home directories, shell history files, backup archives, and application configuration files. The team read these files as a low-privilege user and recovered plaintext credentials for {{COMPANY_NAME}} accounts.

The following paths were readable by users outside the owning account or group:

  • {host1}:/home/*
  • {host1}:/mnt/*
  • {host1}:/etc/{application_config}
  • {host2}:/etc/{application_config}

Shell history files in several home directories contained previously executed commands with credentials supplied inline. The team used the recovered credentials to authenticate to additional {{COMPANY_NAME}} services, confirmed access to corporate resources including JIRA, and established that the compromised account held superuser privileges on the host.

# Impact

World-readable files grant any authenticated user on the system access to content the owning account did not intend to share. When that content includes credentials — embedded in scripts, configuration files, or shell history — an attacker with any foothold on the system can recover them without exploiting any additional vulnerability. Credentials recovered this way are directly usable against any other service where the same credentials are valid.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Audit filesystem permissions on all multi-user systems. Apply the principle of least privilege: home directories should be mode 700 and files containing credentials or configuration should be readable only by the owning account or a defined service group.
  • Remove credentials from shell history files. Establish a practice of prefixing sensitive commands with a space — which most shells exclude from history — or using environment variables rather than inline credential strings.
  • Review and restrict permissions on backup and configuration directories. Confirm that backup jobs do not run as root when a lower-privilege account can access the same data.
  • Where multiple services must share access to a file, use a dedicated service account and a restricted group rather than world-readable permissions.
name: Insecure Filesystem Permissions

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {device_name} device accepted firmware updates from its SD card without verifying the authenticity or integrity of the update image. The team extracted the running firmware, replaced a binary, repackaged the image, and confirmed that the device executed the modified binary after rebooting.

The update process used U-Boot to read a Squashfs image named {filename} from the SD card at each boot. The team extracted the image using unsquashfs, replaced the {filename} binary with a modified version, repackaged the filesystem using mksquashfs, and wrote the resulting image to the SD card. After rebooting the device, boot logs confirmed the image was applied and the replaced binary was executed — with no signature or hash verification performed at any point in the process.

The device's operating system was based on {os}, a {ostype} distribution, which has documented support for verified update frameworks. None were in use on the device.

# Impact

A firmware update process that does not verify cryptographic signatures allows any attacker with physical access to the update media — or the ability to deliver a malicious image — to install arbitrary code at the firmware level. Firmware-level code runs before the operating system and with full hardware access. Depending on the device's deployment context, this access enables credential interception, sensor eavesdropping, network pivoting, or persistence that survives factory resets that do not replace the update media.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Sign all firmware images with a private key held by the manufacturer. The device boot process must verify the signature against a trusted public key stored in tamper-resistant hardware before accepting any update image.
  • Reject unsigned or incorrectly signed images at boot. Log the rejection and halt rather than applying an unverified image.
  • Implement anti-rollback controls that prevent the device from accepting an image with a version number lower than the one currently installed.
  • Where hardware supports it, adopt an A/B partition model: install the new image to the inactive partition, confirm it boots cleanly, then commit. If the new image fails to boot, revert to the previous partition automatically.
name: Insecure Firmware Update Process

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found a domain administrator account with a Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) session that had remained in a disconnected state for {number} days on the system at {system_location}. The team connected to that system using a low-privilege account and attached to the existing disconnected session, assuming the domain administrator's identity without supplying the administrator's credentials.

Windows preserves disconnected RDP sessions in memory when no session time limit or automatic logoff policy is enforced. Any authenticated user who can establish a session on the same host can reconnect to an orphaned session using the native session-switching interface. The team confirmed domain administrator access after reconnecting and collected the following:

  • Trophy 1
  • Trophy 2
  • Trophy 3

The team determined that the Logoff Session after Disconnect group policy setting was not enforced on the system at {system_location}.

# Impact

A disconnected RDP session that is not terminated remains live in memory and is accessible to any user who can authenticate to the same host. Reconnecting to the session does not require knowledge of the original user's credentials. When the orphaned session belongs to a privileged account, an attacker with low-privilege access to the host gains that account's full domain access — including the ability to read password hashes, modify group policy, and reach domain-connected systems — through a low-privilege entry point.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Configure the group policy setting at Local Computer Policy / Computer Configuration / Administrative Templates / Windows Components / Remote Desktop Services / Remote Desktop Session Host / Session Time Limits to enforce a maximum disconnected session duration and automatic logoff when the limit is reached.
  • Apply this policy to all systems where privileged accounts are likely to hold RDP sessions, including domain controllers, jump hosts, and administrative workstations.
name: Insecure Group Policy Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application issued session cookies without the Secure flag. A cookie without Secure is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP as well as HTTPS, exposing it to any attacker positioned to observe or modify traffic between client and server.

When users authenticated to the application, the server set a cookie named Session without the Secure attribute. The team demonstrated interception using ettercap on the local network: the team performed ARP spoofing and injected JavaScript into an existing HTTP response that caused the target browser to open the application's login endpoint in a new window. The browser transmitted the Session cookie over the resulting HTTP request. The team's capture server recorded the cookie value. The team then used it to authenticate to the application without supplying a username or password.

# Impact

A session cookie without the Secure flag is transmitted over both HTTPS and HTTP. An attacker with network access — on the same segment, through a compromised router, or through injected content on any cleartext page the user loads — can capture the cookie and replay it to impersonate the user for as long as the token remains valid. If the cookie is an authentication token, the attacker gains full account access without needing the user's password.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Set the Secure flag on all cookies that carry authentication tokens or other sensitive values. This prevents the browser from transmitting the cookie over unencrypted HTTP.
  • Set SameSite=Strict on session cookies to prevent them from being sent on cross-site navigations.
  • If the Domain attribute must be set, restrict it to the specific hostname where the application is hosted. Do not set it to a parent domain that includes subdomains operated by other teams or services.
  • If the Path attribute must be set, restrict it to the application's URI prefix rather than /.
  • Set Expires or Max-Age on authentication cookies to a value appropriate for the session policy. Avoid tokens with no expiration.
name: Insecure HTTP Cookie Options

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found Helm version 2 deployed in the Kubernetes cluster with its server-side component, Tiller, accepting unauthenticated gRPC connections from any pod in the cluster. Tiller holds cluster-admin privileges by default and performs cluster-wide operations — creating, modifying, and deleting Kubernetes resources — on behalf of any caller that reaches its service address.

The team verified reachability from within the {container_name} container using Telnet to the Tiller gRPC service and confirmed that commands were accepted without credentials. This access allowed the team to deploy and modify workloads across the cluster without requiring any pod-level privilege.

# Impact

Tiller, Helm 2's server-side daemon, runs with cluster-admin privileges and performs no authentication or authorization checks in its default configuration. Any pod in the cluster — including one obtained through a separate vulnerability in an application container — can send API calls to Tiller and perform any action the cluster administrator can perform. This is a direct path from any compromised container to full cluster control, regardless of the pod's assigned service account or RBAC configuration.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Upgrade to Helm 3, which eliminates Tiller. Helm 3 communicates directly with the Kubernetes API server using the client's own credentials, removing the privileged daemon from the cluster entirely.
  • If an immediate upgrade is not possible, remove the Tiller Kubernetes Service and patch the tiller-deploy deployment to bind only to localhost:
    kubectl -n kube-system delete service tiller-deploy
    kubectl -n kube-system patch deployment tiller-deploy --patch 'spec: {template: {spec: {containers: [{name: tiller, ports: [], command: [/tiller], args: [--listen=localhost:44134]}]}}}'
    The Helm CLI uses port forwarding to communicate with Tiller and continues to function after this change.
  • Audit cluster services for other management interfaces accessible without authentication from within the pod network.
name: Insecure Helm Tiller Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application reflected user-supplied URL parameter values in its HTTP responses without restricting the accepted input. The team constructed URLs that placed attacker-controlled text in a position that appeared to be part of the application's own interface, producing content indistinguishable from messages generated by the application itself.

The vulnerable error parameter accepted strings of unrestricted length. HTML special characters were encoded correctly, which prevented script execution in this instance. A recipient who followed a crafted link would see attacker-authored content rendered under the {{DOMAIN}} domain in the browser's address bar — including fabricated instructions, contact addresses, or calls to action that inherit the domain's trust with users.

Variants

LLM Jailbreak: The assessment team found that {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s LLM API implementation did not apply sufficient input restrictions before passing user-supplied content to the model. An authenticated attacker could supply instructions that overrode the model's configured behavior, causing it to respond in ways the application did not intend.

# Impact

Insufficient input validation allows attacker-controlled data to pass through the application and appear in contexts where it influences user behavior or system behavior. In the reflected parameter case, the consequence is phishing via the application's own trusted domain. In the LLM case, an attacker can replace the model's system-level operating instructions, bypassing the application's configured guardrails.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Restrict the error parameter and similar display parameters to a defined set of known values. Validate against a server-side allowlist and reject any value not in it.
  • Where possible, replace free-text URL parameters with integer codes that map server-side to defined messages, removing user control over displayed content entirely.
  • For LLM integrations, maintain system prompts and instruction context server-side. Do not accept model instructions or role definitions from client-supplied request parameters.
name: Insecure Input Validation

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {device_name} device's Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) key-removal routine wrote an all-zero 128-bit key to the cleared slot rather than marking the slot inactive. The device continued to honor BLE authentication attempts using the zeroed key until a new valid key was written to the same slot or a factory reset was performed.

When the mobile application removed a user from the device, it sent a command that invoked the delete_user function with the affected slot's parameters. The function applied {bad_operation} to the key bytes, which zeroed them but left the slot in an operational state. The team wrote a Python script that initiated a BLE session using a zero-filled key for the cleared slot ID, sent an unlock command, and confirmed that the device accepted it and operated the controlled access mechanism.

The team verified the issue end to end: removed a second user account through the mobile application, waited for the device to synchronize and receive the clearing command, confirmed the original key no longer worked, then authenticated successfully with the all-zero key.

# Impact

Cryptographic key material that is zeroed rather than invalidated leaves the associated access control in an exploitable state. An attacker who knows a slot has been cleared — for example, by observing a user's removal from the device's mobile application — can authenticate using a predictable all-zero key without possessing any previously valid key material. In a physical access context, this bypasses access revocation for any user who was removed from the device.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation: • When a key slot is cleared, flag it as inactive before overwriting the key bytes. The device must reject all authentication attempts that reference an inactive slot, regardless of the key value supplied. Mark the slot active only after a new, valid key has been written and confirmed.
name: Insecure Key Management

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_feature} copilot chat endpoint at POST /api/chat/sessions/{sessionId}/messages on {fqdn} constructed its LLM requests entirely from client-supplied values. The request body carried the model's system prompt in the scopeSystemPrompts parameter, the conversation history in conversationHistory, tool definitions in availableTools, and UI action definitions in elements. The back end forwarded these values to the LLM provider without server-side validation, allowing an authenticated user to replace the assistant's operating instructions or submit arbitrarily large token payloads.

The team confirmed that scopeSystemPrompts was an array of strings accepted from the browser and forwarded directly to the model as the system turn. The team also submitted an oversized conversationHistory array, confirmed the back end forwarded it to the model without truncation or rejection, and demonstrated that this path could force unbounded token consumption per request at the attacker's chosen rate — imposing uncontrolled LLM API costs on {{COMPANY_NAME}}.

# Impact

When the system prompt, conversation history, tool definitions, and model parameters are accepted from the browser and forwarded to the LLM without server-side validation, an attacker can replace the model's intended operating instructions with arbitrary directives. This bypasses the application's configured guardrails. A client-supplied conversation history that the back end forwards without a size cap allows the attacker to force arbitrarily large token processing volumes per request, with API costs proportional to the request rate and payload size.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Construct the system prompt server-side. Do not accept scopeSystemPrompts or equivalent instruction content from the client. Store the authoritative prompt keyed to the template and user entitlements and prepend it to each model request in the back end.
  • Maintain conversation history server-side, keyed to the session identifier. Persist each turn as it occurs and reconstruct the history from storage rather than accepting a client-supplied array.
  • Enforce hard limits before invoking the model: cap the number of history messages, the size of each message, and the total input token count. Reject requests that exceed the limits before they reach the LLM provider.
  • Validate availableTools and elements definitions against a server-side allowlist of known tool schemas. Do not forward client-supplied tool definitions to the model.
name: Insecure LLM API Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined through interviews with {application} development teams that no documented guidance existed specifying which security-relevant events must be logged or what fields each log entry must include. Coverage varied by team and by feature, with no shared standard for format, content, or severity classification.

The assessment team also determined that the {application} platform did not provide API-based or export-based log retrieval, and the organization had not developed incident response procedures specific to the platform. Security monitoring teams would have difficulty establishing access timelines, detecting unauthorized activity, or scoping an incident using the available logs.

Variants

Insecure Logging Practices: The assessment team found {number} instances where the application recorded security-relevant events with insufficient context — missing user identifiers, incorrect severity levels, or output formats incompatible with the organization's SIEM — reducing the investigative value of the log record.

# Impact

When security-relevant events — authentication attempts, privilege changes, administrative actions, API key usage, bulk data access — are not logged with sufficient context, incident response teams cannot determine what happened, under which account, or from where. Incomplete logs extend the time between a compromise and its detection and may make it impossible to scope the incident or satisfy regulatory reporting requirements.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Define a mandatory list of security-relevant events that all development teams must log: at minimum, authentication success and failure, privilege escalation, administrative actions, API key creation and use, and bulk data retrieval. Specify the required fields for each event type — timestamp, user identifier, source IP, affected resource, and outcome.
  • Review vendor documentation for log export or API-based retrieval options. Integrate available logs into centralized monitoring infrastructure and establish alerting on high-value event categories.
  • Document incident response procedures specific to the platform, including log query examples for common investigation scenarios such as unauthorized access and bulk data export.
name: Insecure Logging Practices

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the host {{TARGET_HOST}} exported NFS shares accessible to any host that could reach the server's NFS port, without requiring authentication or restricting access by client IP address. The team mounted the exported share and read its contents without supplying credentials.

The team enumerated available exports using showmount -a {{TARGET_HOST}} and mounted the {share_path} export. The server had root_squash and all_squash enabled, which prevented the team from writing files as root. However, the target files were world-readable, so the nobody account produced by the squash configuration was sufficient to read them. The team confirmed access to {description_of_sensitive_contents} from the mounted share.

# Impact

An NFS share with no client IP restrictions and no authentication requirement is accessible to any host that can reach the server's NFS port. If the exported filesystem contains credentials, configuration files, private keys, or sensitive data — as is common with backup and configuration shares — an attacker with network access can read that content without exploiting any application-layer vulnerability. NFS traffic without TLS is also subject to passive interception on any network segment between client and server.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace NFS with a protocol that provides per-connection authentication and encryption by default, such as SFTP or SMB with Kerberos. Securing NFS to an equivalent level requires significant supporting infrastructure and is difficult to maintain in most environments.
  • If NFS must remain in use: configure an IP allowlist in the server's export options that limits connections to the specific hosts with a documented business need, and enable Kerberos authentication with integrity protection (krb5i) and privacy (krb5p) on the NFS server.
name: Insecure NFS Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found the rlogin service active on {{TARGET_HOST}} and configured to accept connections as the root superuser without a password. The team used the standard rlogin client to connect and received a root shell without supplying any credentials.

The rlogin protocol, designed in the 1980s for trusted host-to-host access, transmits all data in cleartext, provides no cryptographic identity verification, and relies entirely on IP-address trust — which is trivially spoofed. The device was a network camera running an embedded Linux image from 2012. From the root shell, the team read /etc/shadow and additional configuration files, and used the access to {post_exploitation_actions}.

# Impact

An exposed rlogin service that accepts unauthenticated root connections gives any network-accessible host unrestricted administrative control of the device. All session traffic is cleartext. No credential exists to capture or guess — the service grants access on connection. Combined with the age of the device's firmware and the absence of any modern OS-level security controls, this leaves the host persistently open to remote takeover.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation: • Disable the rlogin service. Replace it with OpenSSH, configured to use key-based authentication exclusively and to deny direct root login (PermitRootLogin no in sshd_config).
name: Insecure Network Service: rlogin

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} insecure or unnecessarily exposed network services on {{COMPANY_NAME}} systems. On the server at {ip}, port {port} was reachable from both the VPN and the Guest Wi-Fi segments at the {campus_name} campus. The team confirmed a JMX RMI interface on that port accepting connections without authentication.

Although class loaders were disabled on the JMX interface, the team created a malicious JAR file and loaded it through the JMX MBean management interface to achieve remote command execution on the host. Source code for the exploit is included with this report.

# Impact

A JMX RMI interface with no authentication accepts management requests from any host that can reach the port. Even with class loaders disabled, the MBean management interface exposes operations that can execute code in the JVM context. An attacker who reaches this service gains remote command execution under the JVM process account without supplying credentials or exploiting any application logic.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable all network services that have no confirmed business purpose. Document the justification for each exposed service and review the list on a defined schedule.
  • Enable JMX security controls in all production JVMs: require TLS for the JMX connection, enforce password authentication, and restrict the accessible MBean set to the minimum required for operational monitoring.
  • Restrict access to all required services by IP allowlist at the host firewall. Guest Wi-Fi and VPN segments should not have connectivity to management interfaces.
  • Align host configurations to your hardening baseline and conduct periodic assessments to identify services added outside the change management process.
name: Insecure Network Services

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{COMPANY_NAME}} web services accessible over unencrypted HTTP. The team used automated discovery techniques and enumerated {url_count} URLs responding on port 80 across the environment, including services that handled user authentication and sensitive data submission without enforcing transport encryption.

An attacker positioned between a client and one of these services — through ARP poisoning on a shared network, a compromised router, or content injected into any HTTP response the client loads — can read session tokens and credentials submitted over HTTP, modify server responses in transit, and redirect authenticated sessions before the user reaches an HTTPS endpoint.

Variants

AWS: The assessment team found RDS instances and associated connection strings in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment that did not enforce TLS. Traffic between application servers and the database passed in cleartext within the VPC.

Azure: The assessment team found storage accounts, applications, Application Gateways, and databases in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Azure environment without enforced HTTPS. Cleartext paths existed between services and from browsers to the application tier.

GCP: The assessment team found Cloud SQL instances in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} GCP environment that did not require TLS from clients. Database connections were accepted over unencrypted channels.

Heroku: The assessment team found applications in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Heroku environment without SSL certificates configured, or without strict HTTP-to-HTTPS redirection enforced.

FTP: The assessment team found services communicating over FTP. The protocol transmits credentials and file content in cleartext and provides no integrity protection for transferred data.

Redis: The assessment team found Redis instances accepting connections without TLS. Cached data and commands traversed the network without transport protection.

# Impact

Data transmitted over unencrypted channels is readable by any party on the network path. Session tokens captured from HTTP traffic allow session hijacking without any additional credential. Login credentials submitted over HTTP are immediately recoverable. An attacker who can inject content into HTTP responses can redirect users, capture tokens, and execute script in the browser — all before any HTTPS connection is established.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enforce HTTPS on all services. Configure servers and load balancers to return a 301 redirect for any HTTP request to its HTTPS equivalent.
  • Deploy HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) headers with a max-age of at least one year on all HTTPS responses. This instructs browsers to refuse future plaintext connections to the domain.
  • Ensure TLS certificates are valid, issued by a trusted CA, and not expired. Automate renewal to prevent expiry-driven outages.
  • For database and service-to-service connections, require TLS in the connection configuration and reject plaintext connections at the server.
name: Insecure Network Transmission

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {appname} application passed client-supplied cookie values to PHP's unserialize function without validation. The __trigtrans cookie carried a Base64-encoded, gzip-compressed serialized PHP object. The team crafted a malicious FileCookieJar object from the GuzzleHttp library — whose __destruct method writes data to a caller-controlled file path — and encoded it to match the cookie format. When the application deserialized the payload, it instantiated the object and called its destructor, writing a PHP file to a path inside the web root that the team specified.

The team accessed the written file over HTTP and confirmed remote code execution as the www-data user. The team also identified two additional cookies — {parameter_name2} and {parameter_name3} — carrying serialized PHP objects. Due to time constraints, the team did not locate the endpoints responsible for deserializing those values, but any such endpoint would be subject to the same class of attack.

# Impact

PHP's unserialize function reconstructs an object graph from attacker-controlled bytes, instantiating classes present in the autoloaded namespace with attacker-controlled properties and invoking their magic methods. When a reachable class has a destructor, string conversion method, or other magic method that performs a file write, network request, or shell execution, the attacker can trigger that behavior by supplying a crafted payload — no separate vulnerability required. The result is code execution in the web server's process context.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Do not pass client-supplied data to unserialize. Replace the serialized object cookie with a structured key-value payload in JSON or another data-only format, and reconstruct the object server-side from explicitly validated fields.
  • Where serialization across a network boundary is required, use a format that serializes data only — not executable object graphs — and validate the deserialized structure against an explicit schema before use.

Strategic Considerations

  • Use the Data Transfer Object (DTO) pattern to move data between systems. Serialize and deserialize DTOs using a safe, data-only mechanism rather than native language serialization.
name: Insecure Object Deserialization

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application's password reset flow could be exploited for account takeover. In the primary scenario, the reset endpoint accepted a caller-controlled URL in the request body and sent the password reset link to that URL rather than to the address the application held for the account. An attacker with knowledge of a target's username could issue a reset request pointing to an attacker-controlled server, causing the reset token to be delivered to the attacker rather than the account holder.

The team demonstrated this using a test account: the team submitted a reset request with the team's server hostname in the relevant parameter. The target account received a password reset email with a link pointing to the team's server. When the team followed the link, the reset token arrived in the request. The team used the token to set a new password and confirmed full account access.

In a secondary scenario, the application emailed newly generated plaintext passwords to users on reset. The issued password required no immediate change and had no expiration, meaning that any compromise of the user's email account — at any point after the reset email was sent — was sufficient to recover the credential.

# Impact

A reset flow that accepts the redirect URL from the client allows an attacker who can make a request on behalf of any account to intercept the reset token for that account. No current password is required. Sending plaintext passwords over email exposes credentials to anyone who can read the mailbox at any future point, through any means of email compromise that postdates the original reset.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Send single-use reset links, not plaintext passwords. Tokens must be cryptographically random, bound to the account, and expire after a short window — 15 to 60 minutes is typical.
  • Invalidate the reset token immediately after use, or when any password change occurs, whichever comes first.
  • Build the reset link server-side using the application's own known hostname. Do not accept a URL, host, or redirect destination from the client. Validate any configurable hostname component against an allowlist.
  • Transmit the reset token in a path segment or short-lived server-side code, not a URL query string, to reduce exposure through browser history, referrer headers, and server logs.
  • Bind the reset token to the initiating session or source IP and reject it if presented from a different context.
name: Insecure Password Reset Functionality

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found services on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network communicating over protocols that transmit data in cleartext without integrity protection. These protocols expose credentials, session material, and transferred content to any party with access to the network path between client and server.

# Impact

Network protocols without encryption transmit all data — including credentials and session tokens — in a form readable by any observer on the network path. An attacker with a passive capture position can recover credentials without active interference. An attacker with an active position can modify data in transit. Authentication over these protocols provides no meaningful protection, because the credentials are visible alongside the session they are meant to protect.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable unencrypted services that are not required for business operations. Document a justification for any exception before permitting it.
  • For administration interfaces, enforce HTTPS exclusively. Remove or block HTTP access at the server configuration or network perimeter.
name: Insecure Protocols

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a Rails dynamic rendering vulnerability in the {application_name} application that led to unauthenticated remote code execution. The TemplatesController passed a user-supplied path parameter to the Rails render method using the :file keyword argument, which resolves paths relative to the filesystem root rather than the application's template directory. The team supplied a path to a file outside the template directory and confirmed that the application read and executed its contents as a Rails template. The issue was disclosed to the {application_name} team during the engagement and was resolved within one week.

# Impact

The Rails render :file call resolves the supplied path against the filesystem root. User-supplied input to this argument allows an attacker to request any file readable by the application's process. Files containing ERB or Ruby template syntax are executed; others are disclosed. This provides a path to arbitrary file read and, if a writable location the attacker controls is reachable, to arbitrary code execution.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation: • Change the :file keyword argument on the TemplatesController render call to :template. The :template argument resolves paths relative to the application's template directory and does not permit traversal to arbitrary filesystem locations.
name: Insecure Rails Dynamic Rendering

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found insecure S3 bucket configurations in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment. The identified issues included {number} overly permissive buckets, {number} buckets without versioning enabled, and {number} buckets without MFA Delete configured.

The overly permissive buckets granted {access_type} to principals beyond those with a business need. Depending on bucket contents, this allows an attacker who discovers the bucket name to enumerate or retrieve stored objects without valid AWS credentials. Object listings expose filenames and metadata useful for planning further attacks.

Versioning preserves object states on write and delete. Without it, an attacker with write access can overwrite or destroy objects with no recoverable prior state. MFA Delete adds a second authentication factor to bucket deletion operations, raising the barrier against permanent data destruction from a single set of compromised credentials.

# Impact

Overly permissive bucket policies expose stored data to enumeration and retrieval by unauthorized parties. Disabled versioning removes the ability to recover from destructive writes. Disabled MFA Delete removes a protection against permanent data loss. Together, these gaps create a bucket whose contents are readable by any attacker who finds it, whose data can be overwritten or deleted without recovery, and whose destruction requires only a single compromised credential set.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove Everyone and Authenticated Users as grantees from all S3 bucket policies and ACLs. Grant access only to specific IAM principals with a documented business need.
  • Apply the principle of least privilege when defining bucket policies. Separate read, write, and delete permissions and assign each only where required.
  • Enable versioning on all S3 buckets that store data not recoverable from source — configuration files, backups, audit logs.
  • Remove S3 buckets that have no current business purpose.

Strategic Considerations

  • Implement a change management process that tracks S3 bucket creation and policy changes. Require approval before new buckets are created with public or broadly permissive access settings.
  • Enable MFA Delete on buckets containing data that must be protected against permanent deletion.
name: Insecure S3 Bucket Configurations

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified SSH service configurations on {{AFFECTED}} that deviated from current security guidance. The affected hosts supported one or more of the following: deprecated ciphers (RC4, 3DES, Blowfish), CBC-mode ciphers and Encrypt-then-MAC (EtM) algorithm combinations that contribute to CVE-2023-48795 (Terrapin), SHA-1-based key exchange and MAC algorithms, password-based authentication on internet-facing ports, and direct root login.

The Terrapin attack requires an active man-in-the-middle position between SSH client and server. Under the right combination of advertised algorithms — servers offering chacha20-poly1305 or CBC-plus-EtM combinations without strict key exchange — an attacker can modify the SSH connection setup sequence to suppress security extensions or downgrade negotiated algorithm choices. The team verified the contributing algorithm combinations using a verbose SSH client connection against each affected host and confirmed the server's advertised algorithm set without attempting active exploitation.

Password authentication on internet-facing services exposes login endpoints to credential stuffing and brute-force attacks. Allowing direct root login means a successful credential attack immediately yields full administrative control.

Variants

Password Authentication: The assessment team identified {number} SSH configurations on internet-facing hosts permitting password-based authentication, increasing exposure to automated credential attacks against privileged accounts.

Terrapin Attack: The affected SSH servers advertised algorithm combinations that contribute to CVE-2023-48795. Exploitation requires an active man-in-the-middle position at connection time.

Weak Cipher Usage: The assessment team found three external servers on ports 830 and 22 advertising RC4, 3DES, and Blowfish ciphers. These have been deprecated in current SSH guidance and are no longer considered adequate for session confidentiality.

# Impact

An SSH configuration advertising deprecated ciphers, weak hash algorithms, or Terrapin-contributing algorithm combinations increases the attack surface for an adversary with a network position between client and server. Password authentication on internet-facing ports gives automated attacks a direct path to credential compromise. Permitting direct root login means a compromised password yields full host access without requiring any privilege escalation step.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable the ssh-rsa host key algorithm and replace it with rsa-sha2-256, rsa-sha2-512, ssh-ed25519, or an ECDSA variant. Update associated client key files accordingly.
  • Remove SHA-1-based and MD5-based key exchange and MAC algorithms, including diffie-hellman-group14-sha1, diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1, hmac-sha1, hmac-sha1-96, hmac-md5, and their EtM variants.
  • Disable RC4 (arcfour, arcfour128, arcfour256), 3DES (3des-cbc, 3des-ctr), and Blowfish (blowfish-cbc) ciphers.
  • To address Terrapin: disable CBC-mode ciphers and EtM MAC algorithms, remove chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com where strict key exchange is not enforced, and enable strict key exchange in the SSH server configuration.
  • Replace password-based authentication with public key authentication on all internet-facing SSH services. Set PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config.
  • Set PermitRootLogin no in sshd_config on all hosts. Require administrators to authenticate under a named account and escalate to root using sudo for elevated operations.
name: Insecure SSH Service Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified SSL/TLS certificates on {{COMPANY_NAME}} infrastructure that were misconfigured in one or more of the following ways: self-signed, expired, revoked, deployed on a domain other than the one named in the certificate, or generated before their stated validity start date. The team also identified certificates with validity periods exceeding 27 months, RSA keys below 2048 bits, and signature algorithms using MD5 or SHA-1.

Client software cannot distinguish between a misconfigured legitimate certificate and a fraudulent one. Both produce the same warning or error in browsers and API clients. As a result, users and automated systems confronted with a certificate warning may accept it regardless of cause, producing the same exposure they would face with an attacker's forged certificate in a man-in-the-middle position.

Certificates using SHA-1 or MD5 signatures are subject to collision attacks: an attacker with sufficient computational resources can forge a certificate that passes hash verification against the same CA signature. Certificates with small RSA keys are susceptible to factoring. Both conditions are more accessible to well-resourced attackers than when these algorithms were in common use.

# Impact

A certificate that clients cannot trust removes server identity verification from the TLS handshake. Without verified server identity, a client has no basis for distinguishing the legitimate server from an attacker-controlled host at the same address. Weak signature algorithms and undersized keys reduce the computational cost of certificate forgery, narrowing the gap between a valid certificate and one an attacker can produce.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace all self-signed, expired, and revoked certificates with certificates issued by a trusted CA. For internal services, deploy the issuing CA as a trusted root on corporate endpoints.
  • Confirm that each certificate is issued for the hostname where it is deployed. Do not reuse a certificate across different domains.
  • Generate new certificates with validity periods no greater than 27 months for DV and OV certificates.
  • Use RSA keys of at least 2048 bits or prefer ECDSA keys on the P-256 or P-384 curve.
  • Use SHA-256 or stronger as the signature algorithm. Do not generate certificates with SHA-1 or MD5 signatures.
  • Automate certificate renewal to prevent expiry-driven outages.
name: Insecure SSL/TLS Certificate Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s infrastructure advertised deprecated SSL and TLS protocol versions and cipher suites with known weaknesses. The team identified support for SSL 2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1, along with cipher suites using RC4, DES, 3DES, export-grade RSA, and anonymous authentication modes on external and internal services.

The protocol and cipher combinations found expose the environment to the following attacks:

  • POODLE: CBC-mode ciphers over SSL 3 allow a man-in-the-middle to decrypt chosen blocks of an SSL session through adaptive chosen-boundary manipulation.
  • BEAST: CBC-mode ciphers over TLS 1.0 allow an attacker with a predictable-prefix injection point to recover plaintext from an active session.
  • FREAK: Export-grade RSA suites can be forced by a man-in-the-middle, reducing session key size to a range factorable in hours.
  • Logjam: Short Diffie-Hellman parameters allow a man-in-the-middle to downgrade key exchange to 512 bits, which has been precomputed at a national level.
  • Sweet32: 3DES and Blowfish use 64-bit blocks; birthday collisions become feasible in long-lived sessions, enabling plaintext recovery.
  • DROWN: SSL 2 support on any server sharing an RSA private key with HTTPS hosts allows offline decryption of captured TLS 1.x sessions.
  • Bar Mitzvah: RC4's invariance weakness allows statistical recovery of the first 100 bytes of a session — typically session tokens — across many observed connections.

Variants

Heroku: The assessment team found applications in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Heroku environment that did not enforce TLS on private-space network traffic, allowing service-to-service communication without transport encryption.

# Impact

Deprecated SSL/TLS versions and their associated cipher suites expose session traffic to a class of attacks that require only a network position between client and server. Several — POODLE, FREAK, Logjam, DROWN — allow a man-in-the-middle to force weaker cryptography and then decrypt or modify session content. Others — Bar Mitzvah, Sweet32 — allow statistical recovery of session tokens or plaintext across multiple observed connections. All are enabled by the server advertising algorithms the security community has deprecated.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable SSL 2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1 on all services. Where legacy client compatibility is a stated constraint, use server-side usage data to assess impact before disabling.
  • Remove cipher suites using RC4, DES, 3DES, anonymous authentication modes, and export-grade RSA. Restrict to TLS 1.2 AEAD suites (AES-GCM, CHACHA20-POLY1305) and TLS 1.3 cipher groups.
  • Disable CBC-mode cipher suites. Enable TLS 1.3 on all services that support it.
  • Enable TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV to prevent protocol downgrade attacks.
  • Disable TLS-level and HTTP-level compression on all services.
  • If TLS 1.3 is not available, configure the server to reject client-initiated session renegotiation.
  • Use the Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator to produce a server-specific hardened configuration based on your server version and available library support.
name: Insecure SSL/TLS Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} iOS application cached HTTP request and response data — including JWT session tokens and payment tokens — in an unencrypted SQLite database on the device. The cached data persisted in Library/Caches/{package_name}/Cache.db inside the application sandbox after the user exited the application.

The team queried the cache database and confirmed that the storage_policy column for the {endpoint} endpoint was set to 0, indicating the iOS NSURLCache system operated with its default caching behavior and no restrictions. The team extracted the cached request and response objects, decoded the JWT tokens stored in them, and confirmed that session credentials and internal user data encoded in the token payload were recoverable from the cache file directly.

On a non-jailbroken device, accessing the sandbox requires specialized tooling or a device backup. On a jailbroken device, the cache database is directly readable by any process with root access.

# Impact

The iOS NSURLCache system caches HTTP requests and responses in a SQLite database inside the application sandbox by default. If the server does not instruct the client to avoid caching sensitive responses and the client does not override the cache policy for sensitive requests, authentication tokens accumulate in a cleartext file on the device filesystem. An attacker with physical access to the device, access to a backup, or root access on a jailbroken device can read these tokens and replay them to access the application as the affected user.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store to HTTP responses from any endpoint that sends or receives authentication tokens, payment data, or other sensitive values. This prevents NSURLCache from storing the response regardless of the client-side cache policy.
  • Set the NSURLRequest cache policy to ReloadIgnoringLocalCacheData in the iOS client for all requests that handle sensitive data.
  • Clear the NSURLCache shared cache on application termination and on user logout to remove any data that was not prevented by the above controls.
name: Insecure Sensitive Data Caching

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified weaknesses in the {application_name} application's account registration flow that allowed creation or manipulation of accounts in ways the application did not intend.

# Impact

Insecure account registration allows an attacker to create accounts that bypass intended access controls, register under another user's identity, or obtain accounts with elevated permissions through manipulation of the sign-up request. Depending on the specific flaw, this can result in unauthorized access to another user's data, persistent access to the application under a fraudulently created identity, or privilege escalation from registration.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Validate all registration fields server-side. Do not trust client-supplied values for account type, role, or privilege level.
  • Confirm ownership of the supplied email address before activating the account, using a single-use verification link with a short expiration window.
  • Apply rate limiting to the registration endpoint to prevent bulk account creation.
  • Log all registration events with sufficient context — source IP, timestamp, supplied email address — to support investigation of fraudulent account creation.
name: Insecure Sign-Up

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found Elasticsearch instances in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment with dynamic scripting enabled and the cluster API on port 9200 accessible without authentication. The team sent a search request containing embedded Groovy scripts and confirmed execution on the host — reading /etc/hosts and /etc/passwd directly through the scripted query response.

The team staged a JAR payload using the same script execution channel, executed it on the Elasticsearch host, and established a shell. From that position, the team retrieved IAM credentials from the EC2 instance metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254. Because the cluster's requests were load-balanced across multiple hosts, the team issued repeated staging requests to ensure the payload reached all nodes in the cluster.

Variants

DNS: The assessment team found DNS services on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network that responded to root-zone queries with amplified responses more than three times the request size, enabling use of these resolvers as reflectors in DNS amplification attacks.

Drupal Installation: The assessment team found an unfinished Drupal installation accessible to unauthenticated external users. An attacker could complete the installation and gain administrative access to the application and its underlying database.

# Impact

Elasticsearch with dynamic scripting enabled and no authentication accepts arbitrary Groovy code in search requests and executes it in the JVM context. Any host with network access to port 9200 can execute code as the Elasticsearch process account — without credentials and without exploiting any application-layer vulnerability. From the Elasticsearch host, access to the cloud metadata service allows recovery of IAM credentials that may provide access to other AWS resources in the environment.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable dynamic scripting by adding script.disable_dynamic: true to elasticsearch.yml on all nodes.
  • Restrict network access to the Elasticsearch API to the specific services with a documented operational requirement. The cluster API port must not be reachable from workstations, guest segments, or the public internet.
  • Deploy an authentication and authorization framework for the cluster — X-Pack Security or an equivalent control. Require credentials for all API operations.
name: Insecure Software Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {product} application passed user-supplied URL parameters as the first argument to Ruby's send and public_send functions without restricting the accepted method name. The team constructed requests that invoked internal methods the application did not intend to expose, achieved remote code execution on {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s infrastructure, recovered application credentials, and reached production customer data.

# Impact

Ruby's send and public_send functions call any method by name on the receiving object. When an application accepts the method name from external input, an attacker can invoke methods outside the intended call graph — including those that execute shell commands, read the filesystem, or call privileged internal functions. No memory corruption is required; the attack follows directly from treating a user-supplied string as a trusted method selector.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Do not pass external input as the first argument to send or public_send. Parse the input against an explicit list of permitted method names defined in the source code and call the selected method directly.
  • Validate any additional arguments passed to send or public_send against the expected type and format for the target method before the call is made.
name: Insecure Use of Ruby Send Functionality

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application stored user account passwords as plaintext in the database. The team accessed the database from the application host and confirmed that the password column contained recoverable credential strings for user accounts, including the account {user_account}.

The database was not accessible from remote hosts — only from the application host itself — which limited the exposure. Any process with local database access, or any attacker who obtains a shell on the application server, can read all stored passwords directly. Because users frequently reuse passwords, recovery from this application enables attacks against any other service where the same credentials are valid.

# Impact

Plaintext password storage means any database disclosure — through backup theft, local privilege escalation, or direct database access — immediately produces usable credentials for every account. A properly chosen hash cannot be reversed; plaintext can be read by anyone with access to the row. The exposure extends beyond the compromised application to every service where affected users reuse those passwords.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace plaintext storage with a memory-hard, one-way hashing algorithm designed for password storage — bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2. Do not use general-purpose cryptographic hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) for passwords; they are too fast and allow brute-force attacks that make weak passwords recoverable in minutes.
  • Apply a unique random salt to each password before hashing. Store the salt alongside the hash. This prevents precomputed rainbow table attacks and ensures that two users with identical passwords produce different stored hashes.
name: Insecure User Credential Storage

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {device_name} device's setup process used a Wi-Fi network whose security was insufficient to protect the credentials the mobile application transmitted during configuration.

In the WPA2-PSK scenario: the setup network used the device's MAC address as the pre-shared key. The team captured the MAC address by passively monitoring Wi-Fi traffic and used it to decrypt the mobile application's setup traffic in Wireshark, recovering the customer's home Wi-Fi network name and password.

In the open network scenario: the setup network had no encryption. The team captured the mobile application's HTTP POST to the device's setup API without decryption, observing the Wi-Fi SSID, password, and shared secret used for cloud API communication.

In the HTTPS-over-open-Wi-Fi scenario: the setup traffic was encrypted at the application layer with HTTPS, but the unencrypted Wi-Fi network meant an attacker with the device firmware — from which a static private key could be extracted — could either tamper with the setup process actively or, if the client negotiated RSA-based cipher suites without forward secrecy, decrypt captured traffic passively.

# Impact

A setup network that uses a predictable or passively observable key provides no meaningful protection for credentials transmitted during configuration. An attacker within Wi-Fi range can recover the customer's home network credentials without interacting with the device or the mobile application. Exposure of the cloud API shared secret allows the attacker to interact with the vendor's device APIs as the affected customer, reading or modifying their data and device settings.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Use a WPA2-PSK-protected setup network. The pre-shared key must be unique to each device and must not be derivable from any value passively observable on the network, including the MAC address, serial number, or device name.
  • Consider using Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) for the device pairing exchange instead of a Wi-Fi setup network. BLE's shorter range limits the physical area from which an attacker could intercept the setup, and a properly implemented BLE pairing flow can establish a secure channel before any credentials are transmitted.
name: Insecure Wi-Fi Setup Network

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {{COMPANY_NAME}} corporate wireless network used WPA2 Enterprise with PEAP authentication but did not configure a Certificate Authority (CA) certificate in the wireless client profiles. Without a CA certificate, clients cannot verify the identity of the Access Point they connect to. An attacker can stand up a rogue AP advertising the same SSID and capture credentials from clients that associate without identity verification.

The team created a rogue AP using freeradius-wpe and hostapd advertising the {ssid5} SSID. Within three minutes, a wireless client associated and submitted a username and PEAP challenge response, which the team captured.

Variants

WPA2-Enterprise: The assessment team found that the {ssid} wireless network was configured with WPA2 Enterprise authentication but without CA certificate validation enforced on client devices, allowing the team to capture credentials from a rogue AP within range of the network.

# Impact

When wireless clients do not validate the AP's certificate against a trusted CA, they connect to any AP advertising the target SSID. A rogue AP paired with a malicious RADIUS server captures PEAP challenge responses from connecting clients. These responses can be cracked offline to recover plaintext passwords that are typically valid for VPN, email, and internal applications using the same credential set.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Deploy EAP-TLS for all corporate wireless networks. Issue a unique certificate and private key to each authorized user or device. EAP-TLS requires mutual certificate validation and eliminates the credential-capture attack entirely.
  • If EAP-TLS cannot be deployed immediately, configure all wireless client profiles for PEAP-authenticated networks to require a specific CA certificate and validate the RADIUS server's identity against it. Distribute and enforce this configuration through MDM or group policy.
