  • Create a separate isolated wireless segment for devices that cannot support EAP or PEAP. Apply firewall rules limiting that segment to the minimum connectivity the device requires, rather than allowing it on the primary corporate network.
name: Insecure Wireless Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found sensitive API credentials embedded in JavaScript files served by the {application} application to unauthenticated users. The exposed values included an API username and password, HTTP headers required for API calls, an email-delivery authentication key, and a geolocation API key. Because the JavaScript was delivered to any browser that loaded the application, these credentials were publicly accessible without authentication.

Using the exposed API credentials, the team authenticated to the {application} API and queried the FHIR endpoint, confirming access to approximately 4,014,898 patient records containing protected health information (PHI). The email delivery key would allow an attacker to send messages appearing to originate from {email_address}. Combined with the available patient contact data, this creates a direct path for large-scale targeted phishing and social engineering campaigns.

The exposed credentials carried no IP restrictions, no scope restrictions, and no key isolation. A single broad-access key was shared across multiple integrations rather than purpose-limited keys for each use case.

# Impact

API credentials in client-side code are readable by any user who inspects the page source or captures network traffic. They cannot be revoked without replacing the code that contains them, and they may be indexed by search engines or code repositories. In this case, the exposed credentials provided direct access to millions of patient records and the ability to send email from a trusted domain — both of which carry regulatory consequences under HIPAA in addition to operational and reputational impact.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove all API credentials from client-side JavaScript immediately. Any credential currently embedded in client-served code should be treated as compromised and rotated.
  • Move all third-party API calls to a server-side proxy. Client code communicates with the proxy; the proxy holds the credentials and makes the upstream call. No credential reaches the browser.
  • Store all application credentials in a secrets management solution — HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or equivalent. Do not embed credentials in environment variables bundled into client-side builds.
  • Scope each API key to the minimum set of operations it requires. Create separate keys for each integration rather than sharing a single broad-access credential.
  • Restrict keys by source IP where the vendor supports it.
  • Integrate secret scanning into the CI/CD pipeline to detect credentials committed to source control or bundled into build artifacts before deployment.

Strategic Considerations

  • Monitor API usage for enumeration patterns and unusually high request volumes.
  • Define a credential rotation schedule and an incident response procedure specific to credential exposure events.
name: Insufficient API Credential Management

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that authentication endpoints in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment applied no rate limiting, lockout, or challenge to repeated login attempts. The team automated credential submissions against the login endpoint and, after roughly 2,000 attempts — approximately two per account — recovered valid credentials for six accounts. No countermeasure fired at any point during the attack.

The guessed passwords were variations on a common word that met the application's complexity policy. The absence of per-account and per-IP rate limiting allowed the full attempt set to complete without interruption.

# Impact

An authentication endpoint with no anti-automation controls accepts guesses at machine speed. An attacker with a list of usernames and a set of common password patterns can submit thousands of attempts per minute. Testing two guesses per account avoids per-account lockout thresholds while still reaching accounts that use predictable password patterns. Compromised accounts provide direct access to whatever data and functions the account holds.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Apply per-IP rate limiting to authentication endpoints. After a defined failure threshold from a single source, introduce exponential backoff delays before accepting the next attempt — this is more durable than a flat lockout window.
  • Present a CAPTCHA challenge after a threshold of failed attempts from the same IP or browser session, requiring human verification before accepting further submissions.
  • Require multi-factor authentication for all accounts with access to sensitive data or privileged operations. MFA makes a correct guessed password insufficient for login on its own.

Strategic Considerations

  • Use a CDN or WAF with bot-detection capabilities to absorb credential stuffing at scale before it reaches the application tier.
  • Restrict access to authentication portals backed by corporate credentials to known IP ranges or VPN egress points where those portals do not need to be publicly reachable.
name: Insufficient Anti-automation

Description:
# Description

The assessment team reviewed the {{COMPANY_NAME}} application as part of the App Defense Alliance's Cloud Application Security Assessment (CASA) program and determined that the application did not meet the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) requirements for CASA participation. The team identified failed test cases across the ASVS control areas.

The following test cases did not meet the ASVS requirements:

| Test Case | Description |
| --- | --- |
| 2.1.1 | Verify that user-set passwords are at least 12 characters in length. |
| {test_case} | {description} |

# Impact

Each failed ASVS test case represents a gap in the application's security controls against a class of attack the standard defines as a minimum baseline for applications handling sensitive user data. Failing CASA requirements indicates the application does not meet the threshold the App Defense Alliance requires for program participation.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remediate each failed ASVS test case identified in this report. Prioritize authentication, session management, and access control requirements before lower-tier cases.
  • Validate each remediation against the ASVS test procedure for the corresponding case before resubmitting for CASA review.
name: Insufficient Application Security Posture

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that authentication controls on {{AFFECTED}} did not prevent {attack_type}. The team exploited the gap to {impact_observed}.

Specifically, the team determined that {auth_control_detail}. The configuration allowed the team to {attack_method} without triggering lockout, a multi-factor challenge, or an alert.

# Impact

Authentication controls that fall below organizational or baseline requirements make credential guessing and replay more likely to succeed. Weak password complexity requirements allow common passwords to meet policy; absent lockout policies permit unlimited guesses; missing MFA requirements mean a stolen or guessed password is sufficient for access. Each gap reduces the cost of credential-based attacks; in combination they remove most of the friction from account compromise.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Configure password composition, expiry, and lockout settings on {hosts} to meet the requirements of the {benchmark_name} baseline.
  • Disable legacy authentication protocols identified in this finding after confirming that no remaining application depends on them.
  • Enforce multi-factor authentication for all accounts with administrative access.

Strategic Consideration

  • Enforce password policy centrally through {directory_service} so that a locally configured host cannot diverge from the organizational standard without a change management record.
name: Insufficient Authentication Controls

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that authorization controls in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment allowed access to resources and actions reserved for higher-privilege accounts. After compromising the {domain1} domain through a separate finding, the team identified domain controllers in that domain with an excessive number of accounts in the local Administrators group — including broad user groups that should not have held local admin rights on domain controllers.

Because local administrator access on a domain controller is functionally equivalent to domain admin access, the team connected as a low-privilege domain user to a server where domain users held local admin rights, ran secretsdump.py, and recovered NTLM hashes for additional accounts. The team then used a recovered hash through pass-the-hash to compromise the {domain2} domain controller without cracking the underlying password.

Variants

API Authorization Bypass: The assessment team found that an authenticated user could access any customer's asset data through the {api_name} API by substituting a different numeric resource identifier in the request URL. No ownership check was performed server-side.

Claude Code Session: The assessment team found that the claude_code workflow node in the {application_name} workflow engine did not enforce authorization checks on the calling identity before executing operations on the target system.

# Impact

Insufficient authorization controls allow an attacker who has obtained any authenticated access to perform operations or access data reserved for more privileged accounts. In the domain context, a path existed from any domain user account to full domain administrator access through intermediate systems with misconfigured local administrator group membership. In the API context, any authenticated user could access or modify another user's data by iterating resource identifiers.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove all users and groups except domain administrators from the local Administrators group on domain controllers.
  • Remove the {domain1domain} Users Active Directory group from the local Administrators group on {host} and any other host where a broad user group has been granted local admin access.

Strategic Considerations

  • Apply the principle of least privilege to all administrative account assignments. Use separate accounts for day-to-day work and for elevated operations. Use domain administrator accounts only to access domain controllers directly.
  • For API authorization, enforce resource ownership checks on every request server-side. Do not rely on the client to supply or withhold the owner's identifier; verify the requesting identity's relationship to the resource before returning or modifying it.
  • Monitor domain administrator accounts and accounts with local admin access to domain controllers for activity outside normal hours or locations.
name: Insufficient Authorization Controls

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that binaries in the {product} distribution were compiled without one or more OS-level exploit mitigation features. Affected Windows binaries lacked Control Flow Guard (CFG) and SafeSEH. Affected Linux binaries were compiled without stack canaries and FORTIFY_SOURCE. The team identified these gaps using Get-PESecurity on Windows binaries and checksec on Linux binaries. The team did not attempt to exploit any memory corruption condition during the assessment due to time constraints.

ASLR and DEP/NX were enabled on the affected binaries, which limits direct exploitation of stack overflows. However, absent CFG on the Windows binary substantially expands the set of return-oriented programming (ROP) gadgets available to an attacker who identifies a memory corruption condition, because CFG restricts indirect call targets at runtime. Without stack canaries on the Linux binary, a stack buffer overflow provides no automatic detection signal before control flow is redirected.

# Impact

Modern operating systems provide opt-in binary hardening features — ASLR, DEP, stack canaries, CFG, FORTIFY_SOURCE — that increase the difficulty of turning a memory corruption condition into reliable code execution. A binary compiled without these features is not inherently vulnerable, but any memory corruption bug present in it is more likely to be exploitable. The absence of these features raises the value of memory corruption bugs found in the software for an attacker targeting the deployment environment.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• For Visual Studio (Windows): enable /CETCOMPAT, /DYNAMICBASE, /HIGHENTROPYVA (64-bit targets), /NXCOMPAT, and /SAFESEH (32-bit x86 targets).
  • For GCC (Linux): add -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, -fpie -Wl,-pie, -fstack-clash-protection, -Wl,-z,relro, and one of the -fstack-protector variants (-fstack-protector-strong is a reasonable default). Add -fcf-protection=full on supported platforms.
  • For Clang: add -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, -fPIE, -fsanitize=safe-stack, and one of the -fstack-protector variants. Add -fcf-protection=full on platforms that support hardware CFI, or -fsanitize=cfi on those that do not.
name: Insufficient Binary Exploit Mitigation

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that branch protection rules on {{COMPANY_NAME}} source code repositories did not enforce the controls necessary to prevent unauthorized modification of branches that gate production deployments. Missing or misconfigured protections allowed contributors to push directly to protected branches, bypass required code review approvals, or dismiss existing approvals without re-review.

# Impact

Branches without adequate protection can be modified without peer review, required status checks, or change approvals. An attacker who compromises a developer account with push access, or a developer acting outside the intended process, can introduce changes to a protected branch that bypass the security review controls the organization put in place. In a CI/CD pipeline where a protected branch push triggers deployment, this provides a path from repository write access to code execution in production.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable branch protection on all branches that gate production or staging deployments. At minimum: require a pull request review by at least one approver who is not the author, and prevent force-push and deletion of the branch.
  • Require status checks to pass before merging, including automated tests, static analysis, and any required security scans in the CI pipeline.
  • Do not allow administrators to bypass branch protection rules. If emergency bypass is required, log and audit every instance.
  • Restrict the set of identities permitted to push directly to protected branches to the minimum required by the development workflow.
name: Insufficient Branch Protections

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} domains in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} portfolio with DMARC configurations in monitoring-only mode (p=none) or without aggregate reporting configured. Domains set to p=none instruct receiving mail servers to take no action on messages that fail SPF or DKIM authentication — spoofed email from these domains is delivered normally.

Within the p=none population, the team observed two postures. Several domains published aggregate reporting addresses (rua), providing visibility into authentication failures without enforcement. Others combined p=none with missing reporting addresses or permissive subdomain policies (sp=none), providing neither enforcement nor visibility into spoofing attempts against those domains.

The team also found domains enforcing p=reject without aggregate reporting configured. Those domains have strong enforcement but lack the visibility into authentication failures that would inform long-term policy maintenance and identification of misconfigured legitimate senders.

# Impact

A DMARC policy of p=none does not prevent spoofed email from reaching recipients. An attacker can send messages claiming to originate from the domain and most receiving servers will deliver them without rejection or spam classification. Combined with an SPF soft-fail qualifier, which marks unauthenticated senders as suspicious rather than rejecting them, these configurations provide no meaningful barrier against email-based impersonation.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Transition domains at p=none to p=quarantine, then to p=reject, once DMARC aggregate reports confirm that all legitimate sending sources pass authentication. Monitor reports for false positives before tightening the policy.
  • Enable rua aggregate reporting on all domains, including those already enforcing p=reject. Aggregate reports identify misconfigured senders and attempted spoofing.
  • Establish a baseline DMARC policy for the domain portfolio and document approved deviations with a business justification and a review date.
  • Review SPF and DKIM alignment settings to confirm they are appropriate for each domain's sending profile. Tighten from relaxed to strict alignment where the infrastructure supports it.
  • Include DMARC configuration in the recurring email infrastructure maintenance cycle to catch records that drift as vendors and sending services change.
name: Insufficient DMARC Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that RDS instances in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment were deployed in a single availability zone without Multi-AZ replication. An availability zone failure — hardware fault, facility incident, or regional AWS event — would take the affected database instances offline until the zone recovered, with no automatic failover to a secondary instance.

# Impact

A single-AZ RDS instance has no redundancy. When the availability zone hosting the instance is unavailable, the database is unavailable. For services with uptime or recovery time requirements, this is a single point of failure that AWS Multi-AZ deployment is designed to address. The impact depends on which services depend on the affected instances and how long those services can tolerate an outage before business operations are affected.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation: • Enable Multi-AZ deployment for all RDS instances that support services with uptime or recovery time requirements. Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby in a separate availability zone and promotes it automatically on primary failure, typically within one to two minutes.
name: Insufficient Database Replication

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {{DOMAIN}} domain's email authentication configuration did not enforce rejection or quarantine of unauthenticated messages. The SPF record used a soft-fail qualifier (~all) and the DMARC record was set to p=none with no forensic reporting address. A message claiming to originate from {{DOMAIN}} sent from any unauthorized server would be delivered by most receiving mail servers without quarantine or rejection.

The SPF record also contained a duplicate include: entry, consuming one of the ten permitted DNS lookups without adding any coverage. A DKIM selector was configured and mail was routing through Microsoft 365, confirming the underlying authentication infrastructure is in place. The gap is in enforcement policy, not in the availability of the authentication mechanisms.

Variants

AWS: The assessment team found email protection features not enabled for identities in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment, leaving those identities without SPF or DKIM authentication for outbound mail.

# Impact

SPF soft-fail and DMARC p=none together provide no enforcement against email spoofing from the domain. An attacker can send from any server, claim the domain as the sender, and most receiving mail servers will deliver the message to the inbox. The domain name carries trust with employees, customers, and partners — trust a spoofed message inherits without any authentication check blocking delivery.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Change the DMARC policy from p=none to p=quarantine, then to p=reject after monitoring aggregate reports for false positives. Configure rua and ruf reporting addresses before tightening the policy.
  • Change the SPF qualifier from ~all (soft fail) to -all (hard fail) to instruct receiving servers to reject mail from senders not listed in the record.
  • Remove the duplicate include: entry from the SPF record to reduce DNS lookup consumption.

Strategic Consideration

  • Coordinate the DMARC enforcement timeline with any email infrastructure migration or integration work. A strict policy applied mid-migration without confirming all legitimate sending sources can suppress valid mail from newly onboarded services.
name: Insufficient Email Protections

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined through interviews with {team_name} development teams that no formal, organization-wide guidance existed specifying how incoming data should be validated before use. Individual teams had developed informal practices, but there was no shared standard for validation at trust boundaries, no requirements for specific checks by data type, and no guidance directing back-end services to validate data pulled from queues or databases.

The absence of a shared standard means that validation coverage depends on individual developer judgment, producing inconsistent behavior across services and increasing the likelihood of an unvalidated path to a sensitive operation.

# Impact

Without explicit validation requirements, different services handle the same class of input differently. Attacker-controlled data that passes through a service with weak validation can reach a second service that trusts input from the first. The absence of a standardized library or framework for common validation also means the same logic is implemented independently across services, creating inconsistency and raising the probability of logic errors that an attacker can exploit.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Define and publish input validation requirements for each data type the application handles: string length, allowed character sets, numeric ranges, and format patterns. Make these requirements explicit — do not leave them to developer interpretation.
  • Specify which service is responsible for validating each input at each trust boundary. Do not assume data from an internal queue or database has already been validated by the producer; validate at each consumption point.
  • Designate a shared validation library or framework module for common checks. Require its use rather than allowing each service to implement its own version.
  • Include validation requirements in code review checklists and development standards so that gaps are caught before code ships.
name: Insufficient Input Validation Guidance

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that logging options available in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment were not fully enabled. The team identified S3 buckets without server access logging, ELBs without access logging, VPC subnets without flow log capture, and Redshift clusters without activity logging. CloudTrail log file validation was also not enabled, and in some configurations global service activity was not being recorded.

Without these logs, the {{COMPANY_NAME}} security team lacks visibility into access patterns for stored objects, load-balanced traffic, network flows, and database queries. Incident investigations depend on records that document what happened, when, under which identity, and from where.

Variants

GCP: The assessment team found logging options available but unused in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} GCP environment, including Cloud Audit Logs and VPC flow logs not enabled for services handling sensitive data.

Heroku: The assessment team found applications in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Heroku environment without a logging add-on configured. Platform-level logs were unavailable for these applications for investigation and monitoring purposes.

# Impact

Logs that are not collected are not available for incident investigation. When an attacker reads stored objects, moves through load-balanced services, or queries a database, evidence of those actions lives in access logs, flow logs, and audit trails. If those records do not exist, the investigation cannot establish what was accessed, how the attacker moved, or how long they had access. CloudTrail log file validation, when disabled, means a tampered log file is indistinguishable from an authentic one.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable CloudTrail with log file validation and global service logging in all regions where {{COMPANY_NAME}} operates AWS resources.
  • Enable S3 server access logging on all buckets that store sensitive data or are accessed by production workloads.
  • Enable ELB access logging on all load balancers.
  • Enable VPC flow logs on all subnets in use.
  • Enable activity logging on all Redshift clusters.
  • Forward all AWS logs to the {{COMPANY_NAME}} centralized logging infrastructure for monitoring, alerting, and retention.
name: Insufficient Logging

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the Kubernetes clusters in scope did not adequately restrict pod network egress. Depending on the cluster, either no network policy engine was installed — leaving all network policy objects inert — or an installed engine was configured with policies that did not restrict pod access to control plane services, the cloud metadata endpoint, or the public internet.

In the cluster without a network policy engine, the team confirmed that a pod in the default namespace could reach the kubelet service on worker nodes at port 10250. In the cluster with an installed but insufficiently restrictive policy engine, the team accessed the AWS metadata service from a pod using the worker node's attached IAM role, listed the contents of a private S3 bucket, and confirmed internet egress by fetching an external URL. In a separate demonstration, the team established a reverse shell from a pod to a team-controlled external host, confirming that pods could initiate outbound connections to arbitrary internet addresses.

# Impact

Without network policies enforced by an active engine, pods can reach any endpoint within the cluster and, absent external controls, the internet. Access to the cloud metadata endpoint from a compromised pod allows an attacker to retrieve IAM credentials attached to the worker node, which may grant access to S3 buckets, databases, or other cloud resources. Access to the kubelet port provides a path to execute commands in other pods on the same node. Unconstrained internet egress enables data exfiltration and command-and-control channels that bypass cluster-level controls entirely.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Install a network policy engine — Calico is well-supported on EKS and most self-managed clusters — if one is not already active. Network policy objects have no effect without an engine to enforce them.
  • Define NetworkPolicy objects that restrict ingress and egress for each workload namespace to the minimum connections required for the application to function. Deny all traffic not explicitly permitted by a policy.
  • Block pod access to the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) from all namespaces that do not require instance metadata. Use a network policy egress rule, or the cloud provider's pod-identity controls (IRSA, Workload Identity), to scope metadata access to specific workloads only.
  • Restrict outbound internet access from pods to only the external endpoints required by each workload. Log denied egress connections for monitoring.
name: Insufficient Network Security Policies

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified unpatched software on {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} hosts during the host-based review of {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s environment. Affected packages included {library_or_application} at version {current_version}, which carries {cve_id} with a published CVSS score of {cvss_score}. In several cases, patches had been available for {days_outstanding} days or more with no corresponding update applied.

# Impact

Unpatched software gives attackers a known path to exploit. Public proof-of-concept code for many CVEs appears within days of disclosure, so a slow patch cycle is a reliable entry point. Each deferred update widens the exploitable attack surface.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Update all affected packages to their current stable release. Where possible, enforce patching through an automated patch management system on a defined schedule rather than relying on manual review.
  • Remove software that serves no active function. Unused packages accumulate vulnerabilities and cannot be kept current without a clear owner.
  • Establish a tiered remediation SLA: critical and high CVEs patched within {critical_days} days of vendor disclosure, medium within {medium_days} days.
  • Subscribe to vendor security advisories for all software in the environment and route alerts to the team responsible for patching decisions.
name: Insufficient Patch Management

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined that Kubernetes clusters in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s environment lacked enforceable pod admission controls. The clusters used the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy controller—removed in Kubernetes 1.25—and the only active policy, {policy_name}, permitted all privileged operations. Any principal with pod-creation rights could deploy workloads with hostPID, hostNetwork, hostIPC, privileged: true, or hostPath set, each of which provides a distinct path to node compromise.

The team created a pod with all permissive properties enabled, mounted the node filesystem at /host, and located a service account token with cluster-admin privileges. Using that token, the team confirmed full access to every namespace and all secrets across the cluster.

# Impact

An admission controller that permits privileged pod properties allows any workload to interact with the host kernel, mount host filesystems, or observe all host network traffic. Any one of the five sensitive properties—hostPID, hostIPC, hostNetwork, privileged, or hostPath—is sufficient to break container isolation and gain control of the underlying node, which reaches every secret the cluster holds.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy controller with the built-in PodSecurity admission controller or a third-party policy engine such as OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno. Configure the policy to enforce the restricted Pod Security Standard at minimum.
  • Deny pods that set hostPID, hostIPC, hostNetwork, privileged: true, or hostPath volumes unless a documented exception has been reviewed and approved.
  • Require all containers to run as non-root and set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false in all security contexts.
  • Set read-only root filesystems on containers where the application permits it. Mount writable volumes explicitly at the paths the application requires.
name: Insufficient Pod Admission Control

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {system_name} system disk stored all data in plaintext, without partition-level or full-disk encryption. The team removed one drive from the mirrored pair, connected it to an external host, and mounted all partitions without any decryption step. The rootfs partition exposed operating-system files and the {data_partition} partition exposed {data_description}. From those partitions, the team extracted {credential_type} credentials and file encryption keys referenced in the {related_finding} findings included in this report.

# Impact

A device that stores data without encryption cannot prevent disclosure when an attacker gains physical access to the storage medium. Removing a drive and mounting it on another host takes minutes and requires no specialized tooling. All data on the drive is readable to whoever holds it, including credentials, keys, and customer records.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• {linux} Enable LUKS full-disk encryption on all partitions. Configure the bootloader to unseal the decryption key from the onboard TPM during secure boot so the device boots unattended under normal conditions but refuses to decrypt on untrusted hardware.
  • {windows} Enable BitLocker on all volumes, tied to the TPM, with a recovery key stored securely outside the device.
  • Apply the Insecure Bootloader Configuration remediation described in this report before enabling disk encryption. Without a verified boot chain, an attacker can boot an alternate OS that reads the TPM-sealed key and bypasses the encryption entirely.
name: Insufficient Protection of Data at Rest

Description:
# Description

The assessment team reviewed {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s CI/CD pipeline through technical interviews and documentation review. Three categories of automated security control were absent. First, dependencies were not scanned for known vulnerabilities when code was merged; no tooling blocked or flagged pull requests that introduced packages with published CVEs. Second, static application security testing was not triggered on new pull requests, so code reached the main branch before any automated review identified common vulnerability patterns. Third, custom Semgrep rules the security team had written were not integrated into the pipeline; they existed but ran only on demand, with no enforcement gate.

# Impact

A CI/CD pipeline without security gates allows vulnerabilities to merge and deploy unchecked. The later in the development cycle a defect is caught, the more it costs to fix. A dependency scanner that only runs on demand is not a control—it is a manual step that gets skipped under schedule pressure.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add a dependency-scanning step to the pipeline that runs on every pull request and blocks merges when packages with CVEs above a defined severity threshold are detected. Tools such as Dependabot, Snyk, or OSV-Scanner integrate directly as pipeline steps.
  • Configure SAST to run automatically on all pull requests. Tools such as Semgrep, Bandit, or Brakeman can post results directly to the pull request as inline comments.
  • Promote the custom Semgrep rules into a required pipeline gate. Rules that do not block the pipeline are advisory at best; they will be ignored under deadline pressure.
name: Insufficient Protections in CI/CD Pipeline

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified IAM roles in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s AWS environment whose trust policies allowed third-party services to assume them without requiring an external ID or MFA. A role's ARN is a static identifier. If a third-party provider knows the ARN, any customer of that provider can instruct the provider to assume the role—not only {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Without an external ID or MFA requirement, the third-party service cannot distinguish a legitimate request originating from {{COMPANY_NAME}} from one submitted by an attacker who supplies the same ARN.

# Impact

An AssumeRole trust policy without an external ID or MFA condition is susceptible to the confused deputy problem. Any customer of the trusted third party can trigger an assumption of the role by supplying the role ARN. The third-party service acts on the instruction without confirming the requestor is the intended account holder, granting temporary credentials scoped to the role's full set of permissions.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Require an external ID on all IAM roles that third-party services can assume. The external ID must be provisioned and managed by the third party, not {{COMPANY_NAME}}. The trust policy Condition block should enforce sts:ExternalId against the provider-assigned value.
  • Alternatively, require MFA on external AssumeRole calls using the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition key where the third-party workflow supports it.
  • Audit all cross-account and third-party trust policies. Remove or update any that grant AssumeRole to an external principal without at least one of these controls.
name: Insufficient Protections on External AssumeRole Policy

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {policy_name} IAM policy granted iam:PassRole with a wildcard resource. Combined with ec2:RunInstances, this let any principal assigned the policy create an EC2 instance and attach any role in the account to it, including roles with more privileges than the principal held. The team created an EC2 instance, attached a role with broader read permissions, retrieved temporary credentials from the instance metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/{role_name}, and confirmed access to resources the original principal could not reach directly.

# Impact

iam:PassRole with a wildcard resource is a privilege escalation primitive. A principal with this permission and the ability to launch EC2 instances can associate any role in the account with a new instance and retrieve its credentials from the metadata service. The escalation path succeeds whenever a more privileged role has a trust policy that allows ec2.amazonaws.com to assume it.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace the wildcard resource in the iam:PassRole policy statement with a list of specific role ARNs the principal is authorized to pass.
  • Where named ARNs are impractical, scope the policy using an IAM path condition to prevent principals in one team from passing roles that belong to another.
  • Use tools such as Policy Sentry, Cloudsplaining, or PMapper to enumerate all PassRole grants in the account and identify privilege escalation paths.
  • Document each policy's intended PassRole scope in the role description field so reviewers can validate permissions without reconstructing the original use case.
name: Insufficient Restriction on PassRole Permission

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined that the in-scope Kubernetes cluster did not restrict container images to an approved internal registry. The team deployed a pod using the kalilinux/kali-rolling image pulled directly from Docker Hub. The pod started successfully and ran with the same networking and filesystem access as any other workload on the node.

# Impact

Pulling images from public registries without verification allows workloads to run arbitrary code that was never reviewed or approved. An attacker who obtains pod-creation rights can deploy pre-built attack tooling by naming a public image, bypassing all internal software supply chain controls. Public images can also carry malware or backdoors introduced through a compromised upstream build.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enforce an image source policy using a validating admission controller such as OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno. The policy should deny pods whose images do not originate from approved internal registries.
  • Require that all images added to the internal registry pass a security review and are scanned for known vulnerabilities before promotion to the approved list.
  • Require cryptographic signing and signature verification for all images used in the cluster. Cosign with a policy enforced at admission time is one approach to ensuring only signed, verified images run.
name: Insufficient Restriction on Third-Party Images

Description:
# Description

The assessment team discovered IAM policies in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s AWS environment that granted iam:PassRole with a wildcard resource to non-administrative principals. In one escalation path, the team used ec2:RunInstances and iam:PassRole to create an EC2 instance, attach the {role_name} role, retrieve temporary credentials from the instance metadata service, and read all objects in the {bucket_name} S3 bucket, which contained personally identifiable information. In a second path, the team exploited an EKS node role with the same misconfiguration to escalate from the development account to administrative access in the production account, using trust relationships identified during the assessment.

# Impact

iam:PassRole without a restricted resource list enables privilege escalation to any role in the account whose trust policy allows the relevant AWS service to assume it. The attacker needs only the ability to create a resource that can assume the role—an EC2 instance, Lambda function, or CloudFormation stack—to inherit its permissions. Cross-account trust relationships compound this: administrative access in a development account becomes a stepping stone to production.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Scope all iam:PassRole grants to the minimum set of role ARNs the principal needs to pass. Replace wildcard resources with explicit ARN lists or IAM path conditions.
  • Run Cloudsplaining or PMapper against the account to enumerate privilege escalation paths before and after changes are applied.
  • Audit cross-account trust policies and remove any that allow a principal in a lower-privilege account to assume an administrative role in a higher-privilege account unless the relationship is documented and approved.
  • Integrate iam:PassRole scope validation into the deployment pipeline so new policies are reviewed before they reach production.
name: Insufficient Restrictions on IAM PassRole

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified an overly permissive Kubernetes RBAC configuration in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s cluster. A service account in the {namespace_name} namespace was bound to a ClusterRole via a ClusterRoleBinding, granting it permissions across all namespaces including the ability to create pods in kube-system. Any user who could read secrets in {namespace_name} could retrieve that service account's token, impersonate the account, and use its cluster-wide permissions to deploy a pod in kube-system, steal the default service account token there, and obtain cluster-admin rights.

The team logged in as a low-privileged user, retrieved the {service_account_name} token, listed pods in kube-system using that token, and launched a pod that established a reverse shell to a team-controlled server, confirming full cluster access.

# Impact

RBAC ClusterRoleBindings that grant namespace-scoped service accounts cluster-wide permissions allow any principal who can access the account's token to escalate to cluster-admin. No application vulnerability is required—only access to the token and the ability to create pods.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace ClusterRoleBindings for service accounts that operate within a single namespace with RoleBindings scoped to that namespace. A service account that only manages resources in {namespace_name} should never hold cluster-wide permissions.
  • Audit all ClusterRoleBindings and remove any that grant broad permissions to non-kube-system service accounts without a documented architectural justification.
  • Apply least privilege when defining roles: enumerate the exact verbs, resources, and API groups the workload requires and grant nothing beyond that.
  • Review RBAC configurations on a scheduled basis. Permissions that accumulate without periodic review tend toward excess over time.
name: Insufficient Role-based Access Control

Description:
# Description

The assessment team reviewed SPF records across {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} domains associated with {{COMPANY_NAME}} and identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} with weak or incomplete configurations. Most used a soft-fail qualifier (~all), which signals a policy preference without instructing receiving servers to reject unauthorized senders. Several omitted an all mechanism entirely, leaving no explicit guidance on how receiving servers should handle unauthenticated senders. In both cases, spoofed messages can pass or arrive with a warning rather than a rejection, depending on the recipient's filtering policy.

The affected records correctly enumerated legitimate sending infrastructure—the problem was the enforcement directive, not the sender inventory. Affected domains included both primary-brand and subsidiary or legacy domains. Combined with permissive DMARC policies, weak SPF enforcement leaves these domains open to phishing and impersonation attacks.

# Impact

SPF with a soft-fail or absent all mechanism does not prevent spoofing; it defers the enforcement decision to the receiving server's heuristics, which vary by provider. An attacker can send email appearing to originate from an affected {{DOMAIN}} and have it delivered, or delivered with a low-priority warning, to targets whose mail infrastructure does not enforce strict DMARC policy.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Audit all sending sources for each affected domain: transactional mail providers, marketing platforms, and any third-party services that send on the domain's behalf. Confirm each is listed in the SPF record.
  • Replace ~all with -all on each domain once the sender inventory is verified. A hard-fail directive instructs receiving servers to reject mail from unlisted sources outright.
  • For domains that send no email, publish v=spf1 -all with no include or ip4 mechanisms to block all spoofing attempts from those domains.
  • Pair strong SPF enforcement with a DMARC policy of p=reject or p=quarantine to ensure consistent enforcement across receiving infrastructure that may not honor SPF alone.
  • Schedule quarterly SPF record audits to catch drift introduced by new third-party services or discontinued sending sources.
name: Insufficient SPF Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a sandbox bypass in the claude_code workflow node running inside a Firecracker microVM on {application_name}, reachable at POST {target_url} on {target_host}. The sandbox restricted file access through a PreToolUse:Read hook that blocked reads outside the assigned workspace directory. The Bash tool was not subject to any equivalent control. The team submitted a task instructing the agent to read /etc/passwd using a Python one-liner through the Bash tool and received the file's full contents—a file the Read tool had previously refused to open with the message "Path /etc/passwd is outside the workspace."

The team also observed that the workflowOverride object in the request body accepted user-supplied node configuration from a standard authenticated account, including permissionMode: bypassPermissions, maxTurns, and allowedNetworkDomains—settings normally reserved for administrative contexts.

# Impact

A sandbox that restricts one execution mechanism while leaving an equivalent one unrestricted fails to contain the confined actor. Any tool that can run a shell command or interpreter reaches the same filesystem paths as the blocked tool. The Read hook in this case created the appearance of a control while a single Bash invocation bypassed it completely. Controls that are not applied consistently across every execution path fail closed on the paper but open in practice.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enforce the workspace boundary at the OS layer inside the microVM, not at the agent tool layer. Run the agent process under an unprivileged user account inside a dedicated mount namespace where the workspace directory is the only readable and writable path. Mount the rest of the root filesystem read-only or omit it entirely. Any subprocess the agent starts—shell, interpreter, or compiled binary—then inherits the restriction without per-tool configuration.
  • Extend the PreToolUse hook to cover every tool that can access the filesystem or start a process: Bash, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, subagent invocation, and any configured MCP tools. Build the hook as a default-deny allowlist so a newly added or renamed tool fails closed rather than open.
  • Reject user-supplied node configuration in the workflowOverride request body. Fields such as permissionMode, allowedNetworkDomains, maxTurns, and timeoutMs should be controlled by the server, not the authenticated caller.
name: Insufficient Sandbox Protection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team reviewed {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s software development lifecycle through interviews with engineering and security leads and examination of available policy documentation. The SDLC lacked four categories of security process: threat modeling was not performed during feature design; secure coding standards existed at a general level but did not specify which patterns were required or prohibited by language; security-focused code review was not a required step before merging; and security test cases covering authorization and input validation were absent from the test suite.

# Impact

A development lifecycle without security gates produces applications where vulnerabilities are found in production rather than during design or review. Each missing gate—threat model, secure coding standard, security review, security test—is a point where a class of defects passes through unchallenged. Defects found in production cost significantly more to remediate than those caught during design.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Require threat modeling for all new features and significant architectural changes. Make a completed threat model a prerequisite for moving a feature from design to development, with a named owner for each model.
  • Adopt language-specific secure coding standards that enumerate required patterns and prohibited ones. Generic guidelines do not give developers actionable direction.
  • Add a security-focused checkpoint to the existing code review process. Define a checklist of controls reviewers must confirm—authorization boundaries, input validation, secrets handling—before approval.
  • Write automated security test cases for access control and malicious input scenarios. Run these tests in the existing test suite on every build, not only during scheduled security reviews.
name: Insufficient Secure SDLC Processes

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined through interviews with {{COMPANY_NAME}} leadership that the IT organization had approximately {headcount} personnel, none dedicated exclusively to information security. Security responsibilities were distributed across IT staff as secondary duties alongside their primary operational work. The organization had no designated security leader—no CISO, no Information Security Officer—with authority over the security program or representation in strategic planning and risk decisions.

# Impact

Security functions performed as secondary duties by generalist IT staff are deferred when operational workloads compete for time. Threat monitoring, vulnerability management, incident response, and compliance oversight each require sustained attention to be effective. Without dedicated personnel, these functions run at reduced capacity or not at all. Incidents that go undetected longer are costlier to remediate and carry greater reputational and regulatory exposure.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Establish at least one full-time information security role with clear authority over the security program. Title and span of control should match the organization's size and regulatory obligations.
  • Conduct a security staffing assessment to determine the appropriate headcount based on {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s risk profile, technology footprint, and compliance requirements.
  • Integrate security representation into executive decision-making. Security considerations should be present when strategic and technology decisions are made, not applied after the fact.
  • Engage a managed security service provider as an interim measure while building internal capability. Define explicitly which functions the provider covers and which remain internal responsibility.

Strategic Considerations

  • Build a multi-year staffing plan aligned with organizational growth. Security needs scale with system complexity and data sensitivity.
  • Budget for ongoing training and professional development. The threat landscape changes; the team's knowledge needs to keep pace.
name: Insufficient Security Staffing

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {compliance_framework} security controls that were absent or had no verifiable compensating control across {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} hosts in scope. Technical testing confirmed that {control_name} was not configured to the required baseline. For example, real-time antivirus protection was disabled on hosts subject to {compliance_framework} requirements, confirmed by querying the host's protection status through available management tooling.

Missing controls expose {{COMPANY_NAME}} to exploitation of the unprotected attack surface and may constitute reportable gaps under {compliance_framework} independent of whether exploitation occurs.

# Impact

A host that does not meet its required hardening baseline provides attacker capabilities that the compliance framework was designed to prevent. Missing technical controls cannot be substituted by policy statements; they must be applied and verified on each in-scope system.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Apply the {compliance_framework} hardening baseline to all in-scope hosts. Use the framework's specific control requirements as acceptance criteria, not a generic hardening guide.
  • Deliver baseline configuration through a configuration management system—Group Policy, Ansible, Chef, or equivalent—so the baseline is automatically enforced and reapplied when a host drifts out of compliance.
  • Document and formally approve any controls that cannot be applied technically. Compensating controls and accepted risks must be on record for compliance purposes.
  • Schedule periodic compliance scans against the hardening baseline to detect drift before the next formal assessment.
name: Insufficient System Hardening

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified two physical bypass techniques that allowed the {device_name} case to be opened without activating its tamper-detection sensor. First, a rare-earth magnet positioned at a specific point on the device exterior held the sensor arm in its closed position while the service panel was removed. Second, adhesive sprayed through a gap between case panels dripped onto the sensor mechanism and, once cured, permanently immobilized the arm. Both techniques were repeatable and left no visible evidence on the device exterior.

With the sensor bypassed, the team removed the flash storage module and recovered customer transaction data that the device would otherwise have erased on case opening.

# Impact

Anti-tamper hardware protects sensitive data by triggering an erasure response when the device is physically breached. A tamper sensor that can be defeated with a magnet or common adhesive provides no meaningful protection against a physically proximate attacker. Devices designed to operate in environments where an attacker may have brief, unmonitored physical access require tamper resistance that holds against plausible physical attacks, not only against attackers observed in real time.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remediate the specific bypass paths identified: position the tamper sensor so it cannot be influenced by an external magnet without first breaching the case itself; seal panel gaps to a clearance that prevents adhesive injection from the exterior. Evaluate whether an optical or non-magnetic sensor design better resists the observed bypass techniques.
  • Commission a follow-on physical security review of any proposed remediation design before production. Physical security controls are difficult to retrofit; validating the design before manufacturing is significantly less expensive than a post-production fix.
name: Insufficient Tamper Resistance

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined through interviews with {{COMPANY_NAME}} engineering and operations staff that the organization lacked standardized technical design documentation for deployed systems and integrations. Architecture diagrams, dataflow diagrams, and network diagrams did not exist in a maintained central repository. Technical details were distributed across meeting notes, collaboration tools, and design files with no defined ownership or update process.

The absence of these artifacts required the assessment team to reconstruct the architecture through interviews and direct observation, which may have left components undiscovered that would be visible in maintained documentation.

# Impact

Without current architecture and dataflow diagrams, security reviews must reconstruct the system from first principles during each engagement and may miss components not reachable through testing. Missing network diagrams prevent verification that segmentation rules match the intended design. Missing dataflow diagrams make it impossible to confirm that sensitive data—PHI, cardholder data—is protected at every transit and storage point.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Produce architecture diagrams showing all system components, their relationships, and trust boundaries, including internal and third-party integrations.
  • Create dataflow diagrams for each path where sensitive data moves through the system. Mark encryption points, storage locations, and trust boundary crossings.
  • Produce and maintain network diagrams documenting segments, firewall rules, VPN connections, and cloud virtual networks.
  • Store all documentation in a versioned repository with defined ownership and a review cadence—at minimum annually—to keep diagrams current as systems change.
  • Require updated documentation as a prerequisite for deploying new integrations or significant architectural changes.

Strategic Considerations

  • Use threat modeling frameworks such as STRIDE or PASTA in conjunction with architecture and dataflow diagrams to systematically identify and address security risks in the design phase.
  • Align documentation practices with applicable regulatory requirements such as HIPAA technical safeguards and PCI DSS network diagram requirements.
name: Insufficient Technical Design Documentation

Description:
# Description

The assessment team confirmed through technical interviews that {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s engineering teams did not perform threat modeling as part of their development process. Features moved from requirements to implementation without a systematic review of potential attack paths or the security controls required to address them. Security considerations entered the process reactively—through code review feedback or external assessments—rather than during design, when changes are least expensive to make.

# Impact

Features designed without threat modeling carry assumptions about trust boundaries and input sources that are never explicitly tested. Attack paths that would surface in a structured analysis tend to survive through code review and testing because reviewers evaluate correctness, not adversarial use. The result is vulnerabilities discovered in production rather than during design.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Adopt a threat modeling framework and apply it to all new features and significant architectural changes. STRIDE covers Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege and maps directly to security control categories.
  • Make a completed threat model a prerequisite for moving a feature from design to implementation. The model should answer whether trust boundaries, authentication requirements, and input validation are addressed for the data flows in scope.
  • Include developers, product owners, and at least one security reviewer in threat modeling sessions. Different perspectives surface attack paths that a single reviewer may miss.
  • Revisit and update threat models when the system's data flows, components, or trust relationships change significantly.
name: Insufficient Threat Modeling

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found active user accounts in the {application_name} environment with creation dates as early as {earliest_year}. Review of account metadata indicated that provisioning and deprovisioning were performed informally, with no defined workflow tied to employment status changes. Several accounts could not be attributed to a current employee or active business function. The team could not confirm that periodic access reviews had been performed on any of these accounts.

# Impact

Accounts that outlast their owners give former employees, former contractors, and attackers who hold compromised credentials persistent access to systems and data. Dormant accounts draw less monitoring attention than active ones and are less likely to trigger anomaly detection. Accounts that accumulate permissions through role changes without a reset carry excess access that no current business need justifies.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Audit all user accounts in production and non-production environments immediately. Disable or remove accounts that cannot be attributed to a current employee with a documented business need.
  • Connect account deprovisioning to the HR system so that termination or role-change events automatically trigger access removal or downgrade. Manual processes miss events and introduce delay.
  • Implement role-based access control to define permissions by job function rather than individual. This limits the scope of any single account and makes access reviews tractable.
  • Conduct access reviews at least quarterly. Each review should confirm that every active account has a current business owner and appropriate permissions.

Strategic Considerations

  • Evaluate identity governance tooling to automate access certification and provisioning workflows at scale.
  • Extend lifecycle controls to non-production environments. Test and staging environments frequently contain sensitive data and are commonly excluded from formal access management programs.
name: Insufficient User Onboarding and Offboarding Controls

Description:
# Description

The assessment team observed that {{COMPANY_NAME}} staff exhibited behaviors consistent with insufficient security awareness training during the assessment period. Employees engaged with simulated phishing messages, and the team identified gaps in the procedures staff use to verify the identity of internal requestors and to respond to unexpected credential requests.

# Impact

Social engineering attacks succeed by exploiting the gap between what users know they should do and what they do under realistic conditions. Training that covers phishing in theory, without scenario-based practice, leaves staff unprepared for well-crafted attacks. A single successful phishing interaction can provide an attacker with valid credentials and an initial foothold, reducing the value of technical controls that depend on authentication being meaningful.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Update security awareness training to include scenario-based exercises covering: identifying phishing email characteristics, recognizing requests for credentials or access that fall outside normal procedures, and the process for reporting suspicious messages to the security team before clicking links or opening attachments.
  • Define and communicate a procedure for employees to verify the identity of internal requestors before complying with access or credential requests. The procedure should not rely solely on email address or phone number as verification.
  • Run periodic phishing simulations to measure training effectiveness and identify staff who need additional coaching. Track results over time to confirm improvement rather than treating training as a one-time event.
  • Make it easy to report suspicious messages. The lower the friction, the more likely staff are to use the reporting path.
name: Insufficient User Security Awareness

Description:
# Description

The assessment team reviewed {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s source code repository using open-source static analysis tooling and identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} findings, a sample of which the team validated manually within the engagement window. Confirmed issues included SQL queries built by string interpolation from API-provided data in ETL workflows, API keys stored in plaintext in environment files committed to the repository, Docker containers configured to run as root, CI/CD workflow steps susceptible to shell injection via PR branch names, and Kubernetes configurations missing basic hardening controls.

The team observed that the organization used AI-assisted development tooling to generate or modify code but applied no automated security validation step specifically to AI-generated output before it reached the main branch.

# Impact

Code generated by non-deterministic systems does not inherit the reviewer's security intent—only the prompt's. Without a validation gate, AI-generated code that introduces SQL injection, credential exposure, or privilege escalation reaches production on the same path as human-authored code. The volume of output that AI-assisted development produces amplifies both the speed of delivery and the rate at which a vulnerability class can propagate across the codebase.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add deterministic security validation gates—SAST, dependency scanning, configuration linting—to the CI/CD pipeline for all code, regardless of whether it was authored by a human or an AI tool. Apply these gates before code reaches the main branch.
  • Apply AI-assisted code review as a second pass for AI-generated changes. A purpose-built review agent can evaluate generated code against the organization's security standards at the volume that AI-assisted development produces.
  • Add a triage layer that consolidates findings from multiple analysis tools and surfaces high-confidence, actionable results for human review. Raw tool output at scale cannot be effectively reviewed without aggregation and prioritization.
  • Assign clear ownership for approving AI-generated code. The human who accepts the merge is accountable for the security outcome, regardless of which tool produced the code.

Strategic Considerations

  • Establish a formal AI-assisted secure SDLC framework that defines when and how AI systems may generate or modify code, along with mandatory validation steps at each stage of the pipeline.
  • Define clear ownership and accountability for approving AI-generated changes. Responsibility for security outcomes must rest with designated engineering or security personnel, not deferred to the tool.
name: Insufficient Validation of Generated Logic

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a prototype pollution vulnerability in the {feature_name} feature of {application_name}. The feature accepted user-controlled input that was merged into a JavaScript object without filtering the __proto__, prototype, or constructor keys. The team supplied a crafted payload that injected properties onto Object.prototype, which propagated to all derived objects in the application's runtime and achieved {exploitation_outcome}.

# Impact

Prototype pollution in server-side JavaScript gives an attacker control over the base properties of every object created after the injection. Depending on the application's code paths, this produces remote code execution by poisoning properties checked by template engines or deserialization libraries; security control bypass by overwriting flags evaluated in authorization logic; or denial of service by setting properties that cause runtime exceptions in downstream code.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• In all code paths that merge or assign user-controlled data to JavaScript objects, explicitly block the keys __proto__, prototype, and constructor before the merge or assignment. Use an allowlist of expected keys where the input schema is known.
  • Replace recursive object merges with a library that is explicitly safe against prototype pollution, or use Object.create(null) to create target objects without a prototype chain when the data source is untrusted.
  • Set Object.freeze(Object.prototype) at server startup as a defense-in-depth measure. This prevents runtime modification of the prototype even if a vulnerable code path is reached, though it is not a substitute for fixing the input handling.
name: JavaScript Prototype Pollution

Description:
# Description

The assessment team confirmed that the LDAP service on {{TARGET_HOST}} accepted anonymous binds and returned directory data without authentication. Using ldapsearch with no credentials, the team extracted user accounts, email addresses, group memberships, home directories, and login shells from the directory. The query required no username or password.

The returned data included security group memberships, revealing which accounts held elevated access. An attacker could use this information to identify high-value targets for phishing, credential stuffing, or privilege escalation attempts.

# Impact

An LDAP server that accepts anonymous binds exposes its directory contents to any host with network access. User account names, email addresses, group memberships, and organizational structure are standard reconnaissance inputs for targeted attacks. Security group enumeration reveals which accounts hold elevated access, making them primary targets for follow-on exploitation.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable anonymous binds on all LDAP servers. Require every client to authenticate with a valid distinguished name and password before executing any query.
  • Review all LDAP ACLs and restrict read access to the minimum set of attributes each application or service requires. No single service account should be able to read the entire directory without a documented business need.
  • Migrate all client connections to LDAPS and disable cleartext LDAP on port 389. Anonymous binds over cleartext LDAP expose both directory contents and other clients' credentials to any observer on the same network segment.
  • Document and enforce a hardening baseline for all LDAP services and verify compliance on a defined schedule.
name: LDAP Anonymous Access

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified an LDAP injection vulnerability in {application_name}. The {parameter_name} parameter was concatenated directly into an LDAP search filter without encoding or validation. By supplying LDAP filter metacharacters in the parameter, the team altered the search filter's logic and retrieved directory objects outside the intended query scope, including a list of domain administrator accounts in the {{DOMAIN}} domain.

# Impact

LDAP injection gives an attacker control over the structure of a directory query. Depending on the filter and the attributes accessible to the service account running the search, an attacker can retrieve sensitive directory data such as account names, group memberships, and email addresses; bypass authentication checks that evaluate LDAP query results; or enumerate privileged accounts for follow-on attacks.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Use a parameterized LDAP library that separates query structure from input data. Inputs should be passed as values to a structured query builder that applies correct encoding automatically, not concatenated into a filter string.
  • Validate all input against an allowlist of permitted characters before it reaches the LDAP query. For username fields, this is typically alphanumeric characters plus a small set of punctuation; filter metacharacters such as (, ), *, \, and NUL should be rejected per RFC 4515.
  • Where allowlisting is not feasible, apply LDAP special-character escaping to all user-supplied values using the library's escaping function. A denylist of specific characters is incomplete by design and should be used only as a last resort.
name: LDAP Injection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined that {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} LDAP servers in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s environment did not enforce LDAP signing or channel binding. The team confirmed the configuration using nxc, which reported signing: None and channel binding: When Supported on the affected domain controllers. Without signing, a man-in-the-middle attacker can intercept and modify LDAP sessions in transit. Without channel binding, an attacker who coerces NTLM authentication from a target can relay it to the LDAP service from a different protocol context.

# Impact

LDAP signing validates the origin and integrity of each LDAP message using a digital signature, preventing a network-adjacent attacker from tampering with directory queries or responses. Channel binding ties an authenticated session to a specific transport connection, preventing cross-protocol relay attacks such as coercing a target into HTTP authentication and relaying it to LDAP. Without both controls, a network-adjacent attacker can relay coerced credentials to modify Active Directory objects or extract sensitive data.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable and require LDAP signing on all domain controllers via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > "Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements" set to "Require signing".
  • Enable required LDAP channel binding on all domain controllers: set "Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements" to "Always" via Group Policy.
  • Deploy LDAPS and disable cleartext LDAP on port 389 at the firewall where feasible. LDAPS provides encryption in addition to the authentication protections that signing and channel binding supply.
  • Audit all client applications that connect to LDAP to confirm they support signing and channel binding before enforcement. Applications that cannot support these controls should be upgraded or isolated before the requirement is applied.
name: LDAP Protections Not Enforced

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found LM hashes stored alongside NTLM hashes in the credential database on {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s domain controllers. After obtaining domain controller access, the team extracted credentials and identified accounts with non-blank LM hashes. LM hashing splits a password into two seven-character blocks and hashes each independently using DES, so any password of fourteen characters or fewer can be attacked as two independent seven-character keys using commodity cracking hardware.

# Impact

LM hashing is computationally broken. Because the password is split and each half is hashed independently, a 14-character password provides no more brute-force resistance than two separate 7-character passwords. Cracking LM hashes requires no per-hash computation investment beyond the cracking hardware and completes in minutes for passwords drawn from any practical keyspace.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Configure all domain controllers and member computers to stop generating LM hashes via Group Policy: enable "Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change".
  • Force a password reset for all accounts with a non-blank LM hash. The stored hash is not removed until the account's password changes after the policy is applied.
  • Verify that no legacy applications or services require LM authentication before disabling the hash. Any system that requires LM should be upgraded or replaced before the control is enforced domain-wide.
name: LM Password Storage

Description:
# Description

The assessment team decompiled the {application_name} APK by converting it to a JAR with dex2jar and decompiling the JAR with a standard Java decompiler. The resulting source code retained original class and method names, making the application's logic straightforward to navigate with a standard IDE. An attacker could use this output to map authentication flows, identify API endpoints, locate hardcoded values, and search for vulnerability patterns without access to the original source repository.

# Impact

Unobfuscated Android bytecode decompiles to source code functionally equivalent to the original. An attacker can navigate it with standard development tools at no cost beyond the decompilation step itself. While obfuscation does not prevent reverse engineering, it significantly raises the time and skill required. Without it, the APK provides the same view of the application's logic as the source repository.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable R8 code shrinking and obfuscation in the Android build configuration. R8 renames classes and methods to short, meaningless identifiers at compile time. Retain a mapping file for each build to allow stack trace deobfuscation in crash reports and debugging.
  • Apply ProGuard keep rules to protect code R8 must not rename: public API interfaces, reflection targets, and serialization classes. Overly broad keep rules defeat obfuscation; scope them to what the application genuinely requires.
  • For applications that handle sensitive data or high-value transactions, evaluate commercial obfuscation tools that add string encryption, control-flow obfuscation, and anti-decompiler measures beyond R8. Retain the mapping files securely and never include them in the distributed APK.
name: Lack of Android APK Obfuscation

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified Droplets and volumes in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s DigitalOcean environment that had no backup or snapshot configured. Neither automatic backups nor manually created snapshots were present for {{AFFECTED}}, leaving them without any recorded state from which to recover in the event of data loss or corruption.

# Impact

A resource with no backup has no recovery path. Data corruption, accidental deletion, or a destructive attack leaves {{COMPANY_NAME}} with no option but to rebuild from scratch, accepting whatever data loss occurred since the resource was last in a known-good state. The absence of a backup also limits forensic analysis of the resource's state before an incident.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Identify which Droplets and volumes hold data or configuration that cannot be reconstructed quickly from another source. Enable DigitalOcean's automatic backup feature for those resources at minimum.
  • Create an initial snapshot of each critical resource to establish a known-good baseline. Automate subsequent snapshots on a schedule calibrated to how often the data changes and how much data loss is acceptable.
  • Test restoration from backup periodically. A backup that has never been restored is an untested assumption.
  • Document the recovery time objective and recovery point objective for each critical resource and confirm the backup schedule meets them.
name: Lack of Backup Policy

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified Azure database servers and virtual machines in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s environment that were not integrated with Azure Active Directory. These resources used local accounts or resource-specific credentials for access control rather than the centralized identity service governing the rest of the environment.

# Impact

Resources that manage their own identity independently of the central directory do not inherit organizational policies: password complexity, MFA enforcement, and account deprovisioning on employee separation. A user removed from Azure AD retains access to non-integrated resources until each is updated manually, extending the window of unauthorized access after an offboarding event.
