# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• For Azure SQL servers, configure an Azure AD administrator in the SQL server settings. Set the Azure AD admin to a security group rather than an individual account so membership management is centralized.
  • For Azure virtual machines, enable the Login with Azure AD credentials extension and assign the Virtual Machine Administrator Login or Virtual Machine User Login role to authorized users or groups in Azure AD.
  • Disable or remove local accounts on integrated resources after confirming Azure AD authentication is functioning correctly. Local accounts that remain active bypass the centralized control and are not subject to organizational access review.
name: Lack of Centralized Access Control

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined that the {application_name} mobile applications for iOS and Android validated server certificates against the operating system's trusted CA store. The applications accepted any certificate signed by any CA the OS trusted, including user-installed CAs. A device configured with a proxy CA certificate caused the applications to trust the proxy's certificate without error, allowing all application traffic to be inspected and modified in transit.

The team confirmed that certificate transparency was used as a compensating control. Certificate transparency addresses malicious issuance by legitimate CAs but does not address interception by a user-installed or enterprise-managed CA.

# Impact

A mobile application that trusts the OS CA store can be intercepted by anyone who can install a CA certificate on the device: an attacker with physical access, a malicious MDM profile, or an enterprise network performing TLS inspection. An attacker in this position can read and modify all traffic between the application and its servers, including session tokens, authentication responses, and API data used in authorization decisions.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Implement certificate pinning by validating the SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) fingerprint of the server certificate or intermediate CA against a set of known-good values embedded in the application. Hash the SPKI with SHA-256 rather than pinning the raw certificate, to avoid breaking the pin on certificate renewal.
  • Pin the intermediate CA certificate rather than the leaf when {{COMPANY_NAME}} controls the issuing CA. Intermediate pins survive leaf certificate rotation without requiring an application update.
  • Embed at least one backup pin for a certificate not yet in production. A pin with no rotation plan becomes an operational incident when certificates expire.
  • Plan and test the key rotation and pin update procedure before deploying pinning in production.
name: Lack of Certificate Pinning

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {region_count} active AWS regions in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s account where AWS Config was not enabled. Without Config, the account had no automated mechanism to evaluate whether deployed resources conformed to {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s configuration requirements or to detect when a configuration change brought a resource out of compliance.

# Impact

AWS Config is the primary mechanism for detecting configuration drift across an AWS account. Without it, a security group that opens an unintended port, an S3 bucket that becomes publicly accessible, or an EC2 instance launched without encryption can persist indefinitely without generating an alert. Configuration drift that accumulates undetected is difficult to audit and remediate at scale.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable AWS Config in all active regions and configure it to record all resource types. Enable the global resource recorder in the primary region to capture IAM resources.
  • Define Config rules that correspond to {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s configuration requirements. AWS Managed Rules cover a broad set of common checks; custom rules can address organization-specific requirements.
  • Configure SNS notifications or Security Hub integration to alert on Config rule failures so non-compliant resources are addressed promptly rather than discovered at the next scheduled assessment.
name: Lack of Configuration Control

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that no firewall rules were defined in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s DigitalOcean environment. All Droplets were reachable from the internet on any port, and inter-Droplet traffic was unrestricted. Services that should be accessible only internally—database ports, administrative interfaces, monitoring endpoints—were reachable from the public internet without any network-layer control.

# Impact

Without firewall rules, every service port a Droplet listens on is reachable from the internet. Network segmentation cannot be enforced. Any service that is accidentally exposed, or becomes exposed through a configuration change, is immediately accessible to external attackers. The attack surface grows with every service added to the environment.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Audit all Droplets to identify the minimum network traffic each resource requires: which ports, from which sources, to which destinations.
  • Create firewall rules that permit only the identified traffic. Default-deny all other inbound traffic from the internet. Restrict inter-Droplet traffic to the paths required for application function.
  • Apply firewall rules by tag or group rather than by individual Droplet so new resources automatically inherit the correct rules and rules do not require manual updates as the environment changes.
  • Restrict administrative services—SSH, RDP, database ports—to approved IP ranges or access through a VPN or bastion host. Never permit these services from 0.0.0.0/0.
name: Lack of Firewall Rules

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s {location} did not maintain a separate guest wireless network. Visitors, customers, and contractors were provided the corporate Wi-Fi passphrase and connected directly to the same network segment as employee workstations and internal infrastructure. A guest device on this network could reach internal hosts, attempt man-in-the-middle attacks against employee traffic, and interact with services that assumed network adjacency implied trust.

# Impact

Corporate and guest wireless traffic sharing a broadcast domain allows any guest device to attempt ARP poisoning, mDNS spoofing, and direct connections to internal services. Segmentation that depends on the corporate network boundary is defeated when untrusted devices sit inside it. Any guest with wireless access becomes a potential pivot point into the internal network.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Provision a dedicated guest SSID on a separate VLAN that routes to the internet only. Block all communication from the guest VLAN to any internal subnet, including the corporate Wi-Fi network.
  • Enable client isolation on the guest SSID so guest devices cannot communicate with each other directly on the wireless segment.
  • Remove the corporate passphrase from any display, printed material, or communication accessible to guests. Corporate Wi-Fi credentials should be known only to employees.
  • Confirm that the access point or wireless controller enforces VLAN separation at the hardware layer, not only through routing policy.
name: Lack of Guest Wireless Network

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined that the {device_name} was built on a platform that provides no hardware root of trust, secure boot support, or hardware key storage. The platform uses a removable storage medium for the operating system and application data. The team removed the storage card, mounted it on an external host, located the SSH authorized_keys file on the device partition, appended a team-generated public key, reinserted the storage card, and logged into the booted device as root over SSH using the newly added key. The team then retrieved the device's credential store from the running system.

# Impact

A hardware root of trust anchors a device's boot process to a set of trusted measurements and provides a secure location for cryptographic keys that cannot be extracted by software. Without it, the storage medium is readable by any host that can physically access it, the firmware can be replaced by mounting the storage card externally, and there is no chain of trust to verify that the device is running authorized code. An attacker with brief physical access to the device can modify it persistently without leaving evidence.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Evaluate a hardware platform that provides an integrated hardware root of trust—a secure element, TPM, or SoC with a built-in trust anchor—as the basis for future {device_name} revisions. The root of trust must support measured boot and hardware key storage that cannot be read by software running on the main processor.
  • As a near-term mitigation on existing hardware, evaluate a security peripheral such as a hardware security module connected to the platform's expansion interface. Note that peripherals connected via GPIO or I2C are susceptible to hardware interposition and should be treated as a partial control, not an equivalent substitute for an integrated trust anchor.
  • Enable full-disk encryption on the storage medium with keys stored in hardware. Without hardware key storage, disk encryption can be bypassed by extracting the key from a software-accessible location in the firmware.
name: Lack of Hardware Root of Trust

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined that the {application_name} Android application did not verify its own integrity at runtime. The team decompiled the APK using apktool, modified the {filename} class to alter the application's behavior, recompiled the modified APK, signed it with a self-generated developer key, and installed it on a test device using adb. The modified application ran without triggering any integrity check or terminating in response to the signature change.

# Impact

An Android application without integrity checks can be decompiled, modified, and redistributed as a trojanized version that impersonates the original. A user who installs the modified APK from a third-party source encounters an application that behaves like the original while performing actions the developer did not authorize—credential harvesting, traffic interception, or data exfiltration. Legitimate users cannot distinguish the modified application from the original without inspecting the signing certificate.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Implement runtime integrity checks using CRC verification against the application's bytecode, native libraries, and data files. Verify the APK's signing certificate at startup by comparing it against the expected fingerprint embedded in native code.
  • Place integrity check logic in native C or C++ code compiled with the Android NDK. Native code is significantly harder to patch than Dalvik bytecode and is not affected by Java-layer decompilation and recompilation.
  • Obfuscate the application's bytecode using R8 or a commercial obfuscation tool to raise the time required to locate and disable the integrity checks before redistribution.
  • For applications distributed through the Play Store, evaluate the Google Play Integrity API to verify device integrity and confirm the application is unmodified at the server level, supplementing client-side checks.
name: Lack of Integrity Checks

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that {application_name} accepted file uploads and passed them to {downstream_process} without scanning for malicious content. No antivirus or content inspection step was present before the file was processed or stored.

# Impact

An application that processes uploaded files without scanning them can be used to deliver malware into internal storage or downstream systems. If uploaded files are executed, shared with other users, or passed to document-processing pipelines, a malicious file can compromise additional hosts or users beyond the application itself.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Integrate a file scanning step before any uploaded file is processed or stored. Validate the integration using the EICAR standard test file to confirm the antivirus engine is active and current.
  • Scan files in a sandboxed environment isolated from production infrastructure. Do not process or open uploaded files on the same host that serves the application.
  • Restrict uploaded file types to those the application requires and validate the file's actual content type, not only the client-supplied MIME type or filename extension.
name: Lack of Malware Detection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified that {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s {authentication_target} did not require multi-factor authentication. Using credentials obtained through {credential_source}, the team authenticated successfully with a username and password alone. Once connected, the team accessed {accessed_resource} and retrieved {sensitive_data_type}.

Had MFA been enforced, the obtained credentials alone would not have completed authentication without a second factor in the account holder's possession.

Variants

This finding applies to additional authentication targets including remote desktop access to internal jump hosts, where single-factor authentication with domain credentials was also confirmed.

# Impact

Single-factor authentication reduces account security to the strength of the password alone. Credentials obtained through phishing, credential stuffing, or password spray are immediately actionable against services that do not require a second factor. A second factor the attacker does not hold breaks the attack even when the password is known.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enforce MFA on all {{AFFECTED}} identified in this finding. MFA must be required for every authentication session, not only for initial enrollment or administrative access.
  • Configure the {authentication_target} to require MFA as part of the authentication exchange at the gateway level, not as a separate step that client configuration can bypass.
  • Prefer hardware-backed FIDO2 authenticators or platform authenticators over TOTP or SMS, which are susceptible to real-time phishing and SIM-swapping respectively.
name: Lack of Multi-factor Authentication

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified at least one {{COMPANY_NAME}} employee account whose credentials appeared in {breach_count} publicly disclosed data breaches. The team confirmed that the exposed password was still in use by authenticating to {application_name} with those credentials. The account's access level allowed the team to operate as a trusted internal user within the application.

# Impact

Credentials disclosed in a data breach remain valid until changed. An attacker who obtains breach data can test the exposed credentials against any service the account holder reuses the password for. Without breach monitoring, {{COMPANY_NAME}} has no mechanism to identify affected accounts before an attacker does or to force a reset before the account is compromised.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Require {{ACCOUNTS}} to reset their password immediately to a unique credential not present in any known breach dataset.
  • Enforce MFA on {application_name} to limit the impact of credential compromise regardless of whether the password has been exposed in a breach.

Strategic Considerations

  • Integrate a breach monitoring service—such as the Have I Been Pwned API or an equivalent provider—to automatically flag employee accounts whose credentials appear in new public disclosures. Route alerts to the security team for immediate follow-up.
  • At password reset, check the new password against known breach datasets and reject it if it appears. NIST SP 800-63B recommends this as a standard control for credential management.
name: Lack of Password Breach Monitoring

Description:
# Description

The assessment team demonstrated that {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s authentication, configured with TOTP as the second factor, was susceptible to real-time phishing. The team set up Evilginx2 as a transparent proxy between a team-controlled domain and the {{COMPANY_NAME}} authentication portal. A test user navigated to the proxied URL, entered credentials, and completed the TOTP challenge. Evilginx2 relayed the authentication to the legitimate portal, captured the resulting session cookie, and the team injected that cookie into a browser session to gain authenticated access without possessing the user's password or TOTP secret.

# Impact

TOTP, push notification, SMS, and voice second factors are all susceptible to real-time phishing. The attacker does not need to break the second factor—they relay the user's response to the legitimate service and capture the resulting authenticated session. FIDO2 and WebAuthn authenticators are not susceptible to this attack because the challenge-response is bound to the origin domain; a proxy cannot forward a valid response from the attacker's domain to the legitimate service.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable TOTP, push notification, SMS, and voice as authentication options for all {{COMPANY_NAME}} employee accounts.
  • Require FIDO2-compliant authenticators—hardware security keys such as YubiKey, or platform authenticators such as Windows Hello or Touch ID—for all employee authentication. FIDO2 binds the authentication to the origin domain and cannot be relayed by a proxy.
  • Enroll all employees in FIDO2 authentication before disabling legacy second factors. Plan a support path for employees who lose or damage their hardware token.
name: Lack of Phishing-Resistant Authentication

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified deployed workloads in the {cluster_name} Kubernetes cluster that did not define a security context at the pod or container level. By default, Kubernetes containers run as root and retain Linux capabilities including CAP_NET_RAW, which allows sending raw packets and performing network enumeration. The team deployed a test pod without a security context in the {namespace_name} namespace, confirmed it ran as root, and used its default network capabilities to enumerate cluster-internal services, confirming reachability of services that should not be accessible from a standard workload.

# Impact

A pod without a security context runs with whatever capabilities the container runtime provides by default, which typically includes root access and network capabilities sufficient to send raw packets and bind privileged ports. An attacker who gains code execution in an uncontextualized pod has significantly more capability for lateral movement than one running as an unprivileged user with capabilities dropped to the application's minimum.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Define a security context for every pod and container. At minimum, set runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser to a non-zero UID, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, and drop all Linux capabilities except those the workload explicitly requires.
  • Apply a PodSecurity admission policy at the restricted or baseline standard to enforce these requirements cluster-wide, rather than relying on individual workload authors to set contexts correctly on every deployment.
  • Audit existing workloads for missing security contexts and remediate them, prioritizing workloads that process sensitive data or hold privileged service account tokens.
name: Lack of Pod Security Contexts

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that {application_name} did not implement root or jailbreak detection, or that the detection routines present could be bypassed at runtime. On Android, the team installed the application on a rooted device, accessed the application's private data directory, and extracted session credentials stored in the application's sandbox. On iOS, the team installed the application on a jailbroken device, connected via SSH as the root user, and read files from the application's container that the OS sandbox would otherwise have protected.

# Impact

Mobile operating systems confine application data using permission boundaries and filesystem sandboxing that depend on the OS enforcing them. A rooted or jailbroken device removes that enforcement. An attacker who installs the application on a compromised device can read the application's private storage, intercept in-process data, and modify the application's behavior at runtime without any modification to the distributed package.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
Android

  • Implement root detection in native C or C++ code compiled with the Android NDK. Java-layer checks can be patched on a rooted device without recompiling the APK. Checks should look for su binaries, Magisk-related file paths, modified build properties, and known root management packages.
  • Obfuscate detection logic and distribute checks across multiple call sites. A single, identifiable detection function is straightforward to patch.
  • Update detection logic with each release. Root tooling evolves rapidly and detection methods that work today may not work next quarter.

iOS

  • Implement jailbreak detection in native C or assembly. Avoid Objective-C methods that can be swizzled at runtime by jailbreak frameworks.
  • Check for jailbreak indicators: Cydia and Sileo URI schemes, file paths used by jailbreak tools, and dyld image names from common jailbreak frameworks.
  • Use _dyld_image_count() and _dyld_get_image_name() to detect injected libraries at runtime.
  • Randomize check placement throughout the application lifecycle. A single-point patch should not defeat all detection.
name: Lack of Root Detection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team determined through interviews that {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s development team had not received consistent, ongoing security training. Newly hired developers received initial guidance on secure coding, but no retroactive training had been provided to existing developers and no formal annual training cadence had been established. For development work performed by external vendors, the team could not confirm whether vendor developers had completed any security training relevant to the code they were producing for {{COMPANY_NAME}}.

# Impact

Developers who do not receive regular security training write code that reflects how the application will be used, not how it will be attacked. Common vulnerability classes—injection, insecure deserialization, broken access control—are consistently present in code produced by developers without security context. Training shifts detection earlier in the development cycle, where defects are least expensive to fix.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Provide secure development training to all current developers, not only new hires. Training should be specific to the languages and frameworks the team uses, not generic security awareness content.
  • Establish an annual training cadence and track completion. Developers who miss the cycle should complete training before working on high-sensitivity features.
  • For external development vendors, require contractually that developers producing code for {{COMPANY_NAME}} complete annual secure coding training and provide evidence of completion.
name: Lack of Secure Development Training

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified that the {application_name} client-side integration documentation and the application dashboard provided users with a script tag that did not include the integrity attribute. Scripts loaded from a content delivery network without a cryptographic integrity check are accepted by the browser at whatever content the CDN delivers at request time.

# Impact

Subresource Integrity allows browsers to verify that a resource loaded from an external source matches an expected cryptographic hash. Without it, a compromised or manipulated CDN can deliver a modified script to every page that loads the resource. The modification executes in the page's origin context with access to the DOM, cookies, and form data. All users of the integration receive the modified script, not only visitors to a single page.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add the integrity attribute to the script tag provided in integration documentation and the dashboard. Compute the hash using SHA-384 of the script file's current content and encode it as a base64 value: integrity="sha384-{hash}".
  • Add crossorigin="anonymous" alongside the integrity attribute. The browser requires a CORS response for SRI checking to function correctly on cross-origin resources.
  • Update the hash whenever the script changes. Automating hash generation as part of the release process prevents the attribute from falling out of sync with the deployed file.
name: Lack of Subresource Integrity

Description:
# Description

The assessment team coerced authentication from domain controllers in {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s environment using the Coercer tool and captured the resulting authentication attempts with Responder. One domain controller responded using NTLMv1 instead of NTLMv2. The team cracked the captured NTLMv1 hash in approximately two hours and recovered the NT hash for the domain controller machine account. Using that NT hash, the team performed a DCSync against {{DOMAIN}} and extracted the NT hash for the {account_name} administrator account. The team then used that hash to authenticate to the production domain.

# Impact

NTLMv1 hashes are encrypted with DES, a cipher broken in 1999. The hash is split into three 7-byte blocks, each encrypted independently with different DES keys. Cracking NTLMv1 via a known-plaintext attack against the DES key space is feasible in seconds on specialized hardware and in minutes on commodity GPU clusters, without any requirement to know or guess the original password.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable NTLMv1 across the environment via Group Policy: set "Network security: LAN Manager authentication level" to "Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM."
  • Audit the environment for legacy systems and applications that require LM or NTLMv1 authentication. Any system that cannot use NTLMv2 or Kerberos should be upgraded or isolated from the domain.
  • Where Kerberos is viable, prefer it over NTLM entirely. Configure sensitive services to require Kerberos and disable NTLM as a fallback.
  • Enable authentication coercion mitigations alongside: enforce LDAP signing, LDAP channel binding, and SMB signing to reduce the attacker's ability to relay coerced credentials even where NTLMv2 remains in use.
name: Legacy Authentication Protocol In Use

Description:
# Description

The assessment team observed active NBNS, LLMNR, and mDNS broadcast traffic on {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s internal network. The team used Responder in analyze mode to confirm broadcast name resolution requests in the testing machine's broadcast domain. The team then responded to those requests, directing requesting hosts to authenticate to a team-controlled SMB server, and captured {credential_count} NTLM credential hashes. The team cracked the hash for {{ACCOUNTS}} and recovered the cleartext password in {crack_time}.

# Impact

NBNS and LLMNR send name resolution requests as broadcast messages to the local network segment without authentication. Any host on the segment can respond to a request, regardless of whether it is the intended target. An attacker who claims to be the requested host receives an NTLM credential hash from the querying system for offline cracking. No vulnerability in the requesting system is required—only network adjacency. mDNS is susceptible to the same class of attack.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable NBNS on all Windows hosts by configuring DHCP to deliver option 0x2C with a value of 2 (P-node) and setting the corresponding registry value on hosts not managed by DHCP for this setting.
  • Disable LLMNR via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Turn off Multicast Name Resolution, set to Enabled.
  • Disable mDNS by setting HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Dnscache\Parameters\EnableMDNS to 0 on all domain members.
  • Confirm that DNS is authoritative for all names the environment requires before disabling the fallback protocols. Name resolution failures after disabling them indicate DNS gaps to address.
  • Enable SMB signing and LDAP signing and channel binding to reduce the impact of relay attacks that use coerced credentials, even after the legacy protocols are disabled.
name: Legacy Host-Identification Protocols in Use

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} systems running end-of-life operating systems joined to the {{DOMAIN}} Active Directory domain. Using LDAP queries against the operatingSystem attribute, the team located {number} Windows XP Professional hosts and {number_2} Windows Server 2003 hosts with domain logons recorded within the prior year. Both operating system versions reached vendor end of life in 2014; neither has received security patches since that date.

The team confirmed that one of the identified Server 2003 hosts was reachable from a workstation-subnet test VM across subnet boundaries without additional access controls in place. Legacy hosts represent a fixed attack surface: known vulnerabilities accumulate over time with no remediation path and no vendor-validated security software to compensate.

# Impact

Operating systems past vendor end of life no longer receive security patches, leaving any subsequently disclosed vulnerabilities permanently unaddressed. An attacker who reaches a legacy host can apply public exploit code against known CVEs without facing a patched target. Third-party security tools — antivirus, EDR agents — typically lose vendor validation for these platforms as well, removing the compensating controls that partially offset unpatched software risk on supported systems.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• For each legacy host, determine whether a supported operating system replacement is feasible. Migrate systems with active business functions to a supported Windows version before the next patch cycle.
  • For hosts that cannot be migrated immediately, place them behind a dedicated network segment with allowlist-based firewall rules that limit inbound access to named services and source addresses only. Sever shared domain trust with production hosts.
  • Disable unnecessary services on legacy hosts and remove administrative trust relationships with other domain-joined systems. Use distinct local administrator credentials rather than shared domain accounts.
  • Monitor vendor advisory feeds for newly disclosed CVEs against Windows XP and Server 2003 and maintain an active risk register entry for each retained legacy host.
name: Legacy Operating Systems

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} MSSQL servers in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment that did not require Extended Protection or encrypted connections. Using nxc, the team confirmed EncryptionRequired was set to false across the affected hosts, then coerced outbound authentication from a service account and relayed it to a target MSSQL instance using impacket-ntlmrelayx.

The relay succeeded and opened an interactive session authenticated as CORP\svc with dbo permissions in the master database. A subsequent privilege check confirmed the relayed session held sysadmin membership. With that access, the team explored the databases on the host and identified a Microsoft BizTalk Server integration platform, confirming db_owner permissions on {number} of its databases. Password hashes extracted from sys.sql_logins did not crack during the assessment window. The xp_cmdshell stored procedure was disabled at the time of testing; per client instructions, the team did not enable it to avoid service disruption. A real attacker without that constraint could enable the procedure and execute operating system commands as the SQL Server service account.

# Impact

Extended Protection for SQL Server uses service binding and channel binding to verify that an NTLM authentication token was generated for the specific service the client intended to reach. Without it, an attacker who can coerce outbound authentication from a service account — through techniques such as PetitPotam, PrinterBug, or DFSCoerce — can relay those credentials to an MSSQL instance and authenticate as that account. Sysadmin access allows reading and modifying all databases, extracting password hashes, and enabling xp_cmdshell for arbitrary command execution on the underlying host. From a production database server, this typically provides a direct path to domain compromise.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Set Extended Protection to Required on all MSSQL instances. This prevents relay attacks by verifying that the authentication token was generated for the target service's service principal name.
  • Set Force Encryption to Yes on all instances. TLS channel encryption is required for channel binding to function.
  • Roll out these changes in a staged batch. Applications and drivers that do not support channel binding or encrypted connections will fail to connect; test in a non-production environment first and update connection strings or client configurations before enabling in production.
  • Review service accounts with MSSQL logins and apply least-privilege database roles. Accounts that do not require sysadmin permissions should not hold them.
name: MSSQL Protections Not Required

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a mass assignment condition in the {appname} application's profile update endpoint. A PATCH request to /api/users/update_profile accepted and persisted arbitrary fields injected into the preferences object — including attacker-named properties such as isadmin, admin_data, and super_admin — without server-side schema enforcement.

The team confirmed the injected fields survived by calling /api/users/current after submission. The properties did not override root-level permission attributes, so no privilege escalation was achieved during testing. However, the back end stored the attacker-supplied keys without restriction. The read-only test account was also able to modify alert_locations and activity feed filters through a path intended to be managed by a separate dedicated endpoint.

Accepting arbitrary fields in a persisted object is a forward-looking risk: if future code paths read those fields and act on them — an authorization check keyed on isadmin, conditional logic triggered by admin_data — the injected values become an attack surface without any additional user action required.

# Impact

Mass assignment occurs when a server deserializes a user-supplied payload and binds it directly to an object without an explicit allowlist of permitted fields. In weakly typed or reflection-based frameworks — common in MVC architectures — any field name the attacker submits can be mapped to object properties. At minimum this produces data integrity problems; in many cases it enables privilege escalation when role or permission fields are reachable through the same binding path. The risk grows over time as new features add fields to shared objects without accounting for the pre-existing blind spot.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Define a strict schema for the /api/users/update_profile endpoint. Accept only explicitly named fields; reject any payload key that does not appear in the allowlist with a 400 response.
  • Map incoming request data to a dedicated input model or DTO before applying it to the domain object. Avoid binding a raw request body directly to a persistence model.
  • Apply the same schema restriction to the preferences object: define its permitted sub-fields explicitly. Keys outside the schema should not be written to the database, regardless of whether they appear harmful at the time of writing.
  • Audit other update endpoints for the same pattern. Any endpoint that accepts a JSON payload and writes it to a stored object is a candidate for this vulnerability.
name: Mass Assignment

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a memory corruption vulnerability in the {name} Android application caused by unsafe use of the Parcelable deserialization mechanism. A class in the application accepted deserialized objects without verifying that the incoming data was an instance of the expected type, allowing the team to construct a malicious object with arbitrary field values.

The team reviewed decompiled source code and identified the vulnerable class. Because the code did not enforce type identity before proceeding, the team instantiated an arbitrary class using a no-argument constructor, set its fields to attacker-controlled values, and passed the resulting object to the vulnerable code path. The object was ignored or cast to an incompatible type and not immediately consumed — but the Java garbage collector eventually invoked its finalize method, triggering attacker-controlled logic.

By placing data at a predictable memory address before the GC pass, the team caused the finalize execution to reference that address, crashing the application in a controlled way and achieving arbitrary code execution within the application's process context. From that position, the team gained access to the application's private sandbox and the sensitive data stored there.

# Impact

Memory corruption in a mobile application allows an attacker to redirect execution flow to attacker-controlled code. In the Android sandbox model, this provides access to everything the application can reach: stored credentials, cached tokens, session data, and files in the private sandbox directory. Exploitation does not require root access or user interaction beyond delivering the malicious object to the vulnerable deserialization path.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Validate the type of any object being deserialized before accepting it. Reject objects whose class does not match the expected type; do not allow deserialization to instantiate arbitrary classes.
  • Avoid accepting attacker-controlled data as input to native pointer operations. Offset values used in memory address calculations must come from trusted, validated sources — not from deserialized input.
  • Do not use Parcelable deserialization paths to dynamically construct objects from attacker-supplied class names. Prefer static, schema-driven parsing where the set of valid types is known at compile time.
  • Eliminate or restrict use of finalize methods in classes that process external data. GC-triggered execution is difficult to reason about in the presence of adversarial input.
name: Memory Corruption

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified multiple {{COMPANY_NAME}} services that accepted requests from unauthenticated callers and returned sensitive data or permitted privileged operations.

Several application API endpoints responded to requests carrying no authentication token — no session cookie, no Authorization header — and returned records belonging to other customers and tenants. The team iterated through returned identifiers to enumerate cross-tenant data.

During network reconnaissance, the team also identified an exposed Java RMI Registry service on port {port} of {{TARGET_HOST}}. The team confirmed a jmxrmi entry bound to the registry using the rmi-dumpregistry Nmap script, then used a crafted Java class invoking RemoteMBean to execute operating system commands through the JMX interface, landing as a local administrator on a Windows Server 2008 R2 host.

To establish a more durable foothold, the team mounted an SMB share from test infrastructure, copied the SAM and SYSTEM registry hives to it, extracted NTLM hashes using pwdump, and used impacket-psexec in pass-the-hash mode to obtain a full SYSTEM shell on the target host.

Variants

Grafana API: Several Grafana instances — identifiable by sandbox-style hostnames — exposed API endpoints without authentication, returning test user records and organization metadata to unauthenticated callers.

Redis: A Redis instance accepted connections without a password, granting full read and write access to its keyspace. An attacker with network access could read cached data, poison cached values, or use CONFIG SET to write files to the host filesystem.

Weaviate Vector Database: {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} Weaviate instances running on {{COMPANY_NAME}} hosts were reachable without authentication. An attacker with network access could query, modify, or delete vector embeddings and the metadata associated with them.

Webalizer: A Webalizer web statistics interface at {{TARGET_URL}} was accessible without a login prompt, exposing server traffic statistics that reveal internal path structures and usage patterns.

phpMyAdmin: A phpMyAdmin interface was reachable without enforced authentication. Access to phpMyAdmin grants full control over the underlying MySQL databases — reading, writing, and deleting data — and can provide a path to operating system command execution through MySQL's file-write functions.

# Impact

Missing authentication allows any network-adjacent caller to reach functionality or data that should require identity verification. At the API layer this typically means cross-tenant data access and account enumeration. At the network service layer — RMI, Redis, databases — it eliminates the need to obtain credentials entirely, converting network access into immediate service compromise. The severity of each instance scales with the data the service holds and the operations it exposes.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Require authentication on every endpoint and network service before returning application data or invoking privileged operations. Apply the check at the framework routing layer, not inside individual handler functions, to prevent gaps introduced by future endpoints.
  • For the Java RMI / JMX service: enable both SSL and password authentication by passing -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.ssl=true and -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=true at JVM startup. If the service has no legitimate external callers, restrict access to localhost or a named management IP range using host firewall rules.
  • Restrict all network services — Redis, Weaviate, database administration interfaces — to the minimum set of source addresses required for operation. Services that have no external callers should not be reachable outside their host or subnet.
  • Inventory all administrative interfaces (phpMyAdmin, Webalizer, Grafana) and confirm each requires authentication before serving responses. Remove or disable any interface not required for active operations.
name: Missing Authentication

Description:
# Description

During technical interviews, {{COMPANY_NAME}} subject matter experts confirmed that no formal data classification policy governed the data handled by the {application_name} application. The team found no documentation describing what categories of data the application ingests, what sensitivity levels apply to each category, or what handling and retention requirements follow from those assignments.

Without classification, data flows to wherever it is convenient: logging infrastructure, development environments, shared file stores. Sensitive fields end up in systems that apply generic controls rather than controls matched to actual risk. The absence of a policy also makes regulatory compliance harder to demonstrate — HIPAA, PCI DSS, and GDPR all require documented understanding of what data an organization holds and where it travels.

# Impact

A data classification policy establishes what kinds of data an organization handles, assigns a sensitivity tier to each, and specifies the controls required for storage, transmission, and disposal at each tier. Without this baseline, technical controls cannot be calibrated to actual risk. High-sensitivity fields receive the same handling as public data, and violations of data minimization or retention requirements are undetectable until an incident reveals them. The indirect consequences are slower incident response, wider breach scope, and difficulty demonstrating compliance to regulators or auditors.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Define a data classification taxonomy for the {application_name} application. At minimum, establish tiers for public, internal, confidential, and restricted data, with concise definitions covering sensitivity level and handling expectations for each.
  • Inventory the data types the application ingests, processes, and stores. Assign each to the appropriate tier based on the harm its exposure would cause.
  • Document handling requirements per tier: permitted storage systems, encryption requirements at rest and in transit, authorized access roles, and retention and disposal schedules.
  • Publish the policy and incorporate it as a required input for design reviews when new features or integrations add data flows to the application.
name: Missing Data Classification Policy

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application allowed authenticated users to perform {action} without first confirming their identity through a step-up check. The workflow presented no password prompt, biometric request, or MFA challenge before accepting and applying the change.

The team signed in as a test user with role {role}, navigated to {feature}, and invoked {action} directly through the UI. The backend accepted the request and committed the change. The team then confirmed the same outcome through direct API calls, ruling out a UI-only enforcement gap. No re-authentication gate was present in either path, and no recent-auth timestamp was validated on the session before the operation was permitted.

Sensitive operations — credential changes, contact information updates, MFA management, and financial account changes — are high-value targets for attackers who have obtained a session token. A step-up check limits the window of damage to sessions where the attacker can also supply the user's current credentials or second factor: a substantially smaller attack population than all stolen sessions.

# Impact

Missing re-authentication for sensitive operations means a stolen session token is sufficient to perform any action the user could perform, including actions that would normally require the user to prove physical presence or knowledge of their credentials. Shared workstations, unattended sessions, session hijacking, and CSRF attack chains all become full-capability attack paths. The risk is highest for operations that change credentials, disable MFA, or authorize financial transactions — exactly the operations an attacker performs first when they obtain a valid session.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Compile a catalog of sensitive operations in the application — at minimum: password changes, email and phone updates, MFA enrollment and removal, payout or banking changes, bulk exports of PII or financial data, and role and permission modifications. Gate each with a re-authentication check before the operation executes.
  • Implement step-up authentication appropriate to the operation's risk level. Password re-entry is the minimum; phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 / WebAuthn) is preferred for operations with financial or credential impact.
  • Enforce the re-authentication check server-side, keyed on a recent-auth timestamp in the session. Client-side enforcement alone is not sufficient.
  • Set a short validity window on the step-up token — five to ten minutes is a reasonable starting point — and require a fresh check if the window expires before the sensitive operation completes.
name: Missing Re-Authentication for Sensitive Action

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{AFFECTED}} in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Azure environment where optional security features were not enabled. Each missing feature narrows the visibility and detection capability available to defenders, reducing the signal between an attacker and a successful, undetected breach.

The features identified as absent or disabled are described in the table below:

Security FeatureWhat it provides
SQL auditingRecords database and server activity to an audit log. Required to detect unauthorized queries, privilege changes, and schema modifications after the fact.
Azure Defender for SQL / threat detectionIdentifies SQL injection attempts, anomalous access patterns, and brute-force activity against database instances in near-real time.
Dynamic data maskingRestricts what low-privilege accounts can read from sensitive columns — SSNs, payment data, contact information — without altering the underlying stored values.
Network WatcherEnables flow logging and packet capture at the Azure network level, needed for post-incident traffic analysis and anomaly detection across VNets.
Virtual machine endpoint protectionProvides malware detection and behavioral monitoring for VMs; required for coverage in Azure Defender's Security Center recommendations.
Automatic security alert notificationsRoutes Security Center alerts to the security team's inbox, closing the gap between alert generation and human response.
# Impact

Optional cloud security features are optional in the configuration sense; the risks they address are not. SQL auditing and threat detection convert an otherwise-opaque database tier into a monitored one: without them, a successful SQL injection or credential-stuffing attack against a database may leave no recoverable log. Dynamic data masking protects sensitive columns from low-privilege accounts that legitimately need database access for unrelated purposes. Endpoint protection and network monitoring provide the telemetry incident responders need to scope a breach after the fact.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable SQL auditing on all Azure SQL databases and servers. Route audit logs to a Log Analytics workspace or storage account with a retention period that matches the organization's logging policy.
  • Enable Azure Defender for SQL on all database instances. Configure alerts for all threat detection types: SQL injection, anomalous access, potential data exfiltration, and brute force.
  • Configure dynamic data masking rules on columns containing PII, financial data, or authentication values. Restrict unmasked access to accounts with a documented business need.
  • Enable Network Watcher in every Azure region that contains in-scope resources. Turn on NSG flow logs and route them to a Log Analytics workspace.
  • For each VM operating system, install the appropriate endpoint protection extension from the Security Center recommendation list and verify coverage in the Security Center dashboard.
  • In Security Center > Pricing & settings > Email notifications, add the security team's address and set the alert severity threshold to match the team's on-call policy.
name: Missing Security Features

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that HTTP responses from the {application_name} application did not include several security headers that instruct browsers to apply additional protective constraints. Browsers implement these features only when the server explicitly enables them; backward compatibility prevents automatic enforcement.

The following headers were absent from application responses:

HeaderWhat it controls
Strict-Transport-SecurityTells the browser to use HTTPS for all future requests to this origin, preventing downgrade attacks and accidental plaintext connections.
X-Frame-OptionsControls whether the application can be embedded in a frame or iframe by external origins. Prevents UI redressing attacks where a transparent overlay tricks users into clicking application controls.
X-Content-Type-OptionsStops browsers from inferring a response's content type from its body, preventing content-sniffing attacks where a file served under one type is reinterpreted as executable HTML or JavaScript.
Content-Security-PolicyDefines which origins may supply scripts, styles, and other resources to the page. A well-configured CSP prevents XSS execution by blocking script loading from unauthorized sources even when injection is present.
# Impact

HTTP security headers reduce the browser's attack surface on the server's behalf. Without Strict-Transport-Security, a network-adjacent attacker can intercept an initial plaintext request before the browser learns to upgrade it. Without X-Frame-Options or a frame-ancestors CSP directive, the application is frameable by any origin and vulnerable to clickjacking. Without X-Content-Type-Options, uploaded files served with permissive content types may execute as scripts in some browsers. Without a CSP, successful XSS injection faces no browser-side barrier against reading cookies, making authenticated requests, or exfiltrating data.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=86400; includeSubDomains initially. After confirming no HTTP-only dependencies remain, increase max-age to 31536000 and consider submitting the domain to the HSTS preload list.
  • Set X-Frame-Options: DENY unless legitimate framing by a known partner origin is required. If framing is required, use the CSP frame-ancestors directive to name the permitted origins explicitly.
  • Set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on all responses.
  • Define a Content-Security-Policy header starting from a restrictive baseline: disallow unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval in script-src, enumerate the CDNs and first-party origins that serve scripts, and set unused resource types to 'none'. Use CSP reporting mode before enforcement to catch breakage.
name: Missing Security Headers

Description:
# Description

Technical interviews with {{COMPANY_NAME}} engineers confirmed that no Software Bill of Materials existed for the {{COMPANY_NAME}} application at the time of the assessment. The team found no inventory of third-party libraries, open-source dependencies, or their versions — neither as a generated pipeline artifact nor as a maintained document.

NIST and CISA both identify SBOMs as a baseline practice for managing software supply chain risk. Without one, answering the question "are we affected by this CVE?" is measured in days rather than minutes. Organizations with SBOMs at the time of the Log4Shell disclosure identified exposure within hours; those without spent days on manual dependency searches across their codebases.

# Impact

An SBOM is a machine-readable inventory of a software artifact's components, their versions, their licenses, and their known vulnerabilities at the time of publication. Its absence does not introduce vulnerabilities directly, but it makes the impact of vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies harder to scope, slower to remediate, and less visible to auditors and regulators. When an incident responder needs to know whether a component is present, the answer comes from the SBOM — or from manual source inspection, which does not scale under the time pressure of an active incident.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Integrate SBOM generation into the build pipeline using a tool such as Syft, CycloneDX, or the SPDX toolchain. Generate an SBOM artifact on every release build and store it alongside the release artifact.
  • Configure the pipeline to warn or fail when new dependencies carry known high-severity CVEs at the time of addition, using a scanner such as Grype or OWASP Dependency-Check against the generated SBOM.
  • Maintain a mapping from each {{COMPANY_NAME}} application to its corresponding SBOM so that vulnerability notifications can be triaged quickly across the portfolio.
  • Review the SBOM on a defined schedule — quarterly is a reasonable starting cadence — and update it when significant dependency changes occur outside the normal release cycle.
name: Missing Software Bill of Materials

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS ECR repositories with imageTagMutability set to MUTABLE, meaning an existing image tag can be overwritten by pushing a new image with the same tag name. The team queried the ECR API to enumerate affected repositories:

aws ecr describe-repositories --query 'repositories[?imageTagMutability == `MUTABLE`].[repositoryName]' --output text

An AWS principal holding ecr:GetAuthorizationToken and ecr:PutImage — or any caller who obtains those permissions through a compromised credential or overly permissive role — could authenticate to ECR, overwrite a production image tag with a malicious variant, and have that image pulled by any container runtime that references the tag by name rather than by digest. The team identified that some pods in Kubernetes clusters referenced image tags resolving to mutable repositories. Where imagePullPolicy was set to Always, those pods would pull a freshly pushed image on each restart, making a poisoned tag effective immediately upon pod recycling.

# Impact

Container image tags are mutable references by default: a tag like latest or v1.2.3 points to whichever image digest was pushed most recently. When a registry does not enforce tag immutability, any caller with push permissions can silently replace a production image. Workloads that pull by tag rather than by digest execute the replacement without any deployment event visible to operators. The result is arbitrary code execution in the container's security context, with access to the environment variables, mounted secrets, and network paths available to the legitimate workload.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Set imageTagMutability to IMMUTABLE on all ECR repositories. This causes the ECR API to reject any push that would overwrite an existing tag, making tag-based image substitution impossible.
  • Update container manifests and deployment pipelines to reference images by digest (image@sha256:<digest>) rather than by tag. This ensures that running workloads continue using the image they were deployed with, even if a tag is later moved.
  • Restrict ECR push permissions to the CI/CD service account and remove ecr:PutImage from any role not involved in the build pipeline. Use read-only credentials for image pull operations.
name: Mutable Container Image Tags

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified an open redirect on the {{DOMAIN}} application. The {endpoint} endpoint accepted a url parameter and issued a 302 response directing the browser to the supplied destination without validating whether that destination was an approved host. Setting url to an attacker-controlled domain caused the application to redirect the user there using {{DOMAIN}} as the originating URL.

An attacker distributes a link using {{DOMAIN}} as the visible hostname. Recipients who trust the domain follow the link, land on the attacker's site, and are presented with phishing content or browser-targeted payloads — with the application's domain reputation borrowed as the delivery mechanism.

# Impact

Open redirect vulnerabilities let an attacker construct a URL under a trusted domain that delivers users to an arbitrary destination. The attack is useful as a phishing delivery mechanism — users see a recognizable hostname before clicking — and can be chained with OAuth and SAML flows that trust redirect_uri values matching a registered domain prefix. The severity depends on what the attacker does with the redirected session; at minimum it enables convincing phishing against users of the affected application.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove user control over the redirect destination where the use case allows. If the endpoint exists to redirect users after login or logout, use a fixed destination or a server-side session value rather than a query parameter.
  • If redirect destinations must be configurable, validate the supplied URL against a strict allowlist of permitted hosts before issuing the redirect. Reject any value that does not match and redirect to a safe default landing page instead.
  • Store dynamic destination data in the server-side session, not in the URL, to prevent tampering without user interaction.
name: Open HTTP Redirection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified an SMTP server on the {network_name} network at {{TARGET_HOST}} that accepted and forwarded mail to external addresses without verifying the sender's identity or restricting the recipient domain. Using swaks, the team sent a message from an arbitrary sender address to an external recipient through the host; the server accepted it for delivery without an authentication challenge at any point in the SMTP session.

swaks --server {ip} --to {external_recipient} --from relay@test.com
<- 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as {queue_id}

An attacker with network access to the SMTP service can use it to deliver spam or phishing mail at scale. Because the messages originate from {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s mail infrastructure, they inherit whatever sender reputation the domain carries, making them harder for recipients to filter and increasing the value of the relay as an attack tool.

# Impact

An open SMTP relay accepts and forwards messages from unauthenticated senders to arbitrary destinations. The practical consequences are reputational and operational: the organization's IP addresses appear on spam blocklists when the relay is discovered and abused, causing legitimate mail to be rejected by recipients. Beyond spam, an attacker can use the relay to send phishing mail that appears to originate from a trusted domain, bypassing recipient-side filters that weight sender domain reputation. The relay also serves as an anonymization point that obscures the true origin of the campaign.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Determine whether the SMTP service has an active business purpose. If not, disable it and update any applications that reference it to use an authorized mail relay.
  • If the service must remain active, configure it to relay only for explicitly permitted sender domains or authenticated sender accounts. Reject relay requests from unauthenticated external senders.
  • Restrict inbound connections to the SMTP port to the IP addresses of legitimate sending systems. Block all other sources at the network or host firewall level.
  • Verify that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records for {{DOMAIN}} are configured to reject or quarantine mail that fails authentication, reducing the value of the relay as a spoofing tool.
name: Open SMTP Mail Relay

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified an SMTP service at {{TARGET_HOST}} on the {network_name} network that relayed mail to external addresses without sender authentication. The team used swaks to confirm that the server accepted a message from a test sender address and queued it for delivery to an external recipient, with no authentication challenge at any point in the SMTP session.

Anyone who can reach the service on port {port} can use it to send mail under any sender address. This is exploitable for phishing campaigns that impersonate {{DOMAIN}} or for spam distribution that degrades the sending domain's reputation with blocklists over time.

# Impact

An SMTP server configured as an open relay forwards messages on behalf of any sender to any recipient without verifying authorization. Abuse typically begins shortly after discovery — open relays are found quickly by automated probing — and proceeds to bulk spam or phishing campaigns using the organization's sending infrastructure. Reputation damage manifests as blocklist entries and causes delivery failures for legitimate mail sent from the same IP ranges or domains.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Evaluate whether the SMTP service is required. If not, disable it and redirect any applications using it to an authenticated relay service.
  • If the service must remain in operation, restrict accepted sender domains to those the organization legitimately controls and require SMTP authentication for any sender. Reject unauthenticated relay requests.
  • Apply firewall rules that limit SMTP access to known client IP addresses. Do not expose the service to the general internet unless it serves as a public-facing mail exchanger — and even then, disable relay for external senders.
name: Open SMTP Relay

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {{COMPANY_NAME}} Heroku applications running on a stack that reached end of life before the date of this assessment. The {stack_name} stack — the operating system layer underlying each Heroku dyno — is no longer receiving security patches, OS updates, or vendor-supported third-party software validation from Heroku.

Applications on an end-of-life stack run on a fixed OS image. Vulnerabilities discovered after the EOL date accumulate without a remediation path. Newer stacks include updated base packages, improved exploit mitigations, and patches for vulnerabilities in the OS libraries that application code links against.

# Impact

An outdated Heroku stack means the operating system environment running application code is no longer maintained. Vulnerabilities in the base OS — in glibc, OpenSSL, or other system libraries — are not patched on EOL stacks, and exploits against those versions remain effective for the life of the deployment. The risk is proportional to the network exposure of the dyno and the sensitivity of the data the application handles.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Upgrade affected applications to the current supported Heroku stack. Consult the Heroku stack deprecation schedule to confirm the current recommended version before migrating.
  • Test the upgraded stack in a staging environment before promoting to production. OS library version changes between stacks can affect binary compatibility for native extensions and compiled dependencies.
  • Establish a process to monitor Heroku stack deprecation announcements and schedule migrations before EOL dates, not after.
name: Outdated Application Stack

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} iOS application disabled App Transport Security by setting NSAllowsArbitraryLoads to true in the NSAppTransportSecurity dictionary of Info.plist. This key overrides ATS entirely, allowing the application to make plaintext HTTP connections to any host without minimum TLS version enforcement or certificate validation requirements.

With ATS disabled, any network connection the application makes over HTTP is unencrypted and subject to interception. An attacker in a man-in-the-middle position — on the same Wi-Fi network, or operating a rogue access point — can read and modify that traffic without triggering any application-level warning. The configuration also removes ATS enforcement from third-party SDKs and web views loaded within the application, not only from first-party code.

# Impact

App Transport Security enforces HTTPS for all network connections and imposes minimum TLS version and cipher suite requirements, providing a backstop against both plaintext transmission and weak TLS configurations. Setting NSAllowsArbitraryLoads to true removes that backstop globally. Any connection the application or its embedded components makes over HTTP — to fetch content, submit credentials, or carry session tokens — is readable by a passive network observer.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove the NSAllowsArbitraryLoads key from Info.plist, or set its value to false. This restores ATS enforcement for all connections the application makes.
  • If specific domains require HTTP connections for a documented technical reason, use NSExceptionDomains to carve out named exceptions rather than disabling ATS globally. Each exception should be as narrow as possible.
  • Audit third-party SDKs bundled in the application for their own ATS exceptions and remove or replace those that require broad exceptions to function.
name: Overly Permissive App Transport Security (ATS) Settings

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified overly permissive cross-domain policy files on the {application_name} application. The crossdomain.xml policy at {hostname}/crossdomain.xml used a wildcard allow-access-from directive, granting every domain read access to application content from Flash contexts. The team also found a Silverlight policy at {url}/clientaccesspolicy.xml with a wildcard domain uri that permitted any domain to access all resources under the application root.

An attacker who controls content on any domain — including a free subdomain on a shared hosting provider — can use a Flash or Silverlight object to make authenticated requests to the application on behalf of a logged-in user and forward the responses to the attacker's domain.

# Impact

Cross-domain policy files govern which external origins embedded plugin objects may access when making requests to the domain hosting the policy. A wildcard policy is functionally equivalent to removing the same-origin policy for those plugin runtimes: any site can read any response the application returns to a logged-in user. An attacker-controlled page that the victim visits while authenticated to the application can silently exfiltrate any data those endpoints expose.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace wildcard entries in crossdomain.xml with an explicit allowlist of domains that have a documented technical need for cross-domain access. If no such domains exist, set permitted-cross-domain-policies to none or remove the file entirely.
  • Apply the same restriction to clientaccesspolicy.xml: list permitted domains explicitly and restrict grant-to paths to the minimum required.
  • Separate any functionality that must be reachable by third-party sites onto a dedicated subdomain with its own narrowly scoped policy, isolated from the authenticated session context of the main application.
  • Avoid cross-domain wildcards in production environments. Validate each trusted domain before adding it to the allowlist.
name: Overly Permissive Cross-Domain Policy

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified network file shares containing sensitive data that were accessible to all authenticated users in the {{DOMAIN}} domain. Using a low-privilege domain account, the team browsed multiple shares and located files containing personally identifiable information, including Social Security numbers and employee records.

In one case, a spreadsheet contained a full list of names and SSNs accessible to any domain user. In another, a backup of an executive's Outlook PST file was present on an open share. The team did not access or download the PST file given its sensitivity, but its presence on an unrestricted share means any authenticated domain user — or any attacker who has compromised any domain account — can reach it.

# Impact

Overly permissive file shares allow any authenticated domain user to read data that should be accessible only to a defined set of principals. When those shares contain credentials, PII, or financial records, a compromised account — even a low-privilege one obtained through phishing — immediately grants access to that data. File share contents also frequently include credentials embedded in scripts, configuration files, and email backups, providing a path to further privilege escalation.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Audit all file shares in the {{DOMAIN}} domain. For each share, document the intended audience and compare it against the current access control list. Revoke access from any principal that does not have a documented business need.
  • Restrict shares containing sensitive data — PII, credentials, financial records, executive communications — to specific named individuals or groups. Remove domain-wide groups such as Authenticated Users or Domain Users from the ACL.
  • Implement a recurring review process for file share permissions. Access grants should require periodic renewal, and anomalous access to sensitive shares should generate an alert.
  • Scan file shares periodically for files matching credential patterns, SSN formats, or payment card numbers and treat discoveries as remediation items.
name: Overly Permissive File Shares

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified firewall rules in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} GCP environment that did not enforce meaningful network segmentation. The team observed rules permitting unrestricted inbound access on all ports, rules exposing sensitive service ports to all sources, rules allowing broad port ranges, and default GCP firewall rules that Compute Engine applies to every VPC automatically.

The default GCP rules — default-allow-internal, default-allow-ssh, default-allow-rdp, and default-allow-icmp — apply to all VMs in the default VPC unless explicitly removed. default-allow-internal permits all traffic on all ports among VMs in the same network; default-allow-ssh and default-allow-rdp expose ports 22 and 3389 to any source. Combined with public IP assignment or internet-facing load balancers, these defaults expose administrative services to the internet without any active misconfiguration by the administrator.

Variants

Heroku: The team identified overly permissive firewall rules applied to Heroku Private Space configurations in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment, allowing access from broader source ranges than the private space model requires. Network isolation in Heroku Private Spaces depends on correctly scoped space firewall rules; overly broad rules undermine that isolation model.

# Impact

Overly permissive firewall rules extend the attack surface of cloud workloads beyond what their function requires. Default GCP rules apply to every VM in a network without administrator action, so they represent a standing exposure that grows as new VMs are added. Unrestricted SSH and RDP access enables brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks against administrative services. Unrestricted internal traffic means an attacker who compromises any single host can reach all other hosts in the same network on any port, with no network-layer obstacle to lateral movement.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Delete the four default GCP firewall rules from all VPC networks. Create named replacement rules with documented purposes and source ranges limited to the specific addresses or internal CIDR blocks that require access.
  • Audit all existing firewall rules and remove any that allow access on all ports, cover wide port ranges, or accept connections from 0.0.0.0/0 on sensitive ports (22, 3389, 1433, 3306, and others). Replace each with a rule scoped to the minimum ports and sources required.
  • Route administrative access (SSH, RDP) through a VPN or bastion host rather than exposing the service port directly to the internet.
  • For Heroku Private Spaces: review each space's firewall rules and remove allow entries that exceed the required inbound sources. Document the intended network topology and enforce it through named, described rules.
name: Overly Permissive Firewall Rules

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a workflow node in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} platform — accessible through the POST /api/workflows/{workflowId}/stream endpoint — that ran with an AWS IAM execution role whose permissions substantially exceeded its function. The node exposed arbitrary command execution through a Bash tool. Using the AWS SDK default credential chain from within that Bash tool, the team acted as the node's IAM role and confirmed it held permissions to read secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and to list and download objects from a shared multi-tenant S3 bucket.

The team retrieved a live production API key from Secrets Manager. The team then listed the shared S3 bucket and found it contained Claude Code session transcripts for multiple tenants, organized by organization and user IDs. A partial enumeration identified {{AFFECTED_COUNT}} distinct organizations and {number} users. The team downloaded a 265KB session transcript belonging to a different organization, confirming cross-tenant read access to other customers' conversation data.

# Impact

An overly permissive IAM principal converts any capability the workload exposes into an API call an attacker can make against the broader AWS environment. Here the Bash tool was the capability; the excess permissions were Secrets Manager read access and cross-tenant S3 read access. The disclosed data included a live production credential — immediately usable to impersonate the service — and the full conversation transcripts of users across multiple organizations. Cross-tenant data access in a shared platform is a direct breach of each affected tenant's confidentiality, regardless of the attacker's intent.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Reduce the execution role's S3 permissions to the specific path prefix for the current execution's own workspace (workspaces/orgs/<orgId>/users/<userId>/chat/<chatId>/executions/<executionId>/). Apply an explicit Deny on s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject for the rest of the shared bucket.
  • Remove Secrets Manager access from the node's execution role. If a specific secret is needed at runtime, inject only that value through the container environment at launch time rather than granting the runtime broad GetSecretValue access.
  • Rotate the exposed production API key immediately and review CloudTrail for prior GetSecretValue and S3 access events from this role to scope potential historical exposure.
  • Audit all other workflow node execution roles in the platform and apply the same least-privilege pattern: each role should permit only the specific resources and actions the node's documented function requires.
name: Overly Permissive IAM Principal

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified IAM roles in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment whose trust policies allowed a broader set of principals to assume them than the roles' function required. In several cases, trust policies specified account root ARNs as trusted principals. A root-level trust grants sts:AssumeRole to any IAM principal in the trusted account that has been granted that action — not only to a named set of principals.

The team demonstrated lateral movement by following trust relationships that allowed a privileged role in one account to be assumed using credentials obtained in a second account. After assuming an administrative role in the first account, the team used cross-account trust to assume an equivalent role in a second account, gaining administrative access to it as well. The trust relationships made the accounts' privilege boundaries interdependent: compromise of any account with a trust relationship pointing at a privileged role in another account provided a lateral escalation path.

# Impact

IAM role trust policies define which principals can assume a role and inherit its permissions. When a trust policy names an account root — arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root — rather than specific IAM principals, any identity in that account that holds sts:AssumeRole permission can assume the role. For highly privileged roles, this means the impact of a compromised low-privilege account in a trusted account extends to full administrative access in the trusting account. In multi-account environments, overly permissive cross-account trusts can convert a development account compromise into administrative access to production.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
