The application server at {{TARGET_HOST}} sent an HTTP GET request to the team's server and retrieved the specified resource, confirming that the application would fetch any URL a caller supplied. By repeating this process with addresses pointing to internal service names and RFC 1918 ranges, an attacker could map what services the application host can reach and read responses from those services — including cloud provider instance metadata endpoints that return temporary IAM credentials.

# Impact

Server-side request forgery turns a web application into an HTTP proxy. The application sends requests to destinations chosen by the attacker rather than its own logic. The exploitable surface depends on what the application host can reach: internal APIs that trust requests from internal IPs, cloud metadata endpoints that return credentials scoped to the host's role, or other back-end services not exposed to the internet. No credentials are required to trigger the behavior.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Redesign the {endpoint} functionality to fetch XML documents only from a defined allowlist of approved server addresses. Reject any URL not on the list without attempting retrieval.
  • Apply strict input validation to any user-supplied URL: validate the scheme, hostname, and port against the allowlist before making a connection. Reject rather than sanitize invalid input.
  • Implement server-side validation only; client-side validation is bypassed trivially through an intercepting proxy.
  • Disable IMDSv1 on all AWS resources and require IMDSv2 to limit the impact if SSRF reaches the instance metadata endpoint.
name: Server-side Request Forgery

Description:
# Description

The assessment team confirmed that {number} JBoss application servers on the {network_name} network ran the JBoss service process under the root account. After gaining code execution on the service through a separate finding, the team ran id and observed uid=0(root). Every file on the filesystem, every system command, and every configuration file was accessible to the compromised process without any further privilege escalation.

# Impact

A service running as root collapses two distinct attack phases — initial access and privilege escalation — into one. Achieving code execution within the service is equivalent to achieving root on the host. From that position an attacker can read any file, write to any directory, install persistent backdoors, and pivot to adjacent systems using credentials or keys stored on disk, all without needing a separate local escalation step.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Create a dedicated, unprivileged OS user account for each service. Run each service under its own account with no login shell and no membership in administrative groups.
  • Audit the filesystem and network permissions required by each service and grant only those — nothing broader. Review periodically as the application evolves.
  • Apply operating system–level controls such as systemd security directives (PrivateTmp, ProtectSystem, NoNewPrivileges) or equivalent to restrict what a compromised service process can do even if it runs without administrative credentials.
name: Service Running with Unnecessary Privileges

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the local administrator account password was shared across multiple servers in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} {network} environment. After gaining access to {host1} through a separate finding, the team extracted the local administrator's NT hash using secretsdump. The team passed that hash directly to {host2} without cracking it and obtained full administrative access — confirming the password was identical on both hosts.

From {host2}, the team extracted the cleartext password for {user1}, a domain administrator account in the {domain1} domain. That credential provided complete control over all domain-connected systems and data. The same shared local administrator password was present in the {domain2} and {domain3} domains, extending the impact across trust boundaries.

# Impact

Shared credentials convert a single-host compromise into multi-host access. An attacker who extracts an NT hash from one machine can relay or pass it directly to any other machine using the same password — no cracking required. When shared accounts span trust zones, access obtained in a lower-trust segment translates directly to control over higher-trust systems. Audit logs cannot attribute activity to an individual because the account has no individual owner.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Assign a unique password to the local administrator account on every system. Use Microsoft Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) to generate, store, and rotate these passwords automatically through Active Directory.
  • Do not share administrative credentials across heterogeneous resource types such as databases, application servers, and network devices.
  • Remove domain user accounts from the Local Administrators group on workstations and servers unless required for documented business operations.
  • Conduct regular access reviews to confirm that all credentials comply with the principle of unique identifying credentials per resource and per user.
name: Shared Credentials

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified that the {app} application used AES-CBC encryption with a static initialization vector. Encrypting the same plaintext string multiple times produced identical ciphertext each time — a direct consequence of the fixed IV. The team confirmed the pattern by encrypting several known strings and comparing the resulting ciphertext values across invocations.

Because the IV does not change between encryptions, an attacker who can request multiple ciphertexts of chosen plaintexts can build a lookup table mapping plaintext blocks to ciphertext blocks. Entries in that table can decrypt other ciphertexts that share a known first block — without possessing the key.

# Impact

CBC mode chains encryption blocks: each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption. The initialization vector primes that chain for the first block. A static IV means two messages with identical leading bytes always produce identical ciphertext at the first block, leaking structure and enabling chosen-plaintext attacks. For data with limited variability — short identifiers, status values, fixed-format fields — the lookup table can cover the full input space and allow decryption without the key.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Generate a fresh cryptographically random IV for every encryption operation. Use a cryptographically secure random number generator (SecureRandom in Java, os.urandom in Python, or equivalent) — do not derive the IV deterministically.
  • Transmit or store the IV alongside the ciphertext so the decryption party can use it. The IV is not secret; it only needs to be unpredictable before encryption.
  • Consider migrating to AES-GCM, which provides both confidentiality and authenticated integrity in a single operation and does not share the IV reuse vulnerabilities of CBC mode.
name: Static IV in CBC Mode

Description:
# Description

The assessment team observed that the subdomain {domain} in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} DNS configuration resolved to {ip_address}, an address hosted by {third_party_vendor}. The configuration appeared intentional — likely associated with a testing or staging integration — and no security vulnerability was actively exploited. The finding is documented for inventory and risk awareness purposes.

The risk is indirect: if the external service at that address is deprovisioned without {{COMPANY_NAME}} removing the DNS record first, an attacker may be able to register the same resource on the external platform and serve content from the {{COMPANY_NAME}} subdomain without authorization.

# Impact

A DNS record that points an organization-controlled subdomain at an external IP or hostname delegates trust to that external host. Visitors to the subdomain interact with whatever content the external provider serves, under the organization's domain name. If the provider decommissions the resource and the DNS record is not removed, any party who re-registers that resource on the external platform inherits control of the subdomain — a pattern called subdomain takeover.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Confirm whether the DNS record for {domain} pointing to {third_party_vendor} is intentional and still required for a current business function.
  • If the record is no longer needed, remove it from the {{COMPANY_NAME}} DNS zone immediately.
  • If the record is required, confirm that {{COMPANY_NAME}} controls the resource registered on the {third_party_vendor} platform and that it cannot be claimed by a third party if the service is cancelled.
  • Establish a process to audit external DNS records periodically and remove any that no longer point to resources under {{COMPANY_NAME}}'s control.
name: Subdomain Points to External Platform

Description:
# Description

The assessment team extracted the complete system prompts for the {application_name1} and {application_name2} applications using an ASCII art–based jailbreak technique. The approach worked by asking the model to imagine its system prompt content rendered as ASCII art and then provide the underlying text, without producing the visual representation. After a few benign ASCII art exchanges primed the conversation, the model became willing to process sensitive content through this framing.

The team first retrieved a list of high-level section headings from the system prompt, then requested each section's full content individually. The guard rails section, tool configuration, and operational instructions were all recovered this way. Both the internal {application_name1} and the external {application_name2} applications were vulnerable to the same technique.

With the system prompt in hand, an attacker can map the model's stated restrictions, identify available tools, and construct inputs specifically designed to stay within the model's described boundaries while triggering unintended behavior. The same ASCII art framing also coerced the model into producing content it would otherwise decline to generate.

# Impact

A language model's system prompt defines its operational boundaries: what tools it can call, what topics it declines, and what priorities it follows. When the prompt is recoverable, an attacker can study those boundaries to find gaps. System prompts may also contain hard-coded secrets — API keys, internal hostnames, tool credentials — placed there during development and never intended to reach user-visible output.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Explicitly instruct the model not to reference, reproduce, or paraphrase any part of its system prompt in user-visible output. Include this as a guard rail in the system prompt itself and validate it against adversarial probing during QA.
  • Deploy a content inspection layer — regular expressions, classifier models, or a guard model — that flags output matching patterns of system instructions, internal metadata, or secrets before responses reach users.
  • Treat all user inputs that explicitly request the system prompt, internal instructions, or model configuration as high-risk signals. Log them and apply additional scrutiny.
  • Do not embed secrets — API keys, tokens, passwords, internal hostnames — in system prompts. Store them in a secrets manager and inject them at the API call layer, where they are not visible to the model as text.
name: System Prompt Leakage

Description:
# Description

The assessment team discovered {number} Azure App Services in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment that were reachable from the internet without requiring authentication. Azure App Services do not apply authentication controls by default. Without explicit configuration, any caller who can reach the service endpoint can invoke its functionality.

# Impact

An App Service without authentication controls accepts requests from any caller who can reach its endpoint. The exposure depends on what the service does: an internal API that trusts caller identity exposes all of its operations without any credential check, while a service that reads from or writes to storage, databases, or downstream APIs extends that exposure to those back-end resources as well.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• For each App Service that should not accept unauthenticated access, navigate to the Authentication blade in the Azure portal, enable App Service Authentication, and select an appropriate identity provider — Azure Active Directory is the preferred option for internal services.
  • Review all App Services in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment to confirm that authentication requirements match their intended access model. Services that must be public should implement application-layer authentication rather than relying on network controls alone.
name: Unauthenticated App Services

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that Kubernetes etcd encryption was not enabled on the {cluster_name} cluster. Inspecting the kube-apiserver flags confirmed the --encryption-provider-config flag was absent. Kubernetes stores Secrets, ConfigMaps, service account tokens, and other sensitive objects in etcd as plaintext by default. Any party with direct read access to the etcd datastore can retrieve those objects without going through the Kubernetes API or its RBAC controls.

For this cluster, etcd runs on the managed control plane and is not directly accessible to pods or cluster users, which partially limits immediate exposure.

Variants

  • AWS: The assessment team identified AWS resources in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment configured without encryption at rest. AWS managed services support encryption through KMS-managed keys, but encryption must be explicitly enabled — it is not on by default for all resource types.
  • Azure: The assessment team identified Azure resources in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment configured without encryption at rest. Azure supports encryption at rest across most storage services, but customer-managed key configurations and per-service encryption settings must be verified and enabled explicitly.
# Impact

Data stored without encryption is readable in full by anyone who gains access to the underlying storage layer, bypassing any application-level or API-level access controls. For Kubernetes etcd, the stored data includes every Secret in the cluster — TLS private keys, database passwords, service account tokens, and other sensitive values. Regulatory frameworks including PCI DSS, HIPAA, and SOC 2 treat encryption of sensitive data at rest as a baseline requirement.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable etcd encryption using a KMS provider. Configure --encryption-provider-config on the kube-apiserver with an AES-GCM or KMS envelope encryption provider.
  • For AWS environments, manage encryption keys with AWS KMS to automate key creation, rotation, and revocation without additional operational overhead.
  • For Azure environments, enable encryption at rest with customer-managed keys for each resource type where sensitive data is stored, and verify that the setting is applied to existing resources as well as new ones.
  • After enabling encryption, rewrite existing etcd objects to ensure previously stored plaintext data is encrypted. Run kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f - to force a re-write through the encryption provider.
name: Unencrypted Data at Rest

Description:
# Description

The assessment team reviewed the IAM credential report for the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment and found that user accounts with console access — including the root account and accounts holding the AdministratorAccess policy — did not have MFA enabled. The root account has no permission boundary; a session authenticated as root has full, unrestricted access to every AWS service and resource in the account.

The team also found roles with AssumeRole trust policies that did not require MFA as a condition. A password alone is sufficient to assume these roles, which return temporary credentials scoped to the role's permissions.

Variants

  • Heroku: The assessment team found that MFA was not enforced on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Heroku environment. Accounts with administrative access to Heroku can modify application configuration, environment variables, and connected add-ons. MFA is the primary control preventing unauthorized access to these capabilities through a compromised password.
# Impact

Without MFA, a stolen or guessed password is sufficient to open a console or API session. Password exposure can come from phishing, credential reuse from a breach on another service, or retrieval from an unsecured secrets store or repository. MFA adds a time-limited second factor that is not reusable across sessions — a compromised password alone cannot produce a valid session.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Create a custom IAM policy that denies all console and API actions except MFA enrollment for any user who has not enrolled an MFA device. Attach it to all IAM users with console access. AWS publishes a tutorial for this pattern in the IAM documentation.
  • Enable MFA on the root account immediately. Use a hardware token or virtual MFA device and store the recovery codes in a separate, secured location.
  • Add an aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true condition to AssumeRole trust policies on sensitive roles so that assuming them requires an active MFA session.
name: Unenforced Multi-factor Authentication

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {number} applications in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Heroku environment in the default unlocked state. Heroku applications are unlocked by default; locking them restricts visibility of the application's collaborator list, add-on configurations, and permission settings to the application owner.

# Impact

An unlocked Heroku application exposes basic configuration and team membership data to any member of the team to which the application belongs. In environments where team membership is broadly granted, this allows users to view add-on configurations, environment variable keys, and application settings that are not relevant to their role — information that could be used to plan targeted attacks against the application or its integrations.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Lock all production Heroku applications using the Heroku CLI: heroku apps:lock --app {application_name}. Locking prevents team members from viewing application details they do not need access to.
  • Review team membership for each production application and remove collaborators who no longer require access.
name: Unlocked Applications

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a function in the {application_name} API that would disclose session data to any caller who could supply an arbitrary session ID — if the function were reachable through an HTTP route. The getSession function in routes\session.js at line 163 accepted a sessionid path parameter and returned the matching session record from the database, including account state, without any authorization check on the requesting caller.

No HTTP route in the current {application_name} repository exposed a sessionid path parameter, so the function was unreachable in the deployed application. The risk is forward-looking: if a route is added later that includes this parameter, or if the function is reused in another context, the session disclosure path becomes active without any modification to the function itself.

# Impact

Dead code that would expose sensitive data if reachable is not a current vulnerability, but it is a future one. Its presence also signals that the codebase is not being regularly pruned. Removing it eliminates the risk entirely rather than relying on routing constraints that can change through future development without alerting the team to the security consequence.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove the getSession function from routes\session.js entirely if it serves no production purpose. Dead code that handles sensitive data without authorization checks should not remain in the codebase.
  • Incorporate dead code identification into the development and code review process. Any code path that accesses session or account data should require an explicit authorization check on the requesting principal, not rely on the absence of a route that reaches it.
name: Unnecessary Code

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified several categories of files on {{COMPANY_NAME}} servers accessible beyond their intended audience. Maven repository artifacts in /export/home/ directories were world-readable and world-writable (permissions 777). The .ssh directory for the {user} service account — including authorized_keys, known_hosts, and the RSA private key — carried the same permissions, allowing any local user on the server to read the private key or modify who can authenticate via SSH.

On {number} servers in the {environment_name} environment, the team found PCI audit report files that were world-readable and contained entries extracted from /etc/shadow. Those entries included password hashes for {user2}, {user3}, {user4}, {user5}, and {user6}. The hashes can be used as direct input to offline cracking tools without any further access to the systems.

# Impact

Files with overly permissive permissions or files left on systems past their useful life create attack surface disproportionate to their business value. SSH key material and password hashes have immediate value to an attacker; world-writable SSH directories allow any local account to insert its own public key into the authorized_keys file, granting persistent access as the account owner.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Restrict permissions on all .ssh directories to 700 (owner read/write/execute only) and on files within them to 600 (owner read/write only). Apply these permissions to all service account home directories.
  • Review files in home directories across the reported servers and confirm that permissions match intended access. Remove any file without a current business justification for being present.
  • Remove PCI audit report files from production servers after use. If retention is required, store them in a location accessible only to the team responsible for audit review.
  • Include a file permission and content audit step in deployment and maintenance procedures. Apply it each time updates are applied to active systems.
name: Unnecessary Files

Description:
# Description

The assessment team queried the DNS server for the {domain} zone using an AXFR request and received a complete zone transfer, disclosing the hostname-to-IP-address mapping for the entire domain. No source address restriction was configured on the server — the transfer succeeded from the team's external position without authentication.

Zone transfer data provides a ready-made host inventory. It removes the need for slow or potentially alerting port scanning and reduces the time required to identify targets across the environment.

# Impact

DNS zone transfers are designed for replication between authoritative name servers. When unrestricted, any host that can reach the DNS service can pull the complete zone file — a structured map of every hostname in the domain alongside its corresponding IP address, produced by the environment's own infrastructure.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Identify all systems with a legitimate business need to perform zone transfers — typically secondary DNS servers — and restrict AXFR requests to those source addresses only.
  • Verify the restriction by attempting a zone transfer from an unauthorized source after the change is applied. The request should be refused.
name: Unrestricted DNS Zone Transfer

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified Azure resources in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment — including Key Vaults, storage accounts, and SQL servers — that had no network-level access restrictions configured. These services accepted connections from any IP address. Accessing them still requires valid Azure credentials, but without network filtering the credential attack surface is the entire internet rather than a defined set of trusted networks.

# Impact

Service endpoints that accept connections from any source place the full weight of access control on credentials alone. A credential obtained through phishing, discovered in a repository, or reused from another breach gives an attacker direct access to the service from any location. Network-level restrictions do not replace authentication, but they reduce the set of positions from which an attacker can attempt to authenticate — making exploitation harder even when credentials are compromised.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Review each Key Vault, storage account, and SQL server in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} Azure environment to determine whether public internet access is required for its business function.
  • For services that do not require public access, configure network rules to allow connections only from specific trusted IP ranges, Azure Virtual Networks, or private endpoints.
  • For services that must be reachable from the internet, confirm that authentication and authorization controls are sufficient and apply additional monitoring for anomalous access patterns.
name: Unrestricted Service Endpoints

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a code path in the {endpoint} API where a user-supplied URL parameter was passed directly to Python's getattr to select a method to call on a class instance. By submitting the name of a method from a parent class — get_object_or_error on HttpAPI — the team caused the server to attempt to invoke it. The HTTP 500 response that followed included the function's signature in the response body, disclosing internal class structure.

The team was not able to supply the required arguments to the selected method in a way that produced further output beyond the error disclosure. The boundary is narrow: a different target method or one that takes no arguments could allow an attacker to invoke arbitrary server-side behavior without the argument constraint.

# Impact

Reflection calls that accept user-supplied strings to select methods or attributes turn the input into code execution control. An attacker who can name any method on any reachable object can invoke server-side logic the application did not intend to expose through that endpoint. Depending on the methods accessible from the class hierarchy, outcomes range from information disclosure through error messages to arbitrary code execution.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove the getattr call that uses user-supplied input directly. Replace it with an explicit mapping — a dictionary or if/elif chain — that maps allowed operation names to their corresponding methods.
  • If reflection must be used, apply a strict allowlist of permitted method names before passing the value to getattr. Reject any input not on the list and log the attempt.
name: Unsafe Reflection

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {resource_types} in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment that were no longer assigned to active users, groups, or instances. These resources were not exploitable in their current state but their continued presence adds unnecessary complexity to the environment and creates a risk of accidental reuse in future configurations.

# Impact

Unused AWS resources do not represent a current security vulnerability. However, unassigned IAM entities and inactive resources increase the surface area that must be reviewed during access audits and can be mistakenly repurposed in ways that create unintended permissions. Removing them keeps the environment's permission inventory accurate and reduces audit noise.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Delete all unused or unassigned resources identified in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment. Confirm each deletion against current account activity to avoid removing resources that are inactive but still referenced.
  • Establish a periodic review process — quarterly at minimum — to identify and remove AWS resources that are no longer actively used.
name: Unused AWS Resources

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found IAM entities in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} GCP environment assigned basic roles — Viewer, Editor, or Owner — rather than predefined or custom roles. Basic roles predate GCP's IAM system and apply coarse, project-wide permission sets. Each time GCP adds a new service or API to the platform, any principal assigned a basic role automatically gains permissions for it without any review or approval.

# Impact

Basic roles grant broad permissions across the entire project that cannot be scoped to specific resources or services. An Editor-level principal can read and write most project resources regardless of whether those capabilities are relevant to their function. Predefined and custom roles allow permissions to be limited to exactly what a principal needs, making over-permissioned accounts easier to detect and reducing the damage radius of any single account compromise.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Review all IAM entities in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} GCP environment that are currently assigned a basic role.
  • Replace each basic role assignment with a predefined or custom role scoped to the permissions the entity actually requires. Predefined roles exist for most GCP services; custom roles can be defined for combinations not covered by predefined options.
  • Remove basic role assignments once the replacement roles are verified to be functioning correctly.
name: Use of Basic Roles

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that workloads in the {cluster_name} Kubernetes cluster referenced container images by tag rather than by SHA256 digest. A tag is a mutable pointer: it can be reassigned to a different image version without the tag string changing. If the upstream registry does not enforce tag immutability, an attacker with write access to the registry can push a modified image under the same tag and have it pulled by the cluster on the next pod creation or restart.

The team identified tagged images by querying pod specs and filtering out digest references:

$ kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[].spec.containers[].image' | grep -v "@sha256"

The team did not identify any issues with the content of the affected images. The recommendation to use digests is precautionary.

# Impact

Container image tags are labels, not integrity guarantees. An image deployed by tag runs whatever the registry currently associates with that tag. A SHA256 digest is immutable — it is a hash of the image manifest content and always refers to exactly the artifact that was present when the digest was recorded. Substituting a malicious image under an existing tag produces no change in the pod spec that would trigger a review or alert.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Deploy container images using SHA256 digests rather than tags. Replace tag-based image references in pod specs and deployment manifests with the corresponding digest (image@sha256:<digest>).
  • Enable tag immutability in each affected image's registry repository to prevent existing tags from being overwritten.
name: Use of Container Image Tags

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified {number} IAM users in the in-scope {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS accounts. IAM users are assigned long-term credentials — access keys and console passwords — that do not expire automatically. Long-term credentials that are leaked, committed to a source repository, or stored in an unsecured configuration file remain valid until explicitly rotated or revoked.

Several of the identified users held access keys older than {age_threshold}. Keys that have been active for an extended period have passed through backup cycles, deployment pipelines, and environment copies where they may have been logged or retained in locations that are no longer actively monitored.

# Impact

IAM user credentials are long-lived by design, which is a structural disadvantage relative to role-based temporary credentials. Access keys that have been in use for months or years have had more opportunities to be exposed through routine operations. IAM roles generate credentials valid for a bounded session — typically a few hours. When those expire, an attacker must trigger fresh credential issuance, which is logged and auditable, rather than simply reusing a key that has been valid for a year.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Migrate existing workloads that use IAM user access keys to IAM roles with temporary credentials. CI/CD platforms, IaC tools, and automation services all support role-based access.
  • Use federated access for individual user access to the AWS console rather than IAM user passwords. Connect federation to an existing identity provider so accounts are managed centrally.
  • For any IAM user that must remain, rotate access keys on a documented schedule and revoke keys that have not been used within {inactivity_threshold}.
name: Use of IAM Users

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found {number} IAM principals in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment — users, groups, and roles — with inline policies attached directly to them rather than managed policies. Inline policies are scoped to a single principal; when permissions must be updated, each principal holding an inline policy must be modified individually.

# Impact

Inline policies cannot be centrally managed or reused. When a permission set must be updated across multiple principals — for a new service restriction, a compliance change, or a privilege reduction — inline policies require a separate edit on every affected principal. Managed policies propagate changes automatically to all principals they are attached to and appear in a single auditable location in the IAM console.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Convert existing inline policies to managed policies. Create a managed policy containing the same permissions, attach it to the affected principals, and remove the inline policy.
  • Going forward, use managed policies for all IAM permission grants. Document the purpose of each managed policy and apply it consistently according to role or function rather than per-principal.
  • Record IAM policy changes in a formal change management process to maintain an audit trail of when permissions were granted, modified, or removed.
name: Use of Inline Policies

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application used AES in Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode for {encryption_context}. To confirm the behavior, the team encrypted a set of identical plaintexts and observed that the resulting ciphertexts matched exactly each time. ECB encrypts each block independently with the same key, so two equal plaintext blocks always produce equal ciphertext — regardless of where they appear in the message.

{demonstration}

An attacker who can request ciphertexts of chosen plaintexts can build a lookup table mapping ciphertext blocks to their plaintext counterparts. For data with limited variability — short identifiers, status flags, fixed-format fields — the table can cover the full input space and allow decryption without the key.

# Impact

ECB mode reveals plaintext structure through patterns in the ciphertext. Identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks, leaking information about message content without requiring the key. For messages longer than one block, the independent encryption of each block also enables cut-and-paste attacks: ciphertext blocks can be rearranged or substituted to alter the decrypted plaintext at the receiver, without possessing the key.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace AES-ECB with AES-GCM for all encryption operations in the {application_name} application. GCM provides confidentiality through authenticated encryption — the ciphertext cannot be modified without detection, and the mode does not leak block-level patterns.
  • Generate a fresh cryptographically random nonce for each GCM encryption operation. Never reuse a nonce with the same key.
name: Use of Insecure ECB Encryption Mode

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified that the {app_name} application used an unauthenticated cipher for {encryption_type} of {data}. Ciphers in this class — CBC or CTR mode without a message authentication code — encrypt data but provide no mechanism for the receiver to detect whether the ciphertext was modified in transit or at rest. The team obtained a ciphertext through {access_context} and performed a bit-flipping attack: by XORing targeted bytes of the ciphertext, the team produced a controlled change in the decrypted plaintext. The modification caused {abnormal_behavior}.

The application accepted the modified ciphertext without error and processed the resulting plaintext as if it were authentic.

# Impact

Unauthenticated ciphers provide confidentiality but not integrity. The receiver has no way to distinguish a modified ciphertext from the original. In CBC mode, flipping a bit in ciphertext block N corrupts that block's decryption but produces a predictable, controlled change in the plaintext of block N+1 — a property that allows targeted plaintext manipulation without knowing the key. Without an authentication tag, no error is raised on the modified input.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace the unauthenticated cipher with AES-GCM, which provides both confidentiality and integrity authentication in a single operation. AES-GCM rejects any ciphertext that has been modified and produces an authentication error before decryption proceeds.
  • If replacing the cipher mode is not immediately feasible, add an HMAC over the ciphertext and verify it before decryption. Compare the HMAC using a constant-time comparison function to prevent timing-based bypass.
name: Use of Unauthenticated Encryption Ciphers

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} {endpoint_type} process revealed whether a submitted account identifier was registered in the application. Submitting a username that did not exist produced a response that differed from the one returned for a valid account — either a distinct error message, a different HTTP status code, or a measurable difference in response time. The difference was consistent and reproducible across multiple requests.

Using a candidate username list sourced from public data, the team identified the following valid accounts: {{ACCOUNTS}}.

Variants

  • Drupal User Endpoint: The assessment team found Drupal-powered applications on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network where an unauthenticated API endpoint returned registered usernames and email addresses without requiring any credentials.
  • WordPress API: The assessment team identified a WordPress application in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external scope where the /wp-json/wp/v2/users endpoint returned all registered usernames, display names, and user IDs to unauthenticated callers.
# Impact

User enumeration produces a confirmed list of valid account identifiers. That list removes uncertainty from credential attacks: password spraying and credential stuffing can target real accounts rather than guessing both username and password simultaneously. Combined with the target's known email format, enumerated usernames also supply valid addresses for phishing campaigns.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Return the same response — identical status code, body, and response time — for failed authentication, password reset, and account signup requests, regardless of whether the failure is caused by the username or the password. The response must be indistinguishable to the caller.
  • For password reset flows, send the reset email if the address is registered and do nothing if it is not. Surface the same message either way: for example, "If that address is in our system, you'll receive an email shortly."
  • Use constant-time string comparison when checking credentials to prevent timing-based inference of valid accounts.
  • For WordPress and Drupal installations, disable the user listing API endpoint or restrict it to authenticated administrators only.
name: User Enumeration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team confirmed that the {application_name} application at {{TARGET_URL}} could be loaded inside an iframe on an attacker-controlled page. The application sent neither an X-Frame-Options response header nor a Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors directive, so browsers applied no restriction on cross-origin framing.

The team constructed a proof-of-concept page overlaying a transparent iframe of the {application_name} profile settings page at {url2} on top of a fake CAPTCHA prompt. The CAPTCHA image displayed the text hacker@example.com. Input events on the decoy page were captured by the underlying iframe. A user who completed the fake CAPTCHA — typing the displayed text and clicking Submit — would unknowingly update their account's registered email address to one the attacker controls. A subsequent password reset would then transfer account access to the attacker. The attack requires the victim to be logged into {application_name} at the time they visit the attacker's page.

# Impact

Clickjacking frames a target application inside an attacker-controlled page and uses visual deception to capture the victim's input on the target application's controls. The victim interacts with what appears to be the attacker's page; their clicks and keystrokes reach the underlying application. The attack requires no vulnerability in the application's logic — it relies on the browser's willingness to load the application in a cross-origin frame.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add a Content-Security-Policy response header with the frame-ancestors 'none' directive to all {application_name} pages. This prevents the application from being loaded in a frame by any origin.
  • If specific trusted origins must be permitted to frame the application, use frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted-origin.example.com rather than a wildcard.
  • Send the X-Frame-Options: DENY header as a fallback for browsers that do not support frame-ancestors.
  • Notify the account holder by email when their registered email address is changed, so they can detect and report unauthorized changes promptly.
name: User Interface (UI) Redress

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified GCP service accounts in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment configured with user-managed keys. User-managed keys can be downloaded as JSON credential files, are valid until explicitly revoked, and can be stored or transmitted by anyone with access to them. GCP-managed keys are never exposed outside the GCP control plane and rotate automatically every two weeks.

# Impact

A service account key that can be downloaded can leak through any channel: a public repository, a backup file, a developer's local workstation, or a misconfigured secrets manager. Once leaked it remains valid until an administrator revokes it. GCP cannot enforce how user-managed keys are stored, shared, or rotated, so the ability to assert that only the intended service holds the credential is lost the moment the key file is created.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace user-managed keys with GCP-managed keys for all service accounts where user-managed keys are not required by a specific technical constraint. GCP-managed keys cannot be downloaded and rotate automatically.
  • For any service account that must retain user-managed keys for a documented business reason, restrict key creation to the minimum number needed, log all uses through Cloud Audit Logs, and rotate keys on a defined schedule.
  • Audit existing user-managed keys to identify any that are unused or overdue for rotation and revoke them.
name: User-managed Service Account Keys

Description:
# Description

After obtaining a BitLocker recovery key through the {finding} finding and using it to gain local administrator access on {machine1} and {machine2}, the team disabled the endpoint detection and response (EDR) service on both hosts. Local administrator privileges are sufficient to stop or uninstall most EDR agents; no further privilege escalation was required.

With EDR disabled, the team could execute tools on both hosts that would otherwise generate detection events. An attacker who reaches local administrator access on a managed endpoint can reliably remove endpoint-based detection before proceeding with post-exploitation activity.

# Impact

An attacker with local administrator access on a managed endpoint can disable endpoint protection software. Most EDR products include tamper protection, but that protection is enforced through the same privilege level the attacker has already obtained. Removing EDR creates a window for tool execution and lateral movement that does not generate process-level or file-level alerts on the compromised host, extending the attacker's dwell time before detection.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Enable EDR tamper protection features that require communication with the vendor's cloud management plane — not just local administrator credentials — to stop or uninstall the agent.
  • Configure centralized monitoring to alert defensive teams when an EDR agent on any managed endpoint stops reporting. Treat a silent endpoint as a potential compromise indicator.
  • Restrict who can retrieve BitLocker recovery keys from Active Directory or Azure AD. Access to recovery keys should require documented justification and approval through a change management process.
name: Using BitLocker Recovery Keys

Description:
# Description

The assessment team exploited an unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability on the {application} API server, achieving unauthenticated remote code execution. The server processed OGNL expressions embedded in the Content-Type request header — a behavior corrected in Apache Struts releases following the original public disclosure. The team sent a crafted GET request with an OGNL payload in that header and received output from whoami && hostname confirming execution as the Tomcat service account.

From that position, an attacker can read application data, install persistent access mechanisms, pivot to systems on the same network, and exfiltrate any data the Tomcat account can reach on disk or over the network.

Variants

  • Apache: The assessment team identified web servers on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network running potentially vulnerable versions of Apache HTTP Server and Apache Tomcat, identified through error page banners. The applicable CVEs and their severity depend on the specific versions in use.
  • Apache Tomcat: The assessment team identified an Apache Tomcat instance at version {version} on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network. That version is affected by known vulnerabilities; the applicable CVEs depend on the specific patch level.
  • CVE-2025-0133: The assessment team found that {{COMPANY_NAME}} PAN-OS web applications were affected by CVE-2025-0133, a reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability in the GlobalProtect portal. The vendor advisory specifies the affected version range and available patches.
  • EternalBlue: The assessment team identified a host on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} internal network running Windows Server 2012 R2 Standard, which is vulnerable to MS17-010 (EternalBlue). This vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote code execution over SMB port 445.
  • Grafana: The assessment team found a Grafana instance at {domain} on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network running a version affected by CVE-2025-4123. The vendor advisory specifies the affected version range and remediation steps.
  • Jira: The assessment team found that Jira applications on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network allowed unauthenticated enumeration of valid usernames. These usernames can seed targeted credential attacks against accounts on the platform.
  • Nginx: The assessment team identified Nginx instances on {{COMPANY_NAME}} assets running versions affected by {cve_id} and additional known vulnerabilities. The relevant Nginx security advisories list affected version ranges and available patches.
  • OpenSSH: The assessment team found an internet-exposed host on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network running an outdated OpenSSH version with multiple known vulnerabilities. Exploitability in this environment depends on the specific enabled configuration and the CVEs applicable to the observed version.
  • OpenSSL: The assessment team found OpenSSL versions on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} infrastructure affected by known vulnerabilities. The applicable CVEs depend on the specific version; the OpenSSL security advisories list affected ranges and available fixes.
  • RouterOS: The assessment team identified a host at {ip_address} running a RouterOS version affected by CVE-2021-41987, a heap-based buffer overflow in the WPA2 handshake processing path. Successful exploitation requires network adjacency to the device.
  • Ubuntu: The assessment team found {number} websites hosted on a server running an end-of-life Ubuntu operating system version. The OS no longer receives security patches; all vulnerabilities disclosed after the end-of-life date are permanently unpatched on affected hosts.
  • WordPress Plugins: The assessment team found that {{TARGET_URL}} appeared to run outdated WordPress plugins with known vulnerabilities. The most serious was a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability in {plugin_name} version {version}.
  • jQuery: The assessment team identified a jQuery version on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} external network that contains known cross-site scripting vulnerabilities. These are exploitable when the application passes unsanitized input to jQuery's DOM manipulation methods.
# Impact

Vulnerable software is software whose installed version contains a security flaw with a published exploit or detailed technical description. The window between public disclosure and patching is the highest-risk period — attackers routinely scan for version banners and known-vulnerable paths, and the interval between identification and exploitation attempts is frequently hours rather than days.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Update {affected_technology} to its latest stable release, currently version {latest_version}. Apply the update to all instances, not only those identified during this assessment.
  • Establish a process for monitoring vendor security advisories for all software in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} environment. Apply patches for critical and high-severity vulnerabilities on an expedited timeline — within 30 days for critical, 60 days for high.
  • Maintain an accurate inventory of software versions across the environment to support rapid identification of affected systems when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.
name: Vulnerable Software

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified an NTP service on the {{COMPANY_NAME}} network configured to respond to Mode 6 diagnostic queries and monlist requests from any source. Using nmap with the ntp-monlist and ntp-info scripts against {{TARGET_HOST}}, the team confirmed the service returned recent client IP addresses in response to monlist queries without any access restriction.

An attacker can exploit this configuration to conduct a reflection amplification denial-of-service attack. A small spoofed monlist request — listing a victim IP as the source — causes the NTP server to send a response that can be more than 200 times the size of the request to the victim's address, consuming the victim's inbound bandwidth without the attacker generating proportionate traffic themselves.

# Impact

NTP amplification attacks use a publicly accessible, misconfigured NTP server as a traffic multiplier in a denial-of-service attack against a third party. The attacker sends small spoofed packets to the NTP server; the server replies with large payloads addressed to the victim. The {{COMPANY_NAME}} NTP server does not receive the attack traffic — it generates it, which can also degrade the network link shared by legitimate NTP clients and other services hosted on or near {{TARGET_HOST}}.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove the NTP service from public internet exposure if a publicly reachable NTP server is not required. If the service must remain accessible, restrict Mode 6 query responses to trusted source addresses only.
  • Disable the monlist feature by adding noquery to the restrict directives in the NTP configuration, or upgrade to NTPsec which removes monlist entirely.
  • Rate-limit NTP responses to reduce the amplification potential if the configuration change cannot be applied immediately.
name: Vulnerable Software Configuration

Description:
# Description

The assessment team discovered that 13 WCF services on {{TARGET_HOST}} had Metadata Exchange (MEX) endpoints enabled and reachable without authentication. The HTTP default page for each service displayed the svcutil.exe command needed to retrieve the service's full metadata. The team ran that command against all 13 services and generated a complete C# proxy class and client configuration file for each one.

The generated proxy code provided a precise inventory of every operation, parameter type, and data contract across the entire back end. The team used this information to construct the targeted test clients that demonstrated the {other_finding} finding.

# Impact

WCF MEX endpoints describe the service contract in enough detail for a client to generate compatible code without access to the server's source. Exposing them without authentication gives any caller an internal API specification — the full operation signatures, input and output types, and service addresses across all 13 services on the back end. This directly accelerates targeted attack construction.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable MEX endpoints on all WCF services that do not require them for production operation. Remove or comment out the <serviceMetadata httpGetEnabled="true"> element in each service's configuration.
  • If metadata publication is required for a specific integration, restrict access to the MEX endpoint by IP address or require client certificate authentication.
name: WCF Standard Endpoint Exposure

Description:
# Description

The assessment team reviewed the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS account password policy and found that it permitted passwords as short as {number} characters. The team confirmed this by successfully setting a user account password to a single character. The policy also permitted password reuse, allowing users to return to a previously exposed credential after a reset cycle.

Short minimum length requirements allow passwords that fall within the space targeted by online guessing attacks. Permitting reuse means a password reset cannot reliably invalidate a credential an attacker may already hold.

# Impact

Weak minimum length requirements allow passwords that a guessing attack can exhaust quickly, particularly against services without strict account lockout. Very short passwords also fall within seconds against offline cracking once a hash is obtained. Permitting reuse undermines the purpose of a forced rotation: an attacker who obtained the previous password retains access after the reset.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Set the AWS account password policy minimum length to 14 characters. Current NIST guidance treats length as the primary driver of password strength.
  • Prevent password reuse by configuring the password history restriction to at least 24 previous passwords.
  • Enforce MFA on all console users to add a second factor independent of password strength.
  • Avoid complexity requirements (mandatory uppercase, symbols, and so on) unless required by compliance or regulation; research shows they lead to predictable substitution patterns that reduce effective entropy.
name: Weak AWS Password Requirements

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {application_name} application delivered a Content-Security-Policy response header that included directives that undermined its cross-site scripting protections. The policy used unsafe-inline in script-src, which permits inline script execution — the primary XSS attack vector CSP is designed to prevent. Wildcard source values in content directives allowed any subdomain matching the pattern to serve trusted content. An attacker who can control content on any permitted origin can use it to execute script in the {application_name} application's context.

# Impact

A Content Security Policy restricts which sources can supply executable content to a page, limiting the damage from XSS vulnerabilities that do exist. unsafe-inline removes that restriction for inline scripts, restoring the full XSS attack surface the policy was intended to eliminate. Wildcard sources make the policy's effectiveness contingent on the security of every host the wildcard covers; any subdomain compromise under those wildcards can be used against the protected application.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Remove unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval from script-src, style-src, object-src, and default-src. Migrate inline scripts to external files or use nonce-based or hash-based allowlisting instead.
  • Replace wildcard source entries with explicit origins. Audit which domains the application legitimately loads content from and enumerate them individually.
  • Set any directive not actively used to 'none' to prevent unexpected content loading from unconfigured source types.
  • Do not host user-supplied content on origins listed in active content directives such as script-src.
name: Weak Content Security Policy

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a no-op encryption service — NoopInternalEncryptionService — in the {application_name} codebase. Both the encrypt and decrypt methods returned their input unchanged. The application selected this service when no encryption key was present in the instance configuration, and the configuration files in the source code repository did not include an encryption key. Any instance deployed directly from the repository would use the no-op service and store data as plaintext.

Production configuration files were not available for review. The ServerStartup.java file contained checks that blocked the equivalent no-op fallback for external encryption services, but those guards were absent for the internal encryption service path. The internal no-op service could be deployed to production without any configuration error or startup failure to signal the misconfiguration.

# Impact

The no-op service provides no confidentiality: it returns its input unchanged. Any application instance using it stores or transmits data that appears encrypted through the API surface but is in fact plaintext. An attacker who can read the storage layer or intercept traffic has direct access to that data without needing a key or performing any cryptographic operation. The silent fallback design means the misconfiguration produces no observable error that would alert an operator.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Add a startup check that prevents the application from starting if NoopInternalEncryptionService is selected and the environment is not explicitly designated as a development or test environment. Match the guard pattern already applied to the external encryption service path.
  • Remove NoopInternalEncryptionService from the codebase if it serves no current development purpose. Use a test-scoped real encryption configuration with a test key instead.
  • Require a non-empty encryption key in all deployment configurations. Fail the application startup if the key is absent or if the key length does not meet the minimum for the chosen algorithm.
name: Weak Cryptography

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found that the {{COMPANY_NAME}} application's authentication endpoint accepted passwords without regard to letter casing. Sending the same password with varying capitalization — submitting demotestacctsecops1 and then DeMoTeStAcCtSeCOps1 — both produced an HTTP 200 response and a valid session for the same account. Case insensitivity reduces the effective entropy of any mixed-case password by collapsing uppercase and lowercase into a single character set for the full credential space.

Source code was not available for review. The behavior is consistent with passwords being lowercased before hashing, a case-folding step applied during comparison, or storage in a database collation that treats character case as equivalent.

Variants

  • APT: The assessment team found that the {app_name} application accepted passwords as short as {number} characters. Passwords below a meaningful length threshold fall within the space targeted by online guessing attacks without the need for offline cracking infrastructure.
  • IPT: The assessment team, starting from a low-privileged user account in the {domain1} network, compromised all {{COMPANY_NAME}} domains through weak or reused passwords on domain user and service accounts. The specific accounts compromised and the technique used for each are described below.
# Impact

Effective password strength is a product of length and character space. Case insensitivity collapses uppercase and lowercase into a single set, cutting the character space and reducing the number of attempts required to cover it in a brute-force or dictionary attack. Combined with short minimum length or common password patterns, this makes targeted credential attacks materially faster to execute.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Confirm that passwords are stored as hashes produced by a password-specific hashing algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) and that the hash input preserves case exactly as the user supplied it. Do not normalize or fold case at any point in the storage or comparison path.
  • Require passwords to be at least 12 characters long. Length is the primary driver of practical brute-force resistance; enforce it without complexity requirements that lead to predictable substitution patterns.
  • Enforce MFA on all accounts to provide a second factor independent of password strength.
  • Encourage password manager use by accepting any printable characters and removing maximum length restrictions that prevent long, randomly generated passwords.
name: Weak Password Requirements

Description:
# Description

The assessment team identified a cache poisoning vulnerability in the {application_name} application. The X-Forwarded-Host request header influenced the Location value in redirect responses but was excluded from the cache key. A poisoned cache object persists until it expires and is served to every request that matches the same cache key — which, because X-Forwarded-Host was excluded, includes any user requesting the same URL without that header.

The team confirmed the attack by submitting a GET request to {{TARGET_URL}} with X-Forwarded-Host set to an attacker-controlled domain. The server responded with a 301 redirect to that domain, and the cache server stored it. A follow-up request without the X-Forwarded-Host header received the same poisoned redirect from cache. The team scoped all testing to a URL with the dedicated parameter bf_cache_poison to avoid affecting live users. An attacker repeating this process from multiple geographic locations can poison multiple cache nodes and extend the redirect to all users served by those nodes.

# Impact

Web cache poisoning stores a malicious server response in a shared cache so it is returned to subsequent users who request the same resource. The attacker's input causes the server to generate a response it would not otherwise produce; the cache then delivers that response to an arbitrary number of victims. The same mechanism that delivers a redirect here can also carry XSS payloads or other client-side attacks, with the cache amplifying the attacker's reach to all users served by the poisoned node.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Include the X-Forwarded-Host header in the cache key so that requests with different X-Forwarded-Host values produce separate cache entries rather than sharing one.
  • Validate the X-Forwarded-Host header against an allowlist of trusted originating domains before using it to construct redirect URLs. Reject requests where the value does not match.
  • Limit caching to purely static responses. Do not cache responses that depend on request headers supplied by the client.
name: Web Cache Poisoning

Description:
# Description

The assessment team found IAM policies in the {{COMPANY_NAME}} AWS environment that used wildcard values for both the Action and Resource fields. The {name} policy permitted iam:* on Resource: *, granting any principal holding the policy the ability to perform every IAM action on every resource in the account — creating users, modifying policies, assuming roles, and accessing credential reports.

Wildcard policies also expand silently: any IAM action AWS adds to a service namespace in the future is immediately permitted to all principals holding a wildcard policy for that namespace, without any review or approval step.

# Impact

A wildcard in an IAM Action field grants every current and future permission in that service namespace. Resource: * removes any ARN-level scoping. Together they give the attached principal more access than any specific function requires, and that access grows as AWS extends the service. When the wildcard covers a sensitive namespace like IAM, the principal can grant themselves or others access to anything in the account.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Replace wildcard Action values with the specific IAM actions each principal requires. Enumerate the minimum set needed and define them explicitly.
  • Replace Resource: * with specific ARNs where the service supports resource-level permissions. Scope each action to the resources the principal must reach.
  • Review all existing IAM policies for wildcard entries as part of a regular access review cycle. Use IAM Access Analyzer to identify overly permissive policies and generate least-privilege replacements based on actual access patterns.
name: Wildcard Specified in IAM Policy

Description:
# Description

The assessment team exploited an XML external entity injection vulnerability in the {application_name} application's file upload endpoint at {url}. The endpoint accepted .xlsx files and processed their embedded XML using a Java-based document parser with external entity resolution enabled. The team unpacked a legitimate .xlsx archive, replaced xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml with a malicious payload declaring an external DTD reference, and re-packaged the file.

When the application processed the file, the parser fetched the external DTD from the team's server at {server_url}. That DTD defined entities pointing to local file system paths. The parser resolved those entities and exfiltrated the contents of /etc/passwd via an out-of-band HTTP channel back to the team's server, confirming arbitrary local file read access without authentication.

# Impact

XXE injection exploits XML parsers that resolve external entity references — declarations in the document type definition that point the parser to an external resource and substitute its contents into the parsed document. An application that passes user-supplied XML to a parser with external entity resolution enabled exposes every file the application process can read on the server, and can be used as an HTTP client to probe internal services not reachable from the internet.

# Replication Steps
Recommendation:
• Disable DOCTYPE declarations and external entity processing in the XML parser used to handle .xlsx files. For Java SAX parsers, set the http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl feature to true. The OWASP XML External Entity Prevention Cheat Sheet documents the correct configuration for each major Java XML parser.
  • Update the document parsing library to its latest version. Many parser versions released in recent years disable external entity resolution by default; confirm the default configuration is applied and not overridden in application code.
  • Do not expose local file system paths in error responses. The parser's error output in this finding disclosed internal path structure; configure the parser to suppress detailed exceptions in production.
name: XML External Entity (XXE) Processing
